items.content: ICML 2027 Call For Papers The 44th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2027) will be held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, July 31-August 6 , as an in-person event. In addition to the main conference sessions, the conference will include tutorials, workshops and an expo. We invite submissions of papers on original and rigorous research of significant interest to the machine learning community for the main conference proceedings. All papers will be reviewed in a double-blind process and accepted papers will be presented at the conference. Papers must be prepared and submitted as a single file: 8 pages for the main paper, with unlimited pages for references, the impact statement, and appendices. There will be no separate deadline for the submission of supplementary material. The final versions of accepted papers will be allowed one extra page for the main paper. Note: ICML is planning to make some updates to the submission process (but not the submission format). We will announce them by late November, please stay tuned. Change in policy: two-stage reviewing process: ICML 2027 will review submissions in two stages. In the first stage, the area chair assigned to each paper decides whether it should proceed to the second stage. Papers that would clearly not be accepted receive a first-stage rejection. Every proposed first-stage reject must be confirmed by a senior area chair, and when in doubt, papers go to full review. Authors of papers that receive a first-stage rejection will be notified by February 23, 2027 with a short justification. All other papers go through the usual review process, and final decisions will be announced on May 3, 2027. This process is similar to the expedited initial review used by many top journals, where an editor or senior reviewer assesses whether a submission is sufficiently competitive to warrant a full round of external review. We recognize that any early-stage review process carries some risk that a good paper could be rejected prematurely. The requirement that every first-stage rejection be reviewed by both an AC and an SAC, together with the principle that papers should proceed to full review whenever there is doubt, is intended to minimize this risk. The goal of this process is to reduce the number of low-quality papers that go through full review. Change in policy: contribution type in submission/reviewing: ICML 2027 asks all authors to select the Contribution Type that best reflects the primary scientific contribution of their submission. The available types are General (most papers) , Theory , Application-driven , Concept and Feasibility , Negative Results , and Datasets, Evaluations and Benchmarks. Contribution types were introduced at NeurIPS 2026. They will be used to help guide reviewing and as one factor in reviewer and Area Chair matching. Authors should select the type that best represents the main contribution of the paper, recognizing that submissions may naturally contain elements of multiple types. Please see the full ICML 2027 Contribution Types Policy and Guidance for detailed descriptions and reviewing expectations. Change in policy: LLM use in Reviewing: ICML 2027 will use a single policy for LLM use in reviewing, corresponding to Policy B of ICML 2026. In short, reviewers may use privacy-compliant LLMs to help understand the paper and related works and to polish their reviews. Delegating judgement and critique of the paper to LLMs is not allowed, and reviewers remain fully responsible for the content of their reviews. A single policy simplifies reviewer assignment and activities permitted under policy B have broad support even among authors/reviewers that chose policy A at ICML 2026 (see the paper ). The findings from ICML 2026 also suggest that effect of policy B on paper outcomes is minimal. Details and precise guidance for the reviewers are given on the LLM policy page . Change in policy: Use of Generative AI by Authors & Disclosure Policy ICML 2027 requires authors to disclose substantive use of generative AI tools in conducting the research or preparing the submission. This includes uses such as research ideation, mathematical reasoning, experimental design, code generation, data analysis, literature synthesis, and substantial manuscript drafting. Routine editorial assistance, such as spelling, grammar, formatting, and minor clarity edits, does not require disclosure. All submissions must include an AI Disclosure Statement. The statement does not count toward the paper page limit. Authors remain fully responsible for the correctness, originality, and integrity of all submitted content, including any material produced with AI assistance. When generative AI is part of the research methodology itself, its use must also be described in the paper with sufficient detail to understand and reproduce the work. Please see the full ICML 2027 Policy on the Use of Generative AI by Authors for requirements, examples, and guidance. Change in policy: Submission caps and reciprocal reviewing policy. Similar to ICLR 2027, ICML 2027 introduces submission quotas and strengthens reciprocal reviewing to cope with the growth in submissions. No author may appear on more than 20 submissions. Each submission must designate one of its authors as reciprocal reviewer, and an author can be designated as the reciprocal reviewer for at most 6 submissions. Each author may appear on at most one submission in which no author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer. Authors with 3 or more submissions must also serve on the program committee, as a reviewer, area chair or senior area chair. This also means that since serving on the program committee in any role requires meeting the reciprocal reviewer eligibility criteria, an author who does not meet them may appear on at most 2 submissions. Submissions that do not meet these requirements will be desk rejected. Eligibility criteria and further details are given in the guide on Submission Quotas and Reciprocal Reviewing . Please review Author Instructions , an Example Paper , and use the correct Style Files . Submitted papers that do not conform to these policies will be rejected without review. Topics of interest include (but are not limited to): general machine learning (active learning, clustering, online learning, ranking, supervised, semi- and self-supervised learning, time series analysis, etc.) deep learning (architectures, generative models, theory, etc.) evaluation (methodology, meta studies, replicability and validity, human-in-the-loop, etc.) theory of machine learning (statistical learning theory, bandits, game theory, decision theory, etc.) machine learning systems (improved implementation and scalability, hardware, libraries, distributed methods, etc.) optimization (convex and non-convex optimization, matrix/tensor methods, stochastic, online, non-smooth, composite, etc.) probabilistic methods (Bayesian methods, graphical models, Monte Carlo methods, etc.) reinforcement learning (decision and control, planning, hierarchical RL, robotics, etc.) trustworthy machine learning (reliability, causality, fairness, interpretability, privacy, robustness, safety, etc.) application-driven machine learning (innovative techniques, problems, and datasets that are of interest to the machine learning community and driven by the needs of end-users in applications such as healthcare, physical sciences, biosciences, social sciences, sustainability, and climate etc.) Similar to last year, we also invite submissions of position papers (call for paper is coming soon). Submissions will be handled separately from the main track submissions. Papers published at ICML are indexed in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research through the Journal of Machine Learning Research. In addition to the main conference sessions, the conference will include tutorials, workshops and an expo. We invite submissions of papers on original and rigorous research of significant interest to the machine learning community for the main conference proceedings. All papers will be reviewed in a double-blind process and accepted papers will be presented at the conference. Papers must be prepared and submitted as a single file: 8 pages for the main paper, with unlimited pages for references, the impact statement, and appendices. There will be no separate deadline for the submission of supplementary material. The final versions of accepted papers will be allowed one extra page for the main paper. Change in policy: two-stage reviewing process: ICML 2027 will review submissions in two stages. In the first stage, the area chair assigned to each paper decides whether it should proceed to the second stage. Papers that would clearly not be accepted receive a first-stage rejection. Every proposed first-stage reject must be confirmed by a senior area chair, and when in doubt, papers go to full review. Authors of papers that receive a first-stage rejection will be notified by February 23, 2027 with a short justification. All other papers go through the usual review process, and final decisions will be announced on May 3, 2027. This process is similar to the expedited initial review used by many top journals, where an editor or senior reviewer assesses whether a submission is sufficiently competitive to warrant a full round of external review. We recognize that any early-stage review process carries some risk that a good paper could be rejected prematurely. The requirement that every first-stage rejection be reviewed by both an AC and an SAC, together with the principle that papers should proceed to full review whenever there is doubt, is intended to minimize this risk. The goal of this process is to reduce the number of low-quality papers that go through full review. Change in policy: contribution type in submission/reviewing: ICML 2027 asks all authors to select the Contribution Type that best reflects the primary scientific contribution of their submission. The available types are General (most papers) , Theory , Application-driven , Concept and Feasibility , Negative Results , and Datasets, Evaluations and Benchmarks. Contribution types were introduced at NeurIPS 2026. They will be used to help guide reviewing and as one factor in reviewer and Area Chair matching. Authors should select the type that best represents the main contribution of the paper, recognizing that submissions may naturally contain elements of multiple types. Please see the full ICML 2027 Contribution Types Policy and Guidance for detailed descriptions and reviewing expectations. In short, reviewers may use privacy-compliant LLMs to help understand the paper and related works and to polish their reviews. Delegating judgement and critique of the paper to LLMs is not allowed, and reviewers remain fully responsible for the content of their reviews. A single policy simplifies reviewer assignment and activities permitted under policy B have broad support even among authors/reviewers that chose policy A at ICML 2026 (see the paper ). The findings from ICML 2026 also suggest that effect of policy B on paper outcomes is minimal. Details and precise guidance for the reviewers are given on the LLM policy page . items.content: Submission quotas and reciprocal reviewing The number of submissions to ICML keeps growing faster than the number of qualified reviewers. To keep the review process fair and informative for all authors, ICML 2027 introduces submission quotas and strengthens its reciprocal reviewing requirement. These rules are similar to those adopted by ICLR 2027. Submission quotas No author may appear as a co-author on more than 20 submissions. Each author may appear as a co-author on at most one submission in which no author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer (see below). In plain terms: if neither you nor any of your co-authors has published at one of the venues listed below, you may submit at most one paper to ICML 2027. We welcome submissions from researchers who are new to the field, and these submissions are reviewed like all others. Quotas are checked when abstracts are registered. Authors who exceed a quota will be notified and can fix the problem before the full paper deadline (January 22, 2027). If a quota is still exceeded at the full paper deadline, the program chairs will desk reject excess submissions at random until every author is within the quotas. Who is an eligible reciprocal reviewer An author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer if they have at least one paper accepted at one of the following venues by the abstract registration deadline (January 14, 2027): ICML, NeurIPS, ICLR, UAI, AISTATS, JMLR, TMLR (including Datasets and Benchmarks tracks), ACL, EMNLP, EACL, NAACL, IJCNLP-AACL, Computational Linguistics, TACL (including Findings), COLM CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, TPAMI, AAAI, IJCAI, JAIR, 3DV ICRA, IROS, RSS, CoRL KDD COLT Other publications associated with these venues do not count. This includes workshop papers, position papers, short papers, system demonstrations, industry papers and blog posts. Eligibility is determined from OpenReview profiles, so all authors must keep their profiles complete and up to date, including their publications or DBLP link. Incorrect profile information may lead to desk rejection. Reciprocal reviewing requirement Per-submission requirement: each submission must designate one of its authors as its reciprocal reviewer when the abstract is registered. The designated author must: be an eligible reciprocal reviewer; register as a reviewer for ICML 2027; complete their assigned reviews during the reviewing period (February 24–March 16, 2027). An author can be designated as the reciprocal reviewer for at most 6 submissions. Submissions in which no author is eligible are exempt from this requirement, but they count toward the one-submission quota above. Per-author requirement: authors with 3 or more submissions must serve on the program committee of ICML 2027, as a reviewer, area chair or senior area chair. Authors who serve as area chairs, senior area chairs or members of the organizing committee meet this requirement through that role. This also means that since serving on the program committee in any role requires meeting the reciprocal reviewer eligibility criteria, an author who does not meet them may appear on at most 2 submissions. Responsibilities and enforcement Reciprocal reviewers have the same obligations as all other reviewers. They must follow the reviewing guidelines and the LLM policy, submit their reviews on time, and take part in the discussion with authors and area chairs. The program chairs may desk reject the submissions for which an author is the designated reciprocal reviewer if that author: does not submit their reviews; submits reviews of very low quality;. Submissions that do not designate an eligible reciprocal reviewer when one is available among their authors may also be desk rejected.

items.title: Commission hosts Apply AI Summit to boost Europe’s AI innovation and uptake
items.summary: Nearly 1,000 high-level policymakers, start-ups, industry leaders and researchers will take part in the Apply AI Summit in Brussels tomorrow. They will discuss how artificial intelligence (AI) can boost Europe’s competitiveness across 10 strategic sectors and the public sector. The summit will also showcase concrete AI applications, European success stories and innovative projects. They will discuss how artificial intelligence (AI) can boost Europe’s competitiveness across 10 strategic sectors and the public sector. The summit will also showcase concrete AI applications, European success stories and innovative projects. Henna Virkkunen , Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, will host the summit and present the first Apply AI Startup Award to three European start-ups. The award recognises innovative European startups and scaleups developing AI solutions in the strategic sectors. Alongside the in-person event, an online conference platform will run from 16 to 20 November, allowing additional 2,500 participants to join part of the summit. The Apply AI Summit marks one year since the adoption of the Apply AI Strategy , which sets out how to speed up the use of AI in Europe’s key industries and the public sector. It concludes the first European AI Innovation Month , running from 14 October to 17 November 2026, organised by the European Commission in partnership with the Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union. items.content: The European Commission’s AI Office is launching a call for expression of interest for European AI providers to present AI solutions to the network of European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs). GettyImages © ipopba The objective is to facilitate the deployment of European AI solutions among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across Europe. Through this initiative, EDIHs will act as trusted intermediaries between AI providers and SME users, helping identify suitable solutions and supporting their uptake by businesses. As set out in the Apply AI Strategy, this call aims to help bridge AI supply and AI demand. The network of EDIHs, repositioned as Experience Centres for AI, supports organisations in their digital transformation journey by offering services such as test-before-invest opportunities, training and skills, networking and ecosystem support, and support to access finance. European AI providers whose solutions are mature and ready for deployment in SMEs are invited to participate by completing the survey below. The first edition of this call is open to up to 100 AI providers. About this Call for Expression of Interest The purpose of this call for expression of interest is to identify European AI solutions that address the concrete needs of SMEs, including in specific sectors where EDIHs already support large numbers of businesses. The selected solutions will form the basis of a catalogue to be hosted on the AI-on-Demand Platform. The AI-on-Demand Platform is a European platform developed through the EU funded programmes for discovering, developing and deploying artificial intelligence. The solutions will be included in the Business Navigator, and they will be identified in a dedicated catalogue as “EDIH Ready”. This catalogue will serve as a practical resource for EDIHs when identifying suitable European AI solutions for the SMEs they support. To ensure that the catalogue remains a reliable resource for the EDIH network, the Commission reserves the right to remove solutions that are no longer considered suitable for deployment in SMEs. The catalogue may also serve as a basis for possible follow-up activities by the European Commission, the Digital Transformation Accelerator, the EDIH network, and other relevant initiatives. Who can apply This call is open to European AI providers that offer a mature AI solution which is ready to be deployed in SMEs. Solutions should be relevant to SME needs and suitable for practical deployment with the support of EDIHs. How to apply To participate in this call for expression of interest, applicants should: Check the FAQs to confirm that their solution is suitable for this call. Complete the EU survey in English. Ensure that the submission is complete and submitted in the required form. Only expressions of interest submitted in English, using the correct form and duly completed, will be considered. If your AI solution is suitable for this call, please complete this EU survey . For enquiries, please contact CNECT-DIH@ec.europa.eu Deadline Expressions of interest must be submitted by 17 December 2026, 17.00 CET. The call may close earlier if 100 suitable AI solutions have been submitted before the deadline FAQ Questions and answers of broad interest and other important notices will be published at regular intervals. Please consult this website regularly to be informed of any updates and of the questions and answers published. Why should I participate in this Call for Expression of Interest? This call for expression of interest offers European AI providers the opportunity to increase the visibility of their solutions through the European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs), particularly towards small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). A dedicated catalogue of AI providers is foreseen on the AI on Demand Platform. This catalogue is intended to help EDIHs quickly identify suitable AI solutions for the SMEs they support. Altogether, EDIHs have already delivered services to more than 50,000 organisations across Europe. In addition, further engagement formats are planned, such as information sessions, matchmaking events, webinars and use case demonstrations involving the most relevant participating AI solution providers. My AI solution is still under development and not yet ready to be deployed. Can I still participate in this Call for Expression of Interest? This Call for Expression of Interest is explicitly aimed at AI providers whose solutions are ready to be deployed by SMEs. Proofs of concept, purely research-based projects, minimum viable products, or other solutions that have not yet reached market readiness are not suitable for this call. What is meant by a “European” AI solution in the context of this Call for Expression of Interest? For the purposes of this call, eligibility is determined by the location of the provider’s headquarters. The following countries are eligible: EU Member States (27): Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain and Sweden Other eligible countries (countries associated to the Digital Europe Programme): Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, Türkiye, Ukraine and Kosovo. What are the European Digital Innovation Hubs? European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs) are one-stop shops that help companies — especially SMEs — and public sector organisations adopt advanced digital technologies and improve their competitiveness. They provide access to technical expertise, provide “test before invest” services, training and skills, networking and ecosystem support, and support to access finance. Operating through a Europe-wide network, EDIHs combine local and regional support with access to specialist expertise and best practices across Member States. What is the AI on Demand Platform? The AI on Demand Platform (AIoD) is a European platform for discovering, developing and deploying artificial intelligence. It brings together AI tools, datasets, services, computing resources and expertise from across Europe, connecting researchers, businesses, public organisations and technology providers. For AI providers that meet the criteria of this call for expression of interest, a dedicated catalogue of “EDIH Ready” AI solutions will be created on the platform. What is the timeline and what are the next steps? The call for expression of interest will close on 17 December at 17.00 CET. If more than 100 suitable solutions are submitted before that date, the call may close earlier. Information on suitable candidates will then be shared with DeployAI, the EU-funded consortium behind the AI on Demand Platform, which will contact the selected candidates regarding onboarding to the platform. This is expected to take place in the second half of January. Once onboarding to the AI on Demand Platform has been completed, selected providers will appear as “EDIH Ready” in the Business Navigator, and their AI solutions will be featured in a dedicated catalogue on the marketplace. Following this, dedicated information sessions with EDIHs are planned for the first quarter of 2027. Additional workshops focusing on specific AI solutions may also be organised. Will there be more similar Calls for Expression of Interest in the future? At present, there are no concrete plans for a further call for expression of interest. However, depending on the success of this pilot, similar calls may be launched in the future. More broadly, the Commission is exploring different ways to strengthen the link between AI supply and demand through the EDIHs, including options for a more structured and continuous approach. items.content: Featured projects PyTorch Foundation Ambassadors bring people together to learn, share technical knowledge and contribute to PyTorch Foundation projects and the wider open-source AI ecosystem. In this November roundup, we highlight some of our ambassadors’ activities, including local meetups, university sessions, technical articles and practical learning resources. PyTorch Community Meetup in Kampala On September 19, Pacifique Mugisho organized an in-person PyTorch East Africa community meetup at Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda, in collaboration with the IndabaX Makerere Student Chapter and the IEEE Computer Society Makerere Student Branch. The event received 103 registrations and welcomed 32 attendees . Talks explored retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), external knowledge integration and advanced retrieval techniques. Pacifique also led a practical workshop covering embeddings, semantic search and how these components can be combined in PyTorch-based applications. An interactive quiz gave participants another way to engage with the material. Following the event, the community gained 20 WhatsApp members and four LinkedIn members. The gathering also laid the groundwork for further in-person meetups. Technical talks and hands-on learning at the PyTorch East Africa community meetup at Makerere University, Kampala. Hands-on PyTorch on TPUs in Dhaka On October 30, Zaynul Abedin Miah delivered a technical talk and live demonstration, “PyTorch on TPU with TorchTPU,” at a community meetup in Dhaka, Bangladesh. The session showed students and early-career developers how to run native PyTorch on Google TPUs using free Colab notebooks. It covered device setup, tensor operations and torch.compile , with an interactive “predict, then run” exercise. The event received 91 registrations , and all 50 approved seats were filled . Participants travelled from several cities, with some journeys exceeding 330 kilometres. Slides and a runnable notebook were shared with all registrants so they could continue experimenting afterward. View the event . Colab: Link Attendees and a live demonstration at the PyTorch on TPUs community session in Dhaka. Efficient LLM Inference with PyTorch Community Nepal On November 1, Arun Bhandari organized and hosted PyTorch Community Nepal’s first online technical session, “Accelerating LLM Inference with Speculative Decoding at the Edge.” Guest speaker Manjil Nepal , a Research Associate at the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore, discussed speculative decoding in edge–server environments and approaches to improving draft models through local and federated learning. Arun coordinated the speaker, registration, promotion, moderation and audience discussion. The session attracted 86 registrations and 20 attendees , with presentation slides and source code shared afterward. The event created an opportunity for researchers and Nepal’s AI and machine learning community to exchange knowledge and connect through a technical discussion. PyTorch Community Nepal’s online session on efficient LLM inference. AI Research with PyTorch in Nigeria During September, Abdulsalam Yazid Bande delivered two introductory sessions for academic audiences in Nigeria, reaching 75 attendees . “From Research Question to PyTorch Experiment” introduced 35 graduate and postgraduate students to modern AI, neural networks, generative AI and PyTorch’s role in research. A second session, “Getting Started with AI Research Using PyTorch,” welcomed 40 faculty members for a practical introduction to experimentation, model development and machine learning applications in academic research. Together, the sessions helped students and faculty explore how PyTorch could support their own research questions. Introducing AI research with PyTorch to academic audiences in Nigeria. LLM Application Development at Vilnius Tech In September, Eyup Cinar visited Vilnius Tech University in Lithuania to deliver a guest lecture on rapid application development with large language models. Approximately 30 undergraduate and graduate students attended. The session introduced the PyTorch ecosystem and its role in developing, training and deploying LLM-based applications, while providing an opportunity for academic exchange between institutions. A guest lecture on LLM application development at Vilnius Tech. Getting Started with Open Source at Duke University On September 4, Sahdev Zala presented to more than 25 students in Duke University’s AI Engineering master’s program in Durham, North Carolina. The session helped students understand how to get started contributing to PyTorch and Kubernetes. Participants joined both in person and online to explore opportunities to contribute to open-source projects. Exploring open-source contributions with Duke University students. LLM Post-Training at DevFest Kuala Lumpur On November 14, Vensen Mu , PyTorch Foundation Ambassador and RL-Kernel maintainer, delivered “Practical Train–Inference Consistency in LLM RL Post-Training” at Google DevFest Kuala Lumpur 2026. The talk explored numerical discrepancies between training and inference systems in reinforcement learning for large language models. Vensen shared how the open-source RL-Kernel project works toward bitwise consistency across training and rollout workflows, including engineering considerations relevant to PyTorch and vLLM. The session encouraged developers interested in AI infrastructure and reliable RL post-training to explore the problem and collaborate through open source. Read the event announcement and explore RL-Kernel . Sharing PyTorch Updates in Simplified Chinese Zhiqing Xiao published a Simplified Chinese WeChat article introducing PyTorch 2.14. The article received more than 300 views , helping Chinese-speaking readers learn about the release. Read the article in Simplified Chinese . Transfer Learning: Articles, Code and Community Talks Sahdev Zala published an IBM Developer article based on a transfer-learning demonstration using PyTorch and Torchvision’s pretrained ResNet-18 model. He also made the accompanying source code publicly available, giving readers an example to explore and build on. Read the transfer-learning article and explore the accompanying code . Thank You to Our Ambassadors Thank you to our ambassadors for sharing your knowledge, creating learning opportunities and bringing people together around PyTorch.

items.content: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. How PDD Kit works PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab) . Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust. For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements: You only get a token with the right password. Only admin accounts get admin tokens. We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job. Step 1: Questions before code PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. Figure 2. The first decision card. “Only with the right password” on its own is also met by a login that refuses everyone. Proving both ways rules that out. The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways. Step 2: A human readable intent map As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3). Figure 3. PDD Kit’s mental model for login. The field you send picks the window, the window picks the table and with it the role, and nothing prints until the password matches. Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent. Figure 4. An intent map entry after the decision: a login gets a token only with the right password for that account, and always with it. The flowchart shows every way the password check can end. The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token. Figure 5. Two readings of the same sentence. They differ in one cell, and that cell changes what the proof has to establish. Step 3: Proving the login function Before anything gets built, PDD Kit asks the team to sign off on the plan as a whole. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6). Figure 6. Proving more of login means trusting more small wrappers. The card says so before the developer chooses. That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow , carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. PDD Kit then brought the revised plan back for a fresh sign-off, because matching your intent isn’t proof, and it doesn’t approve new trust or a wider scope. Step 4: Where proof stops There are plenty of things you can’t prove about a program, and login runs into most of them: Code the verifier can’t see. bcrypt’s hashing, sqlx’s queries and jsonwebtoken’s signing live in other crates, outside the proof. Facts about the outside world. What SQLite holds right now and what time the clock says are inputs to the program, not something its code can establish. Whether, and how fast, something finishes. The spec says what you get if login answers. A hung query, or a slow one, breaks nothing in it. Anything a person has to judge , like whether an error message helps or a screen makes sense. Whatever nobody wrote down. A proof covers its spec and says nothing about requirements outside it. That’s where empirical verification comes in. PDD Kit spells out the trusted boundary, the part of the TCB this proof leans on. For login, the developer signed off on six pieces: The two lookups, Customer::find_by_email and Admin::find_by_username . Each awaited, successful lookup returns exactly the row its own table holds for that email or username, or none. check_password , a thin wrapper around bcrypt::verify . Figure 7. Where the login proof stops. Verus proves the core for every input. People accept the trusted ring and tests check it. The plan lists what nobody is promising. Figure 8 maps what gets proved and what gets trusted. Each trust decision is its own card. It shows the clauses Verus will take on faith, what the developer is accepting, and which promise falls apart if the assumption is wrong (Figure 9). Every assumed clause then gets an empirical check in the plan’s Empirical verification section, written as Given/When/Then scenarios before any test exists (Figure 10). An entry says planned until it has run, and then it records the command’s result and the commit it ran against. Figure 8. What gets proved and what gets trusted in login. Green functions are proved by Verus for every input. Amber pieces are trusted, accepted by the developer, and checked by the planned tests in the plan’s §4.1. Figure 9. A trust card for check_password . Verus takes these two clauses on faith, so a person accepts them and two tests check them. Figure 10. A planned test for the trusted check_password , written before the test exists. The plan labels a passing test as evidence rather than proof. You might be wondering whether someone now has to read the proof instead of the code. Nobody does, because the coding agent writes the proof and Verus checks every step of it. If Verus accepts the proof, it holds whether or not anyone reads it. The spec is what the proof is held to, so that’s what people review, and this one is short enough to learn to read in a few minutes. Each function gets an ensures block: statements about its result, r, that must hold for every possible input. Verus checks them when you build, and if any clause could fail for even one input, the build fails and Verus points at that clause. Each clause reads as an if-then, and Figure 11 takes apart the clause for the developer’s first requirement. Figure 11. The ensures clause on login_flow for “You only get a token with the right password.” The same account a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. Notice that the same a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. (r matches Ok(t) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == admin_role()) ==> (email is None && username matches Some(u) && admin_on_file(u@) is Some), // An email login's token always carries the customer role. Every login ends in one of a handful of places, and only one of them has a token (Figure 13). The proof covers all of them at once. Figure 13. Every way a login can end, from the plan. login_flow is async: it awaits a database query. Verus can put contracts on async functions, with one rule worth knowing (Figure 14). requires is checked when the call creates the future. ensures describes the value you get when you await it. Nothing promises the future finishes, so a hung query breaks no clause. The doc comment on login_flow says so in as many words: /// ... In the spec, a lookup keeps its code where it is and gets a contract from the outside with external_fn_specification : /// Looks up a customer by exact email. /// Trusted, not proved: the SQL query runs in sqlx, which Verus cannot check. /// Every customer promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_fn_specification] pub async fn ex_customer_find_by_email(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, email: &str) -> (r: Result , sqlx::Error>) ensures // When the query succeeds, it returns the customers row on // file for exactly this email, or None when there is none. r matches Ok(found) ==> found == customer_on_file(email@), { Customer::find_by_email(pool, email).await } The clock is a small wrapper marked #[verifier::external_body] . Verus uses its ensures clause and never reads the body: /// Reads the clock and computes a token's expiry 24 hours ahead. /// Trusted, not proved: chrono's clock is outside the proof. /// It panics if the time is out of range, as today's login does; /// that panic is not promised against. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn expiry_from_now() -> (r: Expiry) ensures // The expiry is exactly 24 hours (86,400 seconds) after the clock reading. r.exp as int == r.now as int + 86_400, { ... } Figure 7 puts the three layers together: what Verus proves, what people accept and tests check, and what nobody is promising. Figure 7. Where the login proof stops. Verus proves the core for every input. People accept the trusted ring and tests check it. The plan lists what nobody is promising. Figure 8 maps what gets proved and what gets trusted. Each trust decision is its own card. It shows the clauses Verus will take on faith, what the developer is accepting, and which promise falls apart if the assumption is wrong (Figure 9). Every assumed clause then gets an empirical check in the plan’s Empirical verification section, written as Given/When/Then scenarios before any test exists (Figure 10). An entry says planned until it has run, and then it records the command’s result and the commit it ran against. Figure 8. What gets proved and what gets trusted in login. Green functions are proved by Verus for every input. Amber pieces are trusted, accepted by the developer, and checked by the planned tests in the plan’s §4.1. Figure 9. A trust card for check_password . Verus takes these two clauses on faith, so a person accepts them and two tests check them. Figure 10. A planned test for the trusted check_password , written before the test exists. The plan labels a passing test as evidence rather than proof. The plan is just as explicit about what nobody is promising: that the login future ever completes, that an out-of-range clock won’t panic, anything about the timing or rate of attempts, and how other endpoints read the role. Step 5: Reading the spec The intent artifact is what the team reviews. It’s the plain-language version of the formal spec PDD Kit writes as Verus contracts. You might be wondering whether someone now has to read the proof instead of the code. Nobody does, because the coding agent writes the proof and Verus checks every step of it. If Verus accepts the proof, it holds whether or not anyone reads it. The spec is what the proof is held to, so that’s what people review, and this one is short enough to learn to read in a few minutes. Each function gets an ensures block: statements about its result, r, that must hold for every possible input. Verus checks them when you build, and if any clause could fail for even one input, the build fails and Verus points at that clause. Each clause reads as an if-then, and Figure 11 takes apart the clause for the developer’s first requirement. Figure 11. The ensures clause on login_flow for “You only get a token with the right password.” The same account a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. Notice that the same a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. For example, imagine a bug where login checks the password against one account but signs the token for another. Bob logs in with his own, correct password and gets back a token for Alice’s account. Each step looks fine on its own, but this clause catches it, because the password check and the token have to name the same account. That’s the kind of wiring bug a test suite rarely thinks to look for. The spec also has to talk about SQLite, bcrypt and JWTs without running any of them. It does that with uninterpreted functions , names with no body: customer_on_file(email) and admin_on_file(username) for the rows the database holds, bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) for what bcrypt would say, and token_claims(token, secret) for what a token carries. Verus knows nothing about them except what the trusted contracts from Step 4 promise. The proof says “whatever the database holds, login does the right thing with it,” and a trusted contract says “the lookup returns what the database holds.” /// The customers row the database holds for /// exactly this email, if any, when login looks. /// Left abstract: only `Customer::find_by_email`'s /// trusted contract says what it is. pub uninterp spec fn customer_on_file(email: Seq ) -> Option ; ... /// What bcrypt says about `password` against a /// stored `hash`: Some(true) when it is the password /// the hash was made from, Some(false) when it is /// not, None when bcrypt cannot read the hash. /// Left abstract: its meaning is bcrypt's, taken on trust through `check_password`. pub uninterp spec fn bcrypt_verdict(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> Option ; /// The password is the right one for the stored hash, by bcrypt's verdict. pub open spec fn password_matches(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> bool { bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) == Some(true) } On top of those, named_account(email, username) says which account a login names: the customers row for the email when one is sent, otherwise the admins row for the username, otherwise none. It’s written like Rust, but it’s a mathematical definition that never runs and only appears in contracts. Code like this is called ghost code , since the verifier checks it but the compiler erases it from the program. With it, the developer’s two-sentence request ends up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow (Figure 12). /// The account a login names: the customers row for /// the email when one is sent (role "customer"), /// otherwise the admins row for the username (role "admin"), otherwise none. pub open spec fn named_account(email: Option , username: Option ) -> Option { match email { Some(e) => match customer_on_file(e@) { Some(c) => Some(NamedAccount { id: c.id@, password_hash: c.password_hash@, role: customer_role() }), None => None, }, None => match username { Some(u) => match admin_on_file(u@) { Some(a) => Some(NamedAccount { id: a.id@, password_hash: a.password_hash@, role: admin_role() }), None => None, }, None => None, }, } } Figure 12. The two-sentence request and the Both ways decision ended up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow. Four of them keep today’s refusals, so the storefront and the existing API tests keep working. Here’s the whole contract, with its doc comment trimmed. Each clause has the plain-English comment above it that the intent artifact shows the team: /// The whole login, awaited end to end: from the /// request's fields to the token or the HTTP error. /// ... pub async fn login_flow(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, config: &Config, email: Option , username: Option , password: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // Neither an email nor a username: 400 with today's message. email is None && username is None ==> (r matches Err(AppError::BadRequest(m)) && m@ == missing_identity_text()), // A token only for the account the login names, with its right // password; it carries that account's id and its table's role. r matches Ok(t) ==> (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.sub@ == a.id && c.role@ == a.role), // The right password for the named account always gets a // token, unless a lookup or signing failure gives 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash)) ==> (r is Ok || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A login naming an account nobody holds gets // 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. ((email is Some || username is Some) && named_account(email, username) is None) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A wrong password for an account whose hash bcrypt // can read gets 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) == Some(false)) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // An account whose stored hash bcrypt cannot read gets 500 and no token. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) is None) ==> r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_)), // The admin role only for an admins row // found by username, with no email sent. (r matches Ok(t) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == admin_role()) ==> (email is None && username matches Some(u) && admin_on_file(u@) is Some), // An email login's token always carries the customer role. (r matches Ok(t) && email is Some) ==> (token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == customer_role()), { unimplemented!() } The trusted boundary shows up in the code too. check_password is one of the functions whose body Verus doesn’t check. Its contract ties it to bcrypt_verdict , an uninterpreted model of bcrypt with no axioms: /// Asks bcrypt whether `password` matches the stored `hash`. /// Trusted, not proved: Verus cannot check bcrypt's hashing, /// so this wrapper's contract is assumed. /// Every password promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn check_password(password: &str, hash: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // bcrypt answers (Ok) exactly when it can read the stored hash. r is Ok <==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) is Some, // Its answer is its verdict: true for the // right password, false for any other. r matches Ok(b) ==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) == Some(b), { bcrypt::verify(password, hash).map_err(|e| e.to_string()) } The doc comment above it says what rests on it: every password promise of login_flow . Every login ends in one of a handful of places, and only one of them has a token (Figure 13). The proof covers all of them at once. Figure 13. Every way a login can end, from the plan. login_flow is async: it awaits a database query. Verus can put contracts on async functions, with one rule worth knowing (Figure 14). requires is checked when the call creates the future. ensures describes the value you get when you await it. Nothing promises the future finishes, so a hung query breaks no clause. The doc comment on login_flow says so in as many words: /// ... items.content: Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU Mehmet Altan Toksöz, PhD Affiliation: Independent researcher, Gölbaşı, Ankara, Türkiye Email: matoksoz@gmail.com Abstract Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters through OpenVINO. On held-out variants scored by deterministic checkers, the pass rate rises from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA) and 37/66 (QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B (QLoRA). Reading all 159 failing programs shows that the adapters remove most errors of convention, such as the sign of a lag, units and array shapes, but few errors in building signals and noise. Applied at run time, the adapter costs 17–19% of the generation speed. † † subheader: November 17, 2026 1 Introduction Signal-processing engineers write much of their code in MATLAB: they synthesise pulses and chirps, correlate channels, filter, take fast Fourier transforms (FFTs) and set detection thresholds. Language models can draft such code, and small models that run on a laptop can do so without sending anything off the machine, which matters where the work cannot leave it. The Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B Gemma Team (2026) are made for this kind of device. On our tasks, however, they often get the conventions of the field wrong: they read the delay with the wrong sign from xcorr , forget the gain N N of an unscaled FFT, write a chirp rate in the wrong unit or mix row and column vectors. Such code runs and prints a plausible number, which makes the errors hard to notice. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) Hu et al. (2022) and its quantized variant QLoRA Dettmers et al. (2023) make supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of such models possible with little memory. We ask how much a small set of checked examples, trained on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of the same laptop, improves the code these models write, and which errors it removes. Answering this needs three things. First, tasks whose answers can be checked automatically. Following the practice of judging generated code by running it Chen et al. (2021) , we wrote 11 parametric subtasks from signal-processing work, run every answer in an emulator of a MATLAB subset, and score it with checkers that also reject values copied from the prompt or computed from a formula instead of measured. Earlier work compared commercial and open models on generating MATLAB code for automated-driving scenarios Yang et al. (2025) ; here the models are small enough to run on a laptop and the domain is digital signal processing (DSP). Second, training data. Instead of collecting the model’s own correct answers, which were too rare, we let the small model write the reasoning for an expert’s solution and then the answer itself, close to the rationalization step of the Self-Taught Reasoner (STaR) Zelikman et al. (2022) , and kept only answers that pass the checkers. Third, a way to train and deploy on a laptop: the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) library Mangrulkar et al. (2022) on the integrated GPU for training, and OpenVINO GenAI OpenVINO toolkit (2026) with 8-bit integer (int8) weights for inference. Our contributions are: • 11 parametric MATLAB signal-processing subtasks with deterministic checkers; the prompts of the held-out variants are listed in appendix A ; • a procedure in which the small model itself writes 66 training examples from expert solutions, with automatic filters and a reading of every example; • LoRA and QLoRA adapters for E2B and E4B trained on a laptop GPU in under an hour each and run with int8 OpenVINO models; • an evaluation on held-out variants in which the adapters double the pass count of E2B and raise that of E4B from 32 to 47 of 66, and an analysis of all 159 failing programs that shows which errors the adapters remove and which they do not. Section 2 describes the subtasks, the emulator and the checkers, section 3 the training data and section 4 the training and deployment. Section 5 gives the results, section 6 the error analysis and section 7 the limitations. 2 Tasks and evaluation 2.1 Subtasks The tasks come from signal processing: delay estimation between two receive channels, matched filtering, FFT-based detection, frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) and linear frequency-modulated (LFM) waveform generation, and synthetic pulse descriptor words (PDWs), which list each pulse with its time of arrival (TOA) and other parameters. In a first measurement, E2B failed every run of most of these complete tasks, so we split them into the steps at which the models failed. This gives the 11 subtasks of table 1 . Each subtask asks for a short MATLAB script that builds a signal, processes it and prints a few numbers. Every subtask is a parametric template. A variant is drawn from a random generator seeded with the subtask name and the variant index, so every variant is reproducible. The generator draws sampling rates, lengths, delays, bandwidths, amplitudes and signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), writes the prompt in English and computes the expected values with NumPy and SciPy. A variant is drawn again when an expected value equals a number in the prompt or a frequent constant (2, 10, 20, 100): such a value could be copied instead of computed. Variants 0–5 of each subtask are used to make training data (section 3 ); variants 6 and 7 are held out for evaluation. The held-out variants come from the same distribution as the training variants, so the evaluation measures generalisation to new parameters of known subtasks, not to new subtasks. Each template also has a reference solution, which scores 100 on both held-out variants of every subtask. Appendix A lists the prompt of variant 6 of every subtask with its expected values. Label Subtask Checks 1 xcorr_delay integer delay between two LFM channels from the xcorr peak integer delay (from xcorr ); channel 2 = delayed channel 1 w 2 xcorr_fine fractional delay in noise: xcorr peak refined by a parabola refined delay ( ± 0.2 \pm 0.2 samples) r ; channel 2 = delayed channel 1 w ; noise level of both channels w 3 noise_power complex tone plus noise at a given SNR; measured powers noise power r ; variance of the real part r ; power of x x r ; x x = tone + noise w 4 matched_output matched filter of an LFM pulse with conv : length, peak index, peak length; peak index; peak magnitude 5 conv_delay delay of a pulse in a receive window from the matched-filter peak peak index; delay from the peak index 6 fft_noise_power mean | X | 2 |X|^{2} of complex noise after an unscaled FFT, measured and theoretical measured mean r ; theoretical mean 7 exp_threshold threshold on | X ⁡ ( k ) | 2 |X(k)|^{2} for a false-alarm probability (exponential law) threshold on | X | 2 |X|^{2} ; threshold on | X | |X| 8 fft_bin_snr tone in noise: peak bin, measured and theoretical SNR after the FFT peak bin (1-based); measured SNR r ; theoretical SNR 9 fmcw_freq instantaneous-frequency vector of a sawtooth or triangular FMCW signal length; minimum; maximum; value at a given time 10 lfm_single one complex baseband linear chirp stored in a vector instantaneous frequency of the vector w 11 pdw_single pulse descriptor words (PDW matrix) of one emitter with constant pulse repetition interval (PRI) number of PDWs; last TOA; PDW matrix w ; rows sorted by TOA w Table 1: The 11 subtasks and the checks that score them. r : noise-dependent value, accepted only if it changes when the code runs again with another seed. w : workspace check on the arrays left by the code rather than on the printed output. Every subtask also scores the error-free run of the code. 2.2 MATLAB emulator We run the generated code in our own MATLAB emulator, since no MATLAB installation was available. The emulator parses a subset of the MATLAB language into a syntax tree and evaluates it on NumPy arrays; it does not translate MATLAB to Python and never calls exec . It provides 445 built-in functions, among them xcorr , conv , fft , randn , repmat , interp1 and polyfit . Code cannot call system or eval , cannot read or write files and can create no array with more than 20 million elements. Error messages start with MATLAB’s own wording, so a model that knows MATLAB errors sees familiar text. N-dimensional arrays, struct arrays, integer types, global and classdef are not supported. items.raw_text: Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU Mehmet Altan Toksöz, PhD Affiliation: Independent researcher, Gölbaşı, Ankara, Türkiye Email: matoksoz@gmail.com Abstract Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters through OpenVINO. On held-out variants scored by deterministic checkers, the pass rate rises from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA) and 37/66 (QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B (QLoRA). Reading all 159 failing programs shows that the adapters remove most errors of convention, such as the sign of a lag, units and array shapes, but few errors in building signals and noise. Applied at run time, the adapter costs 17–19% of the generation speed. † † subheader: November 17, 2026 1 Introduction Signal-processing engineers write much of their code in MATLAB: they synthesise pulses and chirps, correlate channels, filter, take fast Fourier transforms (FFTs) and set detection thresholds. Language models can draft such code, and small models that run on a laptop can do so without sending anything off the machine, which matters where the work cannot leave it. The Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B Gemma Team (2026) are made for this kind of device. On our tasks, however, they often get the conventions of the field wrong: they read the delay with the wrong sign from xcorr , forget the gain N N of an unscaled FFT, write a chirp rate in the wrong unit or mix row and column vectors. Such code runs and prints a plausible number, which makes the errors hard to notice. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) Hu et al. (2022) and its quantized variant QLoRA Dettmers et al. (2023) make supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of such models possible with little memory. We ask how much a small set of checked examples, trained on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of the same laptop, improves the code these models write, and which errors it removes. Answering this needs three things. First, tasks whose answers can be checked automatically. Following the practice of judging generated code by running it Chen et al. (2021) , we wrote 11 parametric subtasks from signal-processing work, run every answer in an emulator of a MATLAB subset, and score it with checkers that also reject values copied from the prompt or computed from a formula instead of measured. Earlier work compared commercial and open models on generating MATLAB code for automated-driving scenarios Yang et al. (2025) ; here the models are small enough to run on a laptop and the domain is digital signal processing (DSP). Second, training data. Instead of collecting the model’s own correct answers, which were too rare, we let the small model write the reasoning for an expert’s solution and then the answer itself, close to the rationalization step of the Self-Taught Reasoner (STaR) Zelikman et al. (2022) , and kept only answers that pass the checkers. Third, a way to train and deploy on a laptop: the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) library Mangrulkar et al. (2022) on the integrated GPU for training, and OpenVINO GenAI OpenVINO toolkit (2026) with 8-bit integer (int8) weights for inference. Our contributions are: • 11 parametric MATLAB signal-processing subtasks with deterministic checkers; the prompts of the held-out variants are listed in appendix A ; • a procedure in which the small model itself writes 66 training examples from expert solutions, with automatic filters and a reading of every example; • LoRA and QLoRA adapters for E2B and E4B trained on a laptop GPU in under an hour each and run with int8 OpenVINO models; • an evaluation on held-out variants in which the adapters double the pass count of E2B and raise that of E4B from 32 to 47 of 66, and an analysis of all 159 failing programs that shows which errors the adapters remove and which they do not. Section 2 describes the subtasks, the emulator and the checkers, section 3 the training data and section 4 the training and deployment. Section 5 gives the results, section 6 the error analysis and section 7 the limitations. 2 Tasks and evaluation 2.1 Subtasks The tasks come from signal processing: delay estimation between two receive channels, matched filtering, FFT-based detection, frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) and linear frequency-modulated (LFM) waveform generation, and synthetic pulse descriptor words (PDWs), which list each pulse with its time of arrival (TOA) and other parameters. In a first measurement, E2B failed every run of most of these complete tasks, so we split them into the steps at which the models failed. This gives the 11 subtasks of table 1 . Everything runs on one laptop with an Intel Core Ultra 5 226V processor, its integrated Arc 130V GPU and 16 GB of memory (15.6 GB usable) shared between the CPU and the GPU. Training uses the GPU through PyTorch 2.9.1 with its XPU back end (PyTorch’s device type for Intel GPUs), Transformers 5.22 and PEFT 0.21; QLoRA adds bitsandbytes 0.50.2. Newer PyTorch builds gave wrong results with the installed GPU driver, so we kept 2.9.1. Adapters. We train three adapters on the same 66 examples (table 2 ): a LoRA adapter on the bfloat16 (bf16) weights of E2B, and QLoRA adapters on E2B and E4B, whose base layers are quantized to the 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) type with double quantization and computed in bf16. E4B has only a QLoRA adapter, because its bf16 weights do not leave enough GPU memory for training. The adapters have rank 16 and α = 16 \alpha=16 , no dropout, and sit on the query, key, value and output projections and the three multilayer perceptron (MLP) projections of every language-model layer. The loss is computed only on the tokens of the thought and the answer, with the prompt formatted by the same chat template as at inference. Training uses AdamW with learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} and no weight decay, one example per step, gradient clipping at 1, gradient checkpointing and 3 epochs with the examples shuffled in every epoch. There was one training run per adapter; we did not tune these settings. The adapter is loaded as saved by PEFT and applied at run time without merging it into the weights, so the adapter trained on bf16 or NF4 weights runs on int8 weights. The adapter evaluations used OpenVINO 2026.4.1. Merging the adapter into the int8 weights would remove this cost; the run-time merge mode of OpenVINO GenAI accepts only floating-point weights. In the evaluations the adapters also shortened the answers, from 1713 to 1283 tokens on average for E4B, so a run took 106 s with the adapter and 121 s without (42 s and 50 s for E2B with and without LoRA).
