items.content: RSI-Prime: Training Models to Train Models Dewu Zheng Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University Email: zhengdw5@mail2.sysu.edu.cn Yang Ye Affiliation: Mind Lab Email: yanye@umich.edu Hongyu Zhang Affiliation: Chongqing University Email: hyzhang@cqu.edu.cn Jun Yu Affiliation: The School of Intelligence Science and EngineeringHarbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen Email: yujun@hit.edu.cn Yanlin Wang † † thanks: Yanlin Wang is the corresponding author. Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University Email: wangylin36@mail.sysu.edu.cn Abstract Enabling large language models (LLMs) to autonomously conduct training and improve target models is an important foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI). As LLMs expand their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime , a dataset for improving model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. To help LLMs learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice, we perform fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation, then apply decision-level loss masking to exclude supervision on low-quality behavior. Experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark for autonomous post-training, show that training on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement in overall performance over the original GLM-5.3, highlighting a path toward future RSI systems in which models autonomously sustain their own advancement. 1 Introduction Recent large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated growing capabilities in planning and executing model-training experiments ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Chan et al., 2024 ; Rank et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . As illustrated in Figure 1 , model training is expanding from researcher-led manual training to model-assisted training, with the prospect of LLMs autonomously planning, executing, and iterating on experiments toward human-specified goals ( Yamada et al., 2025 ) . As LLMs extend their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development, laying a foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI) ( Gao et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) . Figure 1: Three paradigms of model training: manual, model-assisted, and fully automated. Existing research advances model-training automation through improvements to execution harnesses ( Trirat et al., 2024 ; Fang et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Du et al., 2026a ) , data construction ( Du et al., 2026b ; Zhao et al., 2026a ; Zhao et al., 2026b ) , and training algorithms ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . These advances expand the tools and methods available to agents, but their effective use requires LLMs to select suitable training approaches and adapt them to task requirements and experimental feedback ( Lim et al., 2026 ; Yao et al., 2026 ) . This motivates learning from training experience to systematically improve LLMs’ own model-training capability across tasks. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime , a dataset designed to improve model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. These trajectories preserve the full process of planning, training, evaluation, and iterative refinement, providing context for learning from experimental experience. However, long-horizon training involves many experimental decisions, and final success does not guarantee the quality of each decision. To derive high-quality supervision from complete trajectories, we perform fine-grained identification and quality annotation of experimental decisions, then apply decision-level loss masking based on these annotations. The resulting supervision emphasizes high-quality behavior while preserving the full experimental context, enabling LLMs to learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice. We conduct experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark that assesses an agent’s model-training capability through the performance of the target model it trains under bounded resources ( Rank et al., 2026 ; PostTrainBench Team, 2026b ) . Across six tasks, full-trajectory fine-tuning raises the agent’s overall score from 36.56 to 45.61, while decision-level supervision further improves it to 48.24, a 31.95% relative gain over the original GLM-5.3 (Section 5.1 ). Comparisons across supervision granularities highlight the effectiveness of decision-level supervision, which outperforms step-level selection at similar supervision retention levels (Section 5.2 ). Furthermore, behavioral analysis reveals improvements in decision quality across multiple stages of experimentation, indicating that the gains in task performance are accompanied by higher-quality experimental behavior (Section 5.3 ). Our main contributions are as follows: • A dataset for improving model-training capability. We construct RSI-Prime, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories, with environment validation and quality filtering to support learning from training practice. • Decision-level supervision for experimental trajectories. We identify experimental decisions and annotate their action types and quality, enabling selective supervision of high-quality behavior while preserving the full context. • Empirical validation on PostTrainBench. Fine-tuning GLM-5.3 on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement over the original model. Supervision-strategy comparisons and behavioral analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness of decision-level supervision. 2 Related Work 2.1 Self-Evolving Agents Self-evolving agents use interaction experience and environmental feedback to improve their memory, skills, programs, or model parameters ( Gao et al., 2026a ) . For experience accumulation, Reflexion converts feedback into reflective memory, ExpeL extracts reusable knowledge from task experience, and ACE continually accumulates and refines contextual strategies ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026e ) . Voyager and Memento-Skills further support subsequent task execution by building and updating skill libraries, while Agent-Pro improves decision-making through reflection on and revision of beliefs, together with policy search ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Another line of work extends the object of improvement to agent programs and execution systems. ADAS uses a meta agent to program and search for agent implementations, while the Darwin Gödel Machine and SICA improve capabilities by modifying their own code and evaluating candidate versions ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Robeyns et al., 2025 ) . Self-Harness proposes and validates harness modifications based on execution failures, and The Hyperagents framework further makes the meta-level mechanism that generates improvements editable ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) . Parameter learning uses experience to adapt and train the model itself. SEAL learns to generate fine-tuning data and update directives, while Agent Learning via Early Experience derives supervision from future states produced by the agent’s own interactions ( Zweiger et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026d ) . Self-Challenging trains agents through reinforcement learning on self-generated verifiable tasks, while AgentEvolver combines task generation, experience-guided exploration, and contribution attribution to improve learning efficiency ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Zhai et al., 2025 ) . RSI-Prime focuses on model-training capability, turning complete experimental processes in which agents train target models into learning resources to improve their ability to conduct subsequent training experiments. 2.2 Automated LLM Post-Training Automated LLM post-training studies how agents autonomously prepare data, train models, and iterate on evaluation feedback for a target task. PostTrainBench evaluates end-to-end model improvement under bounded resources ( Rank et al., 2026 ) , Curation-Bench and RSIBench-Data focus on training-data strategy design and iteration ( Kang et al., 2026 ; Meng et al., 2026 ) , and Agent 2 RL-Bench further examines agents’ ability to construct and execute reinforcement-learning post-training pipelines, including closed-loop online interaction ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . These benchmarks characterize autonomous model-training capability at different levels. Existing methods advance autonomous post-training through data, strategy, and execution workflows. DataMaster and ANDES explore data discovery and synthesis ( Du et al., 2026b ; Zhao et al., 2026a ) , TREX explores training approaches through tree-based experimental search ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , and Gödel Forest combines co-evolving search trees with shared experience to balance the depth and breadth of data-strategy exploration ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) . AutoTrainess, RSI-Master, and ImproveAnyTask support experimentation through workflow organization, experiment management, and feedback-driven strategy iteration ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Du et al., 2026a ; Yao et al., 2026 ) . Lim et al. (2026) further find that the agents they study can repair implementations and repeatedly execute training, yet rarely revise their initial strategies in response to feedback, highlighting the need to improve experimental decision-making. Learning from training experience offers another path to improving agents’ autonomous post-training capability. RSI-Dojo constructs post-training environments, collects and filters experimental trajectories, and uses them to fine-tune post-training agents ( Gao et al., 2026b ) . RSI-Prime advances this direction through a systematic pipeline for reliable trajectory construction and fine-grained supervision in long-horizon experiments. Pre-execution validation, independent experimental supervision, and interruption recovery that preserves the original session and cumulative budget support reliable, traceable trajectory collection. Fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation then guide decision-level loss masking, enabling selective supervision of high-quality behavior while preserving the full experimental context. Figure 2: Overview of the RSI-Prime pipeline. 3 Methodology 3.1 Overview RSI-Prime provides supervision for improving agents’ model-training capability by constructing complete trajectories of model-training experiments and selecting high-quality behavior within them. As shown in Figure 2 , the pipeline comprises four stages: task collection and validation, trajectory construction and selection, fine-grained trajectory annotation, and decision-level masked training. We first collect benchmarks across seven task categories, integrate them into a common interface, and validate their evaluation protocols, scorers, and runtime workflows to establish reliable task environments for trajectory collection. In these environments, agents conduct training experiments under independent supervision. The resulting trajectories are filtered for protocol compliance and target-model improvement before proceeding to fine-grained annotation. We identify experimental decisions within these trajectories and annotate their quality and action types using source evidence and context, supporting supervision selection and behavioral analysis, respectively. Quality judgments are then mapped to message-level loss masks for selective supervised fine-tuning while preserving the full experimental context. 3.2 Task Collection and Validation We collect and integrate benchmarks into a common task interface, then validate their evaluation protocols, scorers, and runtime environments before trajectory collection. Benchmark identification. To cover diverse model-training objectives, we automatically collect candidate benchmarks from Hugging Face, academic papers, and official repositories across seven task categories: mathematics and reasoning, code, tools and interaction, knowledge and understanding, information processing, language and text, and instruction following ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2022 ) . The pipeline consults original papers, dataset documentation, and implementations to extract task definitions, data splits, and evaluation protocols, then integrates selected benchmarks into a common task interface. This interface specifies the target model, resource budget, and submission requirements, standardizing execution and result recording while preserving each benchmark’s scoring semantics and providing task environments for pre-execution validation. Pre-execution validation. To ensure reliable experimental feedback, we perform three types of validation shown in Figure 2 . Protocol validation checks task scope, model identity, prompts, generation settings, and the primary metric against the original evaluation requirements. Scorer validation replays available Base/Instruct outputs and uses positive and negative controls and coverage checks to verify expected scoring behavior. Runtime validation tests the supplied model’s inference and scoring pipeline on the actual execution host. Tasks must pass all checks before trajectory collection; failures require repair and revalidation. 3.3 Trajectory Construction and Selection We collect complete model-training trajectories through independent supervision and interruption recovery, then filter them for protocol compliance and target-model improvement. The trajectories retain successful and unsuccessful intermediate attempts, providing context for decision identification and quality assessment. Supervised collection. Maintaining reliable execution is challenging in long-horizon training experiments, where agents may encounter interruptions or terminate prematurely ( Rank et al., 2026 ; Du et al., 2026a ) . We use an independent supervisor to monitor experimental progress and a controller to resume interrupted or prematurely terminated runs within the remaining budget. Recovery preserves the original session, artifacts, and cumulative execution time, while supervisor interventions are recorded separately from agent actions. Together, these mechanisms support stable and continuous operation of the trajectory-collection framework. Trajectory filtering. We filter trajectories for protocol compliance and training effectiveness, retaining experimental experience that meets task requirements and substantially improves the target model. Each trajectory must pass PostTrainBench’s four trajectory judges, and its submitted model must satisfy the relative-improvement threshold: g = s post − s base s instruct − s base > 0.5 , g=\frac{s_{\mathrm{post}}-s_{\mathrm{base}}}{s_{\mathrm{instruct}}-s_{\mathrm{base}}}>0.5, (1) where s post s_{\mathrm{post}} , s base s_{\mathrm{base}} , and s instruct s_{\mathrm{instruct}} are the scores of the submitted, base, and reference instruction-tuned models under the same benchmark protocol, respectively. This condition requires the submitted model’s improvement to exceed half the reference Instruct–Base performance gap. 3.4 Decision Identification Each experimental trajectory comprises a sequence of decisions that guide the training process from initial planning through iterative refinement. We define an experimental decision as a choice that determines the course of action in a model-training experiment, such as selecting training data, designing a training approach, or revising a strategy based on evaluation feedback. As shown in Figure 2 , analysis explains the basis for a choice, the choice specifies the action to take next, and execution records how that choice is implemented and the resulting feedback. Together, Analysis, Choice, and Execution capture the progression from rationale to action. We organize content concerning the same choice into one decision, allowing a decision to span multiple messages and a single message to involve multiple decisions. Decision identification. We use an annotation agent to identify decisions in experimental trajectories and link them to their supporting analysis and execution. The agent reads the trajectory in windows that preserve complete interaction rounds, retrieves original messages to recover relevant context, and links related content across windows to the same decision. Content whose association remains unclear at a window boundary is retained as pending and reconsidered with new evidence in subsequent windows, avoiding forced decision splits or attachment to the preceding decision solely because of a window cutoff. Iterative verification. We check the consistency of decision annotations with the original trajectories through iterative independent verification. Each round comprises three independent checks of the same annotation version, assessing decision completeness, evidential support, and the appropriateness of decision boundaries and evidence attribution. Annotations are retained when at least two checks approve them; otherwise, decisions in the corresponding source interval are re-identified and undergo another verification round until majority approval is reached. Annotation reliability is additionally assessed through an independent human audit (Appendix A.4 ). 3.5 Decision Quality Assessment and Action Annotation We annotate experimental decisions along two axes, quality and action type, to support supervision selection and behavioral analysis, respectively. Both annotations draw on the original trajectories and experimental context, rather than judging local behavior solely by final scores. Quality assessment. We assess decision quality along three dimensions: Analysis, Choice, and Execution. Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University Email: wangylin36@mail.sysu.edu.cn Abstract Enabling large language models (LLMs) to autonomously conduct training and improve target models is an important foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI). As LLMs expand their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime , a dataset for improving model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. To help LLMs learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice, we perform fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation, then apply decision-level loss masking to exclude supervision on low-quality behavior. Experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark for autonomous post-training, show that training on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement in overall performance over the original GLM-5.3, highlighting a path toward future RSI systems in which models autonomously sustain their own advancement. 1 Introduction Recent large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated growing capabilities in planning and executing model-training experiments ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Chan et al., 2024 ; Rank et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . As illustrated in Figure 1 , model training is expanding from researcher-led manual training to model-assisted training, with the prospect of LLMs autonomously planning, executing, and iterating on experiments toward human-specified goals ( Yamada et al., 2025 ) . As LLMs extend their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development, laying a foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI) ( Gao et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) . Figure 1: Three paradigms of model training: manual, model-assisted, and fully automated. Existing research advances model-training automation through improvements to execution harnesses ( Trirat et al., 2024 ; Fang et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Du et al., 2026a ) , data construction ( Du et al., 2026b ; Zhao et al., 2026a ; Zhao et al., 2026b ) , and training algorithms ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . These advances expand the tools and methods available to agents, but their effective use requires LLMs to select suitable training approaches and adapt them to task requirements and experimental feedback ( Lim et al., 2026 ; Yao et al., 2026 ) . This motivates learning from training experience to systematically improve LLMs’ own model-training capability across tasks. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime , a dataset designed to improve model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. These trajectories preserve the full process of planning, training, evaluation, and iterative refinement, providing context for learning from experimental experience. However, long-horizon training involves many experimental decisions, and final success does not guarantee the quality of each decision. To derive high-quality supervision from complete trajectories, we perform fine-grained identification and quality annotation of experimental decisions, then apply decision-level loss masking based on these annotations. The resulting supervision emphasizes high-quality behavior while preserving the full experimental context, enabling LLMs to learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice. We conduct experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark that assesses an agent’s model-training capability through the performance of the target model it trains under bounded resources ( Rank et al., 2026 ; PostTrainBench Team, 2026b ) . Across six tasks, full-trajectory fine-tuning raises the agent’s overall score from 36.56 to 45.61, while decision-level supervision further improves it to 48.24, a 31.95% relative gain over the original GLM-5.3 (Section 5.1 ). Comparisons across supervision granularities highlight the effectiveness of decision-level supervision, which outperforms step-level selection at similar supervision retention levels (Section 5.2 ). Furthermore, behavioral analysis reveals improvements in decision quality across multiple stages of experimentation, indicating that the gains in task performance are accompanied by higher-quality experimental behavior (Section 5.3 ). Our main contributions are as follows: • A dataset for improving model-training capability. We construct RSI-Prime, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories, with environment validation and quality filtering to support learning from training practice. • Decision-level supervision for experimental trajectories. We identify experimental decisions and annotate their action types and quality, enabling selective supervision of high-quality behavior while preserving the full context. • Empirical validation on PostTrainBench. Fine-tuning GLM-5.3 on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement over the original model. Supervision-strategy comparisons and behavioral analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness of decision-level supervision. 2 Related Work 2.1 Self-Evolving Agents Self-evolving agents use interaction experience and environmental feedback to improve their memory, skills, programs, or model parameters ( Gao et al., 2026a ) . For experience accumulation, Reflexion converts feedback into reflective memory, ExpeL extracts reusable knowledge from task experience, and ACE continually accumulates and refines contextual strategies ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026e ) . Voyager and Memento-Skills further support subsequent task execution by building and updating skill libraries, while Agent-Pro improves decision-making through reflection on and revision of beliefs, together with policy search ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Another line of work extends the object of improvement to agent programs and execution systems. ADAS uses a meta agent to program and search for agent implementations, while the Darwin Gödel Machine and SICA improve capabilities by modifying their own code and evaluating candidate versions ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Robeyns et al., 2025 ) . Self-Harness proposes and validates harness modifications based on execution failures, and The Hyperagents framework further makes the meta-level mechanism that generates improvements editable ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) . Parameter learning uses experience to adapt and train the model itself. SEAL learns to generate fine-tuning data and update directives, while Agent Learning via Early Experience derives supervision from future states produced by the agent’s own interactions ( Zweiger et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026d ) . Self-Challenging trains agents through reinforcement learning on self-generated verifiable tasks, while AgentEvolver combines task generation, experience-guided exploration, and contribution attribution to improve learning efficiency ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Zhai et al., 2025 ) . RSI-Prime focuses on model-training capability, turning complete experimental processes in which agents train target models into learning resources to improve their ability to conduct subsequent training experiments. 2.2 Automated LLM Post-Training Automated LLM post-training studies how agents autonomously prepare data, train models, and iterate on evaluation feedback for a target task. PostTrainBench evaluates end-to-end model improvement under bounded resources ( Rank et al., 2026 ) , Curation-Bench and RSIBench-Data focus on training-data strategy design and iteration ( Kang et al., 2026 ; Meng et al., 2026 ) , and Agent 2 RL-Bench further examines agents’ ability to construct and execute reinforcement-learning post-training pipelines, including closed-loop online interaction ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . These benchmarks characterize autonomous model-training capability at different levels. Existing methods advance autonomous post-training through data, strategy, and execution workflows. DataMaster and ANDES explore data discovery and synthesis ( Du et al., 2026b ; Zhao et al., 2026a ) , TREX explores training approaches through tree-based experimental search ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , and Gödel Forest combines co-evolving search trees with shared experience to balance the depth and breadth of data-strategy exploration ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) . AutoTrainess, RSI-Master, and ImproveAnyTask support experimentation through workflow organization, experiment management, and feedback-driven strategy iteration ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Du et al., 2026a ; Yao et al., 2026 ) . Lim et al. (2026) further find that the agents they study can repair implementations and repeatedly execute training, yet rarely revise their initial strategies in response to feedback, highlighting the need to improve experimental decision-making. Learning from training experience offers another path to improving agents’ autonomous post-training capability. RSI-Dojo constructs post-training environments, collects and filters experimental trajectories, and uses them to fine-tune post-training agents ( Gao et al., 2026b ) . RSI-Prime advances this direction through a systematic pipeline for reliable trajectory construction and fine-grained supervision in long-horizon experiments. Pre-execution validation, independent experimental supervision, and interruption recovery that preserves the original session and cumulative budget support reliable, traceable trajectory collection. Fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation then guide decision-level loss masking, enabling selective supervision of high-quality behavior while preserving the full experimental context. Figure 2: Overview of the RSI-Prime pipeline. 3 Methodology 3.1 Overview RSI-Prime provides supervision for improving agents’ model-training capability by constructing complete trajectories of model-training experiments and selecting high-quality behavior within them. In these environments, agents conduct training experiments under independent supervision. The resulting trajectories are filtered for protocol compliance and target-model improvement before proceeding to fine-grained annotation. We identify experimental decisions within these trajectories and annotate their quality and action types using source evidence and context, supporting supervision selection and behavioral analysis, respectively. Quality judgments are then mapped to message-level loss masks for selective supervised fine-tuning while preserving the full experimental context. 3.2 Task Collection and Validation We collect and integrate benchmarks into a common task interface, then validate their evaluation protocols, scorers, and runtime environments before trajectory collection. Benchmark identification. To cover diverse model-training objectives, we automatically collect candidate benchmarks from Hugging Face, academic papers, and official repositories across seven task categories: mathematics and reasoning, code, tools and interaction, knowledge and understanding, information processing, language and text, and instruction following ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2022 ) . The pipeline consults original papers, dataset documentation, and implementations to extract task definitions, data splits, and evaluation protocols, then integrates selected benchmarks into a common task interface. This interface specifies the target model, resource budget, and submission requirements, standardizing execution and result recording while preserving each benchmark’s scoring semantics and providing task environments for pre-execution validation. Pre-execution validation. To ensure reliable experimental feedback, we perform three types of validation shown in Figure 2 . Protocol validation checks task scope, model identity, prompts, generation settings, and the primary metric against the original evaluation requirements. Scorer validation replays available Base/Instruct outputs and uses positive and negative controls and coverage checks to verify expected scoring behavior. Runtime validation tests the supplied model’s inference and scoring pipeline on the actual execution host. Tasks must pass all checks before trajectory collection; failures require repair and revalidation. 3.3 Trajectory Construction and Selection We collect complete model-training trajectories through independent supervision and interruption recovery, then filter them for protocol compliance and target-model improvement. We use an independent supervisor to monitor experimental progress and a controller to resume interrupted or prematurely terminated runs within the remaining budget. items.title: Commission preliminarily finds Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act for failure to tackle the sale of illegal products
items.summary: The European Commission preliminarily found Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to put in place reasonable, proportionate and effective measures to mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform. The Commission preliminarily found that Temu's mitigation measures include ineffective controls to check the compliance of products; a weak content moderation system; and an ineffective sanction system. Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, said: Shopping online should not mean risking the purchase of illegal and unsafe products. Under the Digital Services Act, platforms are responsible for protecting users from the risk of illegal content and goods. The preliminary findings against Temu mark another step towards making the online world safer. Read the full details in the press release Find further information about: Supervision of the designated very large online platforms and search engines under D

items.title: Make America Healthy Again
items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans. Trump Advances Wildfire Suppression briefings & statements Presidential Message on American Education Week November 17, 2026 Read more : Presidential Message on American Education Week presidential actions Nominations Sent to the Senate November 16, 2026 Read more : Nominations Sent to the Senate promises made, promises kept 01 The Trump administration made incredible strides in its effort to Make America Healthy Again, with roughly 35% of the American food industry — including major corporations like Walmart, Hershey and Nestlé — agreeing to eliminate artificial dyes from their products. 02 At President Trump’s direction, the Department of Health and Human Services revised its childhood vaccine recommendations from 72 shots for 11 diseases to 10 “consensus vaccines.” 03 President Trump established the Make America Healthy Again Commission, tasked with investigating and addressing the root causes of America’s escalating health crisis, with an initial focus on childhood chronic diseases. 04 Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins signed a slew of waivers allowing states to remove junk food from SNAP. 05 The Department of Health and Human Services removed COVID-19 vaccines from the list of shots recommended for healthy children and pregnant women. 06 Following negotiations with the Trump Administration, a variety of major pharmaceutical companies have agreed to bring American drug prices in line with the lowest paid by other developed nations, ending decades of Big Pharma exploiting U.S. consumers. 07 President Trump secured $50 billion in funding for rural hospitals. 08 President Trump signed the Whole Milk for Health Kids Act into law, restoring nutritious whole and 2% milk in American schools. 09 The Trump Administration Rollins released new dietary guidelines that prioritize whole, nutrient-dense foods over processed junk. items.content: NVIDIA Expands Commitments With Supply Chain Partners to Support AI Infrastructure Buildout Long-Term Supply Agreements Across Multiple Critical Inputs Position NVIDIA for Sustainable Growth November 17, 2026 News Summary: New agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics support additional substrate capacity and expanded production capabilities at existing factories. NVIDIA’s work with Amkor and SPIL expands advanced packaging capacity for current and next-generation accelerated computing platforms. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs began volume shipments in the third quarter, leveraging TSMC’s 5nm, 3nm and CoWoS advanced packaging technologies. Foxconn is deepening its collaboration with NVIDIA, drawing on its global production network to support next-generation GPU and networking platforms. NVIDIA today announced expanded commitments with supply chain partners to support sustainable long-term growth, aligning supply and manufacturing capacity with demand for its accelerated computing and AI infrastructure platforms. Working with Amkor Technology, Foxconn, Kinsus Interconnect Technology, Samsung Electro-Mechanics , Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and TSMC, NVIDIA is expanding manufacturing capacity across substrates, advanced packaging, wafer and contract manufacturing to scale production of its current and next-generation accelerated computing platforms. “Our supply chain is a strategic advantage,” said Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations at NVIDIA. “Our work with these partners builds on our manufacturing foundation for long-term growth, expanding capacity across components, advanced packaging and system production to deliver the accelerated computing platforms our customers need.” Increasing Substrate Capacity and Production Capabilities NVIDIA is expanding its substrate supply commitments with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics, adding manufacturing capacity and improving production capabilities at existing factories. Under a new agreement with NVIDIA, Kinsus plans to expand its advanced ABF package substrate manufacturing capacity dedicated to NVIDIA by more than 3.5x over current levels from its Youth campus in Taoyuan, Taiwan. Production is expected to begin in the second half of 2027, with the additional capacity targeted for the third quarter of 2028. This multiyear agreement builds on the companies’ existing supplier relationship and supports NVIDIA’s long-term supply planning for its accelerated computing platforms. “We believe AI will be one of the most important technology transitions of our lifetime,” said Scott Chen, CEO and president of Kinsus. “After more than a decade of partnership with NVIDIA, we are excited to continue building the future together.” NVIDIA and Samsung Electro-Mechanics have amended their existing substrate supply agreement to improve operational capabilities at existing factories in support of increased production of NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platforms. The amendment builds on the companies’ previously announced multiyear collaboration supporting substrate manufacturing in Sejong and Busan, South Korea, for NVIDIA’s compute and high-speed networking technologies. “By combining our world-class substrate fine-processing technology and high-reliability MLCC technology, we will perfectly fulfill our role as a total solution provider so that NVIDIA’s AI platform can be supplied to the global market on time, with the highest performance and quality,” said Duck-Hyun Chang, CEO of Samsung Electro-Mechanics. Scaling Advanced Packaging Through Multiyear Agreements NVIDIA’s advanced packaging plans include a new capacity expansion with SPIL and previously announced agreements supporting Amkor’s manufacturing expansion in the U.S. and South Korea. NVIDIA is supporting Amkor’s expansion of advanced packaging capacity in Arizona and South Korea through multiyear agreements announced in July and October 2026, totaling nearly $3 billion. The agreements include prepayments to help Amkor scale manufacturing capacity for NVIDIA’s long-term production needs. “Our agreements with NVIDIA support investments in Arizona and South Korea that will serve multiple generations of AI platforms,” said Kevin Engel, president and CEO of Amkor. “That long-term planning allows us to advance our packaging technologies and add manufacturing capacity as NVIDIA’s production needs grow.” NVIDIA and SPIL are expanding advanced packaging operations in Taiwan under a multiyear agreement supported by multibillion-dollar funding from NVIDIA. The expansion will increase contracted advanced packaging capacity dedicated to NVIDIA by mid-2029. The project includes new production lines with turnkey support spanning bumping, interposer wafer fabrication, assembly and testing. These capabilities support semiconductor products with demanding requirements for computing performance, bandwidth, power efficiency and system integration. “SPIL is proud to strengthen our collaboration with NVIDIA,” said C.W. Tsai, CEO and chairman of the board of SPIL. “This agreement enhances our ability to support next‑generation packaging technologies and deliver the performance and reliability required for future AI systems.” Next-Generation Technologies for Agentic AI The third quarter marked the first volume shipment of NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs for agentic AI. These products take advantage of TSMC’s 5nm, 3nm and CoWoS advanced packaging technologies. “TSMC and NVIDIA share a longstanding partnership built on semiconductor innovation,” said Dr. Kevin Zhang, senior vice president and deputy co-COO at TSMC. “This deep collaboration allows us to plan for future technology requirements and prepare our manufacturing capabilities as NVIDIA brings new platforms to market.” Leveraging Global Manufacturing Footprint for GPU and Networking Platforms “Foxconn continues to deepen its collaboration with NVIDIA across next-generation GPU and networking platforms,” said Young Liu, chairman of Foxconn. “By leveraging its integrated global production network spanning Asia, North America, and Europe, Foxconn is well-positioned to support the volume ramp-up of next-generation AI infrastructure.” Building on Global Supply Chain Expansion These commitments build on NVIDIA’s decades-long partnerships and recent commitments announced in October for manufacturing expansions with Amkor, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Samsung Electro-Mechanics, SPIL and Unimicron. Those plans included an aggregate 2.5x increase in substrate capacity over three years, expanded advanced packaging, a doubling of semiconductor testing capacity from 2026 to 2027 and a 15x increase in SPIL’s optical-engine capacity by mid-2027, with aims for another doubling by the end of 2028. “Our strong and long-standing collaboration with NVIDIA has continued to develop in the area of high-performance IC package substrates,” said Koji Kawashima, president and chief executive officer at IBIDEN. “Through the expansion of our Ono Plant, we will continue to strengthen our production capabilities and meet growing demand.” “Our work with NVIDIA demonstrates the value of close collaboration between chip design and semiconductor testing,” said Gauss Chang, president at KYEC. “Expanding our testing operations into the United States builds on that relationship and brings our capabilities closer to NVIDIA’s growing U.S. manufacturing supply chain.” “As AI reshapes industries and societies around the world, trusted partnerships and supply chain collaboration have never been more important,” said SC Chien, chairman of Unimicron. “The advanced substrate capacity investment underscores the strength of our partnership with NVIDIA and our shared commitment to support the rapid growth of AI infrastructure. By investing in advanced substrate technologies and manufacturing capabilities, Unimicron is well-positioned to help customers unlock new opportunities and share in the tremendous growth of the AI era.” About NVIDIA NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) is the world leader in AI and accelerated computing. items.content: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars: Synthetic enterprise environments : simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation Figure 1: Components of Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ? In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. Synthetic enterprise environments Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve. Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful. Grounding in real world signals To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources. O*NET data from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates. Online job postings provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions. SEC filings inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization. Figure 2: Real signals from public datasets that are used to ground the evaluation data generation Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure. Industry specific simulation We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage: A pharmaceutical environment that includes regulatory submission workflows, clinical trial discussions, and cross functional safety review meetings A capital markets environment featuring deal pipelines, compliance communications, and client portfolio reviews An IT/software company that simulates sprint planning, code review discussions, and product launch coordination Figure 3: Industries targeted for industry evaluation data generation This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes. Automated query generation While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in. The six-stage pipeline Figure 4: Query customization pipeline that turns generic query templates into realistic, industry-specific queries We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios. Validating synthetic quality Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions: Structural fidelity : Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships? Contextual relevance : Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns? Behavioral realism : Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics? Content safety : Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals? End-to-end automation While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including: Reproducibility : Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases. Scale : The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand. Iteration speed : Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles. Cross-team consistency : Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels. This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results. Privacy and safety by design Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline . Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk. Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline. This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible. Results and impact Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions. On synthetic data quality , our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments. On scale and efficiency , each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs. On organizational adoption , our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure. Conclusion As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety. Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next. At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale . Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets ! items.content: At a glance Developers use AI coding agents in the same codebases day after day, yet agents often start each session from scratch: rediscovering familiar facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches. TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model. Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable. AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error. In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. Figure 1. Each finished session teaches TokenEconomizer something about the repository, so later sessions cost less tokens. Where the tokens go We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred: Rediscovering the same facts . After a repository had accumulated at least five completed tasks, 30% of tool calls repeated an action from an earlier task in that repository. Only 7% matched an action in another repository’s history. Paying for unused tools . The agent received 23 tool descriptions on every turn, but 16 were never called. Getting stuck on failures . The 17% of tasks that failed accounted for 32% of the spending. We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere. How TokenEconomizer works After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2. Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it. Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use , while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed. Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself. Figure 2. TokenEconomizer works alongside an unchanged coding agent. Micro-skills add learned facts, tool pruning trims the loaded tools, and failure-loop intervention redirects stuck work. Each finished session updates all three. The controller is designed to revise its decisions as new evidence arrives. Reported savings also account for the cost of TokenEconomizer’s own model calls. Saving costs in every repository We evaluated TokenEconomizer on 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, using five different AI coding agent and model combinations. For each repository, TokenEconomizer started with no prior session history. TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9%, as shown in Figure 3, and saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss. By contrast, lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation. Figure 3. On SWE-Bench, TokenEconomizer lowered mean cost per task by 18.4–30.9% across five agent–model combinations (left), while Pass@1 rose in four of them (right). Savings grow as experience accumulates. Early tasks can cost more while TokenEconomizer learns, but cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task, shown inFigure 4. Each mechanism contributes savings on its own, and combining all three delivers the largest reduction. Figure 4. Cumulative cost change relative to default over each repository’s tasks, using Claude Code. Starting with no history, every repository becomes cheaper by the sixth task. The savings also carried over to sequential web development, with costs 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench. On security auditing, where every task is in a new repository, costs were 6.4–19.6% lower. Looking ahead TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model. The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know. TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model. Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable. AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error. In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. Figure 1. Each finished session teaches TokenEconomizer something about the repository, so later sessions cost less tokens. Where the tokens go We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred: Rediscovering the same facts . After a repository had accumulated at least five completed tasks, 30% of tool calls repeated an action from an earlier task in that repository. Only 7% matched an action in another repository’s history. Paying for unused tools . The agent received 23 tool descriptions on every turn, but 16 were never called. Getting stuck on failures . The 17% of tasks that failed accounted for 32% of the spending. We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere. How TokenEconomizer works After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2. Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it. Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use , while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed. Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself. Figure 2. TokenEconomizer works alongside an unchanged coding agent. Micro-skills add learned facts, tool pruning trims the loaded tools, and failure-loop intervention redirects stuck work. Each finished session updates all three. The controller is designed to revise its decisions as new evidence arrives. Reported savings also account for the cost of TokenEconomizer’s own model calls. The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers.
