items.content: Back to Articles Decision Models in Hugging Face Published November 10, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 101 +95 Aritra Roy Gosthipaty ariG23498 Follow Lysandre lysandre Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow Tom Aarsen tomaarsen Follow Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text. Consider a customer support system receiving the following message: "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today." The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers. llama cli -hf ggml-org/gemma-4-e4b-it-GGUF:Q4_0 > We have the following customer support ticket, "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today." , which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. Give the answers in JSON. [Start thinking] ... [end thinking] ```json { "team_to_handle" : "Billing" , "urgency" : "High" , "request_refund" : true } But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text ? from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } ) # { # 'department': { # 'type': 'choice', # 'choice': 'billing', # 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975, # 'probabilities': { # 'billing': 0.9982666969299316, # 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616, # 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412 # } # } # } This is the key idea behind decision models . What are decision models? A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands. TypeSafe AI introduced Jev , describing it as a System One model . The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2). The community has converged to the term decision model , because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". ( A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models ) For a decision model, the fundamental interface is: State + Questions + Allowed Answers → Decisions + Probabilities Why not use LLMs for everything? We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks. However, there are a few problems with this approach. LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices. Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work. Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work. How are decision models different from classification models? Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification. Traditional classification Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments: Billing Technical support Sales A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution. The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head . If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model. Zero-shot classification Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time. For example: from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification" , model= "facebook/bart-large-mnli" , ) classifier( "My payment was deducted twice." , candidate_labels=[ "billing" , "technical support" , "sales" ], ) # {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.', # 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support'], # 'scores': [0.8466812372207642, 0.0962134450674057, 0.05710534751415253]} Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs. from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification" , model= "facebook/bart-large-mnli" , ) classifier( "My payment was deducted twice." , candidate_labels=[ "billing" , "technical support" , "sales" , "legal" ], ) # {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.', # 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support', 'legal'], # 'scores': [0.8185835480690002, 0.09302053600549698, 0.05521026626229286, 0.03318570926785469]} One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis. This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is. Where decision models differ Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul). More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions . Consider these three approaches: Property Classification Zero-shot classification Decision model Probability over choices Yes Yes Yes Labels defined at inference No Yes Yes Multiple typed questions No No Yes Ordered scoring and yes/no decisions Task-specific Possible with adaptation Native primitives The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions. The decision model interface A decision model request has the following two components: state questions State The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models. For example: { "customer_message" : "I was charged twice. Please refund me today." , "subscription" : "pro" , "previous_tickets" : 2 } Questions and their primitives Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions: Choice: Select one of several possible answers. Score: Evaluate something on an ordered scale. Noul: Answer a yes/no question probabilistically. Let's go over them one by one. Choice: A probability distribution over options Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification. Suppose we ask: Which department should handle this customer request? The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales. from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } ) # { # 'department': { # 'type': 'choice', # 'choice': 'billing', # 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975, # 'probabilities': { # 'billing': 0.9982666969299316, # 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616, # 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412 # } # } # } The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z 1 , … , z K z_1,\ldots,z_K z 1 ​ , … , z K ​ , (with K K K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax: p i = exp ⁡ ( z i ) ∑ j = 1 K exp ⁡ ( z j ) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} p i ​ = ∑ j = 1 K ​ exp ( z j ​ ) exp ( z i ​ ) ​ Here, K K K is the number of choices. Consider this illustrative distribution: Choice Probability Billing 0.998 Technical support 0.001 Sales 0.001 The probabilities sum to one: ∑ i = 1 K p i = 1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i = 1 ∑ K ​ p i ​ = 1. The model chooses the option with the largest probability: y ^ = arg ⁡ max ⁡ i p i \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y ^ ​ = ar g i max ​ p i ​ In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives. Score: The expectation of an ordered distribution Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale? Consider the question: How urgent is this customer request? We define three levels: 0: Low urgency 1: Medium urgency 2: High urgency from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is the request?" , "criteria" : [ "low" , "medium" , "high" ] }, } } ) # { # 'urgency': { # 'type': 'score', # 'score': 1.7053890228271484, # 'legend': { # '0': 'low', # '1': 'medium', # '2': 'high' # }, # 'confidence': 0.5580834252759814, # 'probabilities': { # '0': 0.014908230863511562, # '1': 0.26479458808898926, # '2': 0.7202972173690796 # } # } # } The model again produces a probability distribution: Level Probability 0 — Low 0.01 1 — Medium 0.26 2 — High 0.72 Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index . For a random variable X X X representing the level, the expectation is: E [ X ] = ∑ i = 0 K − 1 i p i \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E [ X ] = i = 0 ∑ K − 1 ​ i p i ​ For our example: E [ X ] = 0 ( 0.01 ) + 1 ( 0.26 ) + 2 ( 0.72 ) = 1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E [ X ] = 0 ( 0.01 ) + 1 ( 0.26 ) + 2 ( 0.72 ) = 1.7 The reported score is therefore 1.7 . This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7. Noul: A Bernoulli decision The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question. For example: Is the customer requesting a refund? from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "refund" : { "type" : "noul" , "instructions" : "Is the customer requesting a refund?" } } } ) # { # 'refund': { # 'type': 'noul', # 'noul': 0.9947046637535095 # } # } Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli). Let Y Y Y represent a binary outcome: Y ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( p ) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y ∼ Bernoulli ( p ) where P ( Y = 1 ) = p , P ( Y = 0 ) = 1 − p . P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P ( Y = 1 ) = p , P ( Y = 0 ) = 1 − p . If the model returns: { "type" : "noul" , "noul" : 0.92 } it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No. The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it. Confidence: How certain is the model? So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score. The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that. For a Choice with K K K options, the confidence is: p max ⁡ − 1 K 1 − 1 K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1 − K 1 ​ p m a x ​ − K 1 ​ ​ where p max ⁡ p_{\max} p m a x ​ is the largest predicted probability. The intuition here is: A uniform distribution has confidence 0. p max ⁡ = 1 K p_{\max} = \frac{1}{K} p m a x ​ = K 1 ​ . This means the model estimates that all choices are equally likely. A distribution concentrated entirely on one option has confidence 1. p max ⁡ = 1 p_{\max} = 1 p m a x ​ = 1 The larger the winning probability relative to a uniform distribution, the higher the confidence. In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998: C = 3 ( 0.998 ) − 1 2 = 0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C = 2 3 ( 0.998 ) − 1 ​ = 0.997 Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558. Decision models in the Hugging Face ecosystem Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations. Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation . A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once: inference engines like llama.cpp can serve any decision model through the same API the Hub can package and surface them consistently and training tools can target shared primitives instead of individual architectures The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces. 1. Serving with Transformers Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline , AutoModelForDecision , and the DecisionConfig classes. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture. For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones. 4. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API. Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. Please refund me." , "refund" ), ( "My package has not arrived." , "shipping" ), ( "The application crashes when I open it." , "technical" ), ( "I want my money back." , "refund" ), ( "Where is my delivery?" , "shipping" ), ( "I cannot log into my account." , "technical" ), ] options = { "refund" : "Billing issues and refunds" , "shipping" : "Orders and deliveries" , "technical" : "Software and account issues" , } def preprocess ( text, label ): request = { "state" : text, "questions" : { "category" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Classify the support request." , "criteria" : options, } }, } (inputs, questions), = model.decision_config.prepare_inputs( request, tokenizer ) inputs[ "marks" ] = inputs[ "marks" ].unsqueeze( 0 ) inputs[ "num_options" ] = torch.tensor([[ len (questions[ 0 ].options)]]) inputs[ "question_type_ids" ] = torch.tensor([[ 1 ]]) # choice inputs[ "labels" ] = torch.tensor( [questions[ 0 ].options.index(label)] ) return inputs dataset = [preprocess(text, label) for text, label in examples] class DecisionTrainer ( Trainer ): def compute_loss ( self, model, inputs, return_outputs= False , **kwargs ): inputs = inputs.copy() labels = inputs.pop( "labels" ) logits = model(**inputs) logits = logits.unsqueeze( 0 ) # [3] -> [1, 3] loss = F.cross_entropy(logits. float (), labels) return (loss, logits) if return_outputs else loss trainer = DecisionTrainer( model=model, args=TrainingArguments( output_dir= "./decision-toy" , max_steps= 30 , per_device_train_batch_size= 1 , learning_rate= 1e-3 , logging_steps= 5 , save_strategy= "no" , report_to= "none" , remove_unused_columns= False , ), train_dataset=dataset, data_collator= lambda batch: batch[ 0 ], ) trainer.train() First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL ( huggingface/trl#8040 ), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open. If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head. Final thoughts Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software . Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text. Consider a customer support system receiving the following message: "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today." The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers. llama cli -hf ggml-org/gemma-4-e4b-it-GGUF:Q4_0 > We have the following customer support ticket, "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today." , which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. Give the answers in JSON. [Start thinking] ... [end thinking] ```json { "team_to_handle" : "Billing" , "urgency" : "High" , "request_refund" : true } But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text ? from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } ) # { # 'department': { # 'type': 'choice', # 'choice': 'billing', # 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975, # 'probabilities': { # 'billing': 0.9982666969299316, # 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616, # 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412 # } # } # } This is the key idea behind decision models . What are decision models? A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands. TypeSafe AI introduced Jev , describing it as a System One model . The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2). The community has converged to the term decision model , because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". ( A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models ) For a decision model, the fundamental interface is: State + Questions + Allowed Answers → Decisions + Probabilities Why not use LLMs for everything? We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks. However, there are a few problems with this approach. LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices. Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work. Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work. How are decision models different from classification models? Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification. Traditional classification Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments: Billing Technical support Sales A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution. The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head . If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model. Zero-shot classification Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time. For example: from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification" , model= "facebook/bart-large-mnli" , ) classifier( "My payment was deducted twice." , candidate_labels=[ "billing" , "technical support" , "sales" ], ) # {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.', # 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support'], # 'scores': [0.8466812372207642, 0.0962134450674057, 0.05710534751415253]} Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs. from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification" , model= "facebook/bart-large-mnli" , ) classifier( "My payment was deducted twice." , candidate_labels=[ "billing" , "technical support" , "sales" , "legal" ], ) # {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.', # 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support', 'legal'], # 'scores': [0.8185835480690002, 0.09302053600549698, 0.05521026626229286, 0.03318570926785469]} One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis. This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is. Where decision models differ Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul). More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions . Consider these three approaches: Property Classification Zero-shot classification Decision model Probability over choices Yes Yes Yes Labels defined at inference No Yes Yes Multiple typed questions No No Yes Ordered scoring and yes/no decisions Task-specific Possible with adaptation Native primitives The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions. The decision model interface A decision model request has the following two components: state questions State The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models. For example: { "customer_message" : "I was charged twice. Please refund me today." , "subscription" : "pro" , "previous_tickets" : 2 } Questions and their primitives Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions: Choice: Select one of several possible answers. Score: Evaluate something on an ordered scale. Noul: Answer a yes/no question probabilistically. Let's go over them one by one. Choice: A probability distribution over options Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification. Suppose we ask: Which department should handle this customer request? The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales. from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } ) # { # 'department': { # 'type': 'choice', # 'choice': 'billing', # 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975, # 'probabilities': { # 'billing': 0.9982666969299316, # 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616, # 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412 # } # } # } The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z 1 , … , z K z_1,\ldots,z_K z 1 ​ , … , z K ​ , (with K K K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax: p i = exp ⁡ ( z i ) ∑ j = 1 K exp ⁡ ( z j ) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} p i ​ = ∑ j = 1 K ​ exp ( z j ​ ) exp ( z i ​ ) ​ Here, K K K is the number of choices. Consider this illustrative distribution: Choice Probability Billing 0.998 Technical support 0.001 Sales 0.001 The probabilities sum to one: ∑ i = 1 K p i = 1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i = 1 ∑ K ​ p i ​ = 1. The model chooses the option with the largest probability: y ^ = arg ⁡ max ⁡ i p i \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y ^ ​ = ar g i max ​ p i ​ In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives. Score: The expectation of an ordered distribution Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale? Consider the question: How urgent is this customer request? We define three levels: 0: Low urgency 1: Medium urgency 2: High urgency from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is the request?" , "criteria" : [ "low" , "medium" , "high" ] }, } } ) # { # 'urgency': { # 'type': 'score', # 'score': 1.7053890228271484, # 'legend': { # '0': 'low', # '1': 'medium', # '2': 'high' # }, # 'confidence': 0.5580834252759814, # 'probabilities': { # '0': 0.014908230863511562, # '1': 0.26479458808898926, # '2': 0.7202972173690796 # } # } # } The model again produces a probability distribution: Level Probability 0 — Low 0.01 1 — Medium 0.26 2 — High 0.72 Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index . For a random variable X X X representing the level, the expectation is: E [ X ] = ∑ i = 0 K − 1 i p i \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E [ X ] = i = 0 ∑ K − 1 ​ i p i ​ For our example: E [ X ] = 0 ( 0.01 ) + 1 ( 0.26 ) + 2 ( 0.72 ) = 1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E [ X ] = 0 ( 0.01 ) + 1 ( 0.26 ) + 2 ( 0.72 ) = 1.7 The reported score is therefore 1.7 . We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli). Let Y Y Y represent a binary outcome: Y ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( p ) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y ∼ Bernoulli ( p ) where P ( Y = 1 ) = p , P ( Y = 0 ) = 1 − p . P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P ( Y = 1 ) = p , P ( Y = 0 ) = 1 − p . If the model returns: { "type" : "noul" , "noul" : 0.92 } it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No. The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it. Confidence: How certain is the model? So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score. The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that. For a Choice with K K K options, the confidence is: p max ⁡ − 1 K 1 − 1 K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1 − K 1 ​ p m a x ​ − K 1 ​ ​ where p max ⁡ p_{\max} p m a x ​ is the largest predicted probability. The intuition here is: A uniform distribution has confidence 0. p max ⁡ = 1 K p_{\max} = \frac{1}{K} p m a x ​ = K 1 ​ . This means the model estimates that all choices are equally likely. A distribution concentrated entirely on one option has confidence 1. p max ⁡ = 1 p_{\max} = 1 p m a x ​ = 1 The larger the winning probability relative to a uniform distribution, the higher the confidence. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558. Please refund me." , "refund" ), ( "My package has not arrived." , "shipping" ), ( "The application crashes when I open it." , "technical" ), ( "I want my money back." , "refund" ), ( "Where is my delivery?" , "shipping" ), ( "I cannot log into my account." , "technical" ), ] options = { "refund" : "Billing issues and refunds" , "shipping" : "Orders and deliveries" , "technical" : "Software and account issues" , } def preprocess ( text, label ): request = { "state" : text, "questions" : { "category" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Classify the support request." , "criteria" : options, } }, } (inputs, questions), = model.decision_config.prepare_inputs( request, tokenizer ) inputs[ "marks" ] = inputs[ "marks" ].unsqueeze( 0 ) inputs[ "num_options" ] = torch.tensor([[ len (questions[ 0 ].options)]]) inputs[ "question_type_ids" ] = torch.tensor([[ 1 ]]) # choice inputs[ "labels" ] = torch.tensor( [questions[ 0 ].options.index(label)] ) return inputs dataset = [preprocess(text, label) for text, label in examples] class DecisionTrainer ( Trainer ): def compute_loss ( self, model, inputs, return_outputs= False , **kwargs ): inputs = inputs.copy() labels = inputs.pop( "labels" ) logits = model(**inputs) logits = logits.unsqueeze( 0 ) # [3] -> [1, 3] loss = F.cross_entropy(logits. float (), labels) return (loss, logits) if return_outputs else loss trainer = DecisionTrainer( model=model, args=TrainingArguments( output_dir= "./decision-toy" , max_steps= 30 , per_device_train_batch_size= 1 , learning_rate= 1e-3 , logging_steps= 5 , save_strategy= "no" , report_to= "none" , remove_unused_columns= False , ), train_dataset=dataset, data_collator= lambda batch: batch[ 0 ], ) trainer.train() First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL ( huggingface/trl#8040 ), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open. If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head. Final thoughts Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software . Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions. items.content: Back to Articles BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model Team Article Published November 11, 2026 Upvote 36 +30 Milan Gritta milangritta Follow qvac Jihye Back happy-jihye Follow qvac JinUk, Cho jucho2725 Follow qvac ohjoon kwon joooon Follow qvac Patrik Lambert patrik-lambert Follow qvac Mathias Buus mafintosh Follow qvac Amril Nurman Nurman Follow qvac Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models. Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information. 🤗 Model (safetensors) | 📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4) Figure 1: BotPsy-0.8B significantly outperforms its base model and leads five of the six tool-use and agentic benchmarks, including against Qwen3.5-2B-Think (2.5× its size); only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think edge ahead. Figure 2: Knowledge: tool-use training preserved and improved BotPsy's general knowledge compared to similarly sized models, though overall knowledge still scales primarily with parameter count. Instruction following: BotPsy excels at following explicit instructions and multi-turn tasks, though its performance drops as instructions accumulate and lags in lower-resource languages. Copyright Complaints We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement. Key Highlights Benchmark results Twice the performance of its base model: BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic capability of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think on key benchmarks: BFCL v4 rises from 23.4 to 44.0, ACEBench from 30.1 to 58.7, and τ-bench from 23.2 to 51.5 (mean of the retail, telecom and banking subsets). Best agent in its category: BotPsy outperforms leading models in the ≤1.2B-parameter weight class (Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think, LFM2.5-1.2B-Think, MiniCPM5-1B-Think) on all six tool-use and agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4, ACEBench, τ-bench, ToolSandbox, Claw-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus. Outperforms its larger sibling: BotPsy has the highest score of all models tested on five of the six benchmarks, beating Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size, on BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 37.7), ACEBench (58.7 vs 55.4), τ-bench (51.5 vs 46.5), ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 41.2) and BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 2.8). Only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think lead (48.9 vs 46.5). Model capabilities More reliable in multi-turn workflows: On τ²-bench, where the agent must hold a long customer conversation, follow a strict policy, and act on the customer's behalf, it scores 82.5 in telecom, ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think (69.3). On BFCL v4's multi-turn tasks, it rises from 7.5 to 46.1 over its base, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8). Grouped by application, its multi-step scores lead all models tested in commerce and services (58.3 vs 47.4 for the next best, Qwen3.5-2B-Think) and in device and system management (46.1 vs 31.9). Knows when (not) to call tools: An agent that acts must also know when not to act. On BFCL v4's hallucination tests, which check that the model declines when no appropriate tool exists, BotPsy scores 86.1, the highest of all models tested. On ACEBench's special cases, where the request is incomplete, contains wrong parameters, or cannot be served by the given tools, it scores 51.3, up from 13.7 for its base model. Follows instructions while preserving knowledge: BotPsy specializes in tool use while preserving general skills. Instruction following improves sharply, with IFEval rising from 59.7 to 90.8 and IFBench from 22.0 to 55.9, the highest IFBench score of all models tested. General knowledge also improves, with GPQA Diamond rising from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9. On all four benchmarks, BotPsy outperforms every other model of 1.2B parameters or fewer that we tested. Safety, efficiency and deployment Safer than leading models in its category: In automated red-teaming across six harm categories, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time, compared with 36% for its base model. This is the lowest rate of all models of up to 1.2B parameters (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35%; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 47%). Under prompt-injection attacks, which matter most for agents that read untrusted tool outputs, the unsafe rate drops from 46% for its base model to 31%. More efficient reasoning and less looping: On questions that all five models answer correctly, BotPsy reaches the answer with about 3× fewer reasoning tokens than its base model on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563) and 2.7× fewer on MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105). Across all IFBench attempts, its rate of getting stuck in repetitive reasoning loops falls from 22.9% to 1.4%, and runs that hit the 32k-token limit fall from 28.3% to 0.2%. Shorter, more decisive reasoning should reduce latency on-device. Open-source and ready to use: BotPsy will be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license for research and educational use. It will be available in three precisions (bf16, Q8, Q4), as Hugging Face safetensors and as GGUF files for the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp. Broader Vision Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps users entirely in control of their digital lives. Methodology BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3). Figure 3: BotPsy training recipe. The student goes through four stages. Three specialist Qwen3.5-4B teachers, each RL-trained for one skill, guide it during the distillation stage. Training procedure: four stages, three types of feedback Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards. Learning from demonstrations (SFT) We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called. Learning from teachers (MOPD) Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4). Figure 4: Mean score of each capability group after each training stage. SFT boosts tool use but pushes knowledge and instruction following below the base model; distillation brings both back above base, and the RL stages add further gains on all three. Learning from rules and environments (RL stages) Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth. The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling. Data composition Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use. Figure 5: Approximate training-data composition per stage, grouped by capability. Results Tool use & agents BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5). Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× BFCL v4¹ 44.0 23.4 37.7 28.1 22.8 ACEBench² 58.7 30.1 55.4 39.4 24.5 τ-bench³ 51.5 23.2 46.5 6.5 28.8 Claw-Eval⁴ 46.5 39.3 48.9 31.6 31.0 BrowseComp-Plus⁵ 4.5 1.9 2.8 0.2 0.8 ToolSandbox⁶ 64.6 30.5 41.2 45.7 28.1 Average 45.0 24.7 38.8 25.3 22.7 Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined ; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Knowledge Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× GPQA Diamond⁷ 38.1 33.2 59.9 35.0 15.8 MMLU-Pro⁸ 48.9 41.6 65.5 39.4 40.0 Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Instruction following BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× IFEval⁹ 90.8 59.7 80.0 85.6 78.4 IFBench⁹ 55.9 22.0 40.9 33.9 40.6 Multi-IF¹⁰ 67.2 43.2 66.9 68.2 53.4 Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Multi-turn conversations The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1). Figure 6: Multi-turn agentic tasks: BFCL v4 multi-turn, ACEBench Agent, τ²-bench (retail, telecom) and τ³-bench (banking). BotPsy leads four of the five benchmarks; on τ³-banking, every model stays below 5. Weak spots BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8). Where it works: app-level performance breakdown BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ. Single tool calls work well everywhere Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70). Figure 7: Mean per-scenario score (0–100, higher is better) by app group, for simple (left) and complex (right) scenarios. n gives the number of simple / complex scenarios in each group; the bottom row is the unweighted mean of the seven groups. The largest gains are in multi-step tasks On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks. Multi-step information retrieval is the weak spot Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14). Inference efficiency BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer. Figure 8: Accuracy against reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench. Tokens are measured on questions all five models answer correctly; accuracy is over all questions. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each. Figure 9: Pass rate against assistant turns per solved task on τ²-bench retail and telecom. Turns are measured on tasks all five models solve; pass rate is over all tasks. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9): τ²-retail: 10.7 turns, against 11.7 for the base (9% fewer) and 10.6 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. τ²-telecom: 13.1 turns, against 17.6 for the base (26% fewer) and 13.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think (5% fewer). It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks. Intended Use and Limitations BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty . BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models. Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information. 🤗 Model (safetensors) | 📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4) Figure 1: BotPsy-0.8B significantly outperforms its base model and leads five of the six tool-use and agentic benchmarks, including against Qwen3.5-2B-Think (2.5× its size); only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think edge ahead. Figure 2: Knowledge: tool-use training preserved and improved BotPsy's general knowledge compared to similarly sized models, though overall knowledge still scales primarily with parameter count. Instruction following: BotPsy excels at following explicit instructions and multi-turn tasks, though its performance drops as instructions accumulate and lags in lower-resource languages. Copyright Complaints We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement. Key Highlights Benchmark results Twice the performance of its base model: BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic capability of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think on key benchmarks: BFCL v4 rises from 23.4 to 44.0, ACEBench from 30.1 to 58.7, and τ-bench from 23.2 to 51.5 (mean of the retail, telecom and banking subsets). Best agent in its category: BotPsy outperforms leading models in the ≤1.2B-parameter weight class (Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think, LFM2.5-1.2B-Think, MiniCPM5-1B-Think) on all six tool-use and agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4, ACEBench, τ-bench, ToolSandbox, Claw-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus. Outperforms its larger sibling: BotPsy has the highest score of all models tested on five of the six benchmarks, beating Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size, on BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 37.7), ACEBench (58.7 vs 55.4), τ-bench (51.5 vs 46.5), ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 41.2) and BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 2.8). Only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think lead (48.9 vs 46.5). Model capabilities More reliable in multi-turn workflows: On τ²-bench, where the agent must hold a long customer conversation, follow a strict policy, and act on the customer's behalf, it scores 82.5 in telecom, ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think (69.3). On BFCL v4's multi-turn tasks, it rises from 7.5 to 46.1 over its base, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8). Grouped by application, its multi-step scores lead all models tested in commerce and services (58.3 vs 47.4 for the next best, Qwen3.5-2B-Think) and in device and system management (46.1 vs 31.9). Knows when (not) to call tools: An agent that acts must also know when not to act. On BFCL v4's hallucination tests, which check that the model declines when no appropriate tool exists, BotPsy scores 86.1, the highest of all models tested. On ACEBench's special cases, where the request is incomplete, contains wrong parameters, or cannot be served by the given tools, it scores 51.3, up from 13.7 for its base model. Follows instructions while preserving knowledge: BotPsy specializes in tool use while preserving general skills. Instruction following improves sharply, with IFEval rising from 59.7 to 90.8 and IFBench from 22.0 to 55.9, the highest IFBench score of all models tested. General knowledge also improves, with GPQA Diamond rising from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9. On all four benchmarks, BotPsy outperforms every other model of 1.2B parameters or fewer that we tested. Safety, efficiency and deployment Safer than leading models in its category: In automated red-teaming across six harm categories, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time, compared with 36% for its base model. This is the lowest rate of all models of up to 1.2B parameters (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35%; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 47%). Under prompt-injection attacks, which matter most for agents that read untrusted tool outputs, the unsafe rate drops from 46% for its base model to 31%. More efficient reasoning and less looping: On questions that all five models answer correctly, BotPsy reaches the answer with about 3× fewer reasoning tokens than its base model on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563) and 2.7× fewer on MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105). Across all IFBench attempts, its rate of getting stuck in repetitive reasoning loops falls from 22.9% to 1.4%, and runs that hit the 32k-token limit fall from 28.3% to 0.2%. Shorter, more decisive reasoning should reduce latency on-device. Open-source and ready to use: BotPsy will be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license for research and educational use. It will be available in three precisions (bf16, Q8, Q4), as Hugging Face safetensors and as GGUF files for the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp. Broader Vision Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps users entirely in control of their digital lives. Methodology BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3). Figure 3: BotPsy training recipe. The student goes through four stages. Three specialist Qwen3.5-4B teachers, each RL-trained for one skill, guide it during the distillation stage. Training procedure: four stages, three types of feedback Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards. Learning from demonstrations (SFT) We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called. Learning from teachers (MOPD) Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4). Figure 4: Mean score of each capability group after each training stage. SFT boosts tool use but pushes knowledge and instruction following below the base model; distillation brings both back above base, and the RL stages add further gains on all three. Learning from rules and environments (RL stages) Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth. The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling. Data composition Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use. Figure 5: Approximate training-data composition per stage, grouped by capability. Results Tool use & agents BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5). Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× BFCL v4¹ 44.0 23.4 37.7 28.1 22.8 ACEBench² 58.7 30.1 55.4 39.4 24.5 τ-bench³ 51.5 23.2 46.5 6.5 28.8 Claw-Eval⁴ 46.5 39.3 48.9 31.6 31.0 BrowseComp-Plus⁵ 4.5 1.9 2.8 0.2 0.8 ToolSandbox⁶ 64.6 30.5 41.2 45.7 28.1 Average 45.0 24.7 38.8 25.3 22.7 Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined ; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Knowledge Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× GPQA Diamond⁷ 38.1 33.2 59.9 35.0 15.8 MMLU-Pro⁸ 48.9 41.6 65.5 39.4 40.0 Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Instruction following BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× IFEval⁹ 90.8 59.7 80.0 85.6 78.4 IFBench⁹ 55.9 22.0 40.9 33.9 40.6 Multi-IF¹⁰ 67.2 43.2 66.9 68.2 53.4 Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Multi-turn conversations The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1). Figure 6: Multi-turn agentic tasks: BFCL v4 multi-turn, ACEBench Agent, τ²-bench (retail, telecom) and τ³-bench (banking). BotPsy leads four of the five benchmarks; on τ³-banking, every model stays below 5. Weak spots BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8). Where it works: app-level performance breakdown BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ. Single tool calls work well everywhere Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70). Figure 7: Mean per-scenario score (0–100, higher is better) by app group, for simple (left) and complex (right) scenarios. n gives the number of simple / complex scenarios in each group; the bottom row is the unweighted mean of the seven groups. The largest gains are in multi-step tasks On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks. Multi-step information retrieval is the weak spot Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14). Inference efficiency BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer. Figure 8: Accuracy against reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench. Tokens are measured on questions all five models answer correctly; accuracy is over all questions. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each. Figure 9: Pass rate against assistant turns per solved task on τ²-bench retail and telecom. Turns are measured on tasks all five models solve; pass rate is over all tasks. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9): τ²-retail: 10.7 turns, against 11.7 for the base (9% fewer) and 10.6 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. τ²-telecom: 13.1 turns, against 17.6 for the base (26% fewer) and 13.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think (5% fewer). It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks. Intended Use and Limitations BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty . BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.
