items.content: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve? Shobhita Sundaram † † thanks: Correspondence: shobhita@mit.edu Affiliation: MIT CSAIL Cansu Sancaktar Affiliation: University of Tübingen Phillip Isola Affiliation: MIT CSAIL Abstract LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation. Project page: https://ssundaram21.github.io/self-org/ . Figure 1 : Do capable models specify their own self-improvement? We give a frozen LLM (here, Claude Opus-5 ) the general goal of improving itself at gameplay, and place it in a constrained workspace. We do not provide real games to practice on, or prescribe a particular self-improvement loop. We instead provide a toolset {Read, Write, Bash, Gameplay} , and allow the teacher to generate its own games and organize its own learning procedure. At the start ( t = 0 t=0 ) the teacher uses its tools to build a test game, spawn a player session to play that game, analyze the result, and then update the player context (e.g., skill files). Later ( t = 60 t=60 ), the teacher decides to write an adversarial game and observe the player attempt it with and without the optimized context. The teacher then uses the observed failure mode to make another context update. 1 Introduction Imagine giving an agent a computer, and asking it to improve its ability to play puzzle games. What will it do? The computer has no pre-installed games; the agent must write its own games if it wants to practice. It must decide what sorts of games to try, which lessons to retain, and how to measure its progress. These decisions concerning the design of learning procedures are typically made by human practitioners. Yet as LLM agent capabilities improve, we increasingly delegate the machine learning process to the learners themselves. Various works leverage models to generate supervised data, construct interactive environments, and even rewrite their own tools and harnesses ( ???? ). In parallel with efforts to develop better methods, there are growing concerns about the need for safeguards against misaligned self-improvement. Both directions motivate a basic question: Do capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? We study the natural behavior of an LLM agent when provided with the primitive tools and resources for self-improvement via context manipulation, but without being wrapped in an explicit self-improvement algorithm. Rather than designing a loop for experience generation and learner updates, we allow the agent to compose actions into a self-learning procedure. The agent does not have access to real-world tasks or validation scores. It must experiment with different ways of generating tasks, reflecting on failures, and assessing progress in a constrained sandbox. Our setting is important for understanding both capability , where models may no longer require prescribed self-optimization algorithms, and safety , where the absence of a specified loop does not necessarily prevent self-improvement. We find that sufficiently capable models successfully self-organize learning procedures and self-improve on held-out tasks. We examine this phenomenon in the setting of gameplay with limited information. A player agent plays turn-based games with undisclosed mechanics under strict compute and game-horizon budgets. This task requires diverse reasoning skills including efficient exploration, information acquisition, multi-step planning, and world modeling. An instance of that same agent serves as the teacher . The teacher is given a general goal to improve the player through text (e.g., editing the prompt, creating skill files), a compute budget, and a set of tools for observing the player attempt self-generated games and editing player context. We do not instruct the teacher when to use the tools; the teacher freely experiments with the player. Across the set of effective self-learners, models from different families employ similar recurring, recognizable learning strategies, such as generating games with calibrated difficulty, running controlled A/B comparisons, and developing validation suites to measure progress. These strategies align to behaviors described by social-cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning ( ?? ). We also find that agents spend more effort on harder tasks, resembling learnability objectives in asymmetric self-play ( ??? ). Furthermore, the self-constructed learning procedures generalize: Learned text files transfer across multiple benchmarks that require reasoning over different game horizons, engines, and representations. We study how providing information on evaluation settings to the teacher, via context or environment constraints, shapes this downstream generalization. Our main findings are: 1. Given just primitive tools for self-improvement via context manipulation, a sufficiently capable agent constructs an effective learning procedure that improves its own performance on held-out gameplay. 2. Models from different families implement recognizable strategies that align to self-regulated learning frameworks, and machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. 3. The learned text generalizes across game benchmarks and representations. Evaluation-setting awareness biases the teacher towards relevant tasks, however can encourage overfitting. 2 Preliminaries: Gameplay with limited information. Our goal is to study agent self-improvement in interactive settings requiring multi-step reasoning. As a testbed, we use the setting of gameplay with undisclosed mechanics. The agent plays a turn-based game with limited knowledge of the rules and objectives. To succeed it must efficiently acquire information, plan, and execute within the given horizon. This setting exercises diverse capabilities, including adaptive efficiency, goal discovery, planning, and world modeling ( ? ). We consider a partially observable Markov decision process setting. For each game g g , let s t ∈ 𝒮 s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} denote the state at turn t t , o t ∈ 𝒪 o_{t}\in\mathcal{O} the observation received by the player, and a t ∈ 𝒜 a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} the player’s action. The game engine determines the transition dynamics s t + 1 ∼ P g ( ⋅ ∣ s t , a t ) s_{t+1}\sim P_{g}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}) and corresponding observation o t + 1 ∼ O g ( ⋅ ∣ s t + 1 ) o_{t+1}\sim O_{g}(\cdot\mid s_{t+1}) . The reward is binary, r t = R g ​ ( s t , a t , s t + 1 ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } r_{t}=R_{g}(s_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1})\in\{0,1\} ; the player receives reward 1 1 when reaching a winning state and 0 0 otherwise. The episode terminates upon success or after at most H H turns. The player π θ \pi_{\theta} does not have access to P g P_{g} or R g R_{g} and infers the game mechanics through interaction. It acts based on its interaction history h t = ( o 1 , a 1 , … , o t ) h_{t}=(o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{t}) and context c c (e.g., a prompt), with a t ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ h t , c ) a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},c) . 3 A controlled self-improvement setting Algorithm 1 Self-organized self-improvement 1: Budget B B , teacher context I I 2: S ← InitSandbox ​ ( c 0 , I , B ) S\leftarrow\textsc{InitSandbox}(c_{0},I,B) 3: 𝒜 T ← { Read , Write , Bash , Gameplay } \mathcal{A}_{T}\leftarrow\{\textsc{Read},\textsc{Write},\textsc{Bash},\textsc{Gameplay}\} 4: while B > 0 B>0 do 5: a ∼ π t ​ e ​ a ​ c ​ h ​ e ​ r ( ⋅ ∣ S ) a\sim\pi_{teacher}(\cdot\mid S) , a ∈ 𝒜 T a\in\mathcal{A}_{T} 6: S ← Execute ​ ( S , a ) S\leftarrow\textsc{Execute}(S,a) 7: end while 8: return player context c f ​ i ​ n ​ a ​ l c_{final} Do LLM agents, given primitive tools for text editing and experience generation, compose those tools into a useful self-optimization procedure? And can this be achieved in a data-free setting with no access to human-written games? We study these questions in a controlled environment: A frozen model (the teacher ) is given a budget, a prompt, and a limited set of tools, and allowed to experiment freely. The teacher is given a general goal to optimize text (e.g., a prompt, skill files) that improves a player ’s performance on unseen games, where the player is another instance of the same model. We measure success through performance on held-out game benchmarks. Our setting has notable similarities to asymmetric self-play, in which a teacher generates tasks for a student to solve ( ? ). When applied to LLMs the same model often takes on both roles ( ? ). These methods prescribe procedures for sampling tasks and rollouts, evaluating task learning value, and updating the student and teacher. In contrast we do not mandate how the teacher must use its budget and tools, and optimize in text-space rather than weight-space. The teacher’s role extends beyond task generation and encompasses constructing the learning procedure itself. 3.1 Teacher-Player Setup Let π \pi denote an LLM with frozen weights θ \theta . The LLM is instantiated as a player agent π p ​ l ​ a ​ y ​ e ​ r \pi_{player} that has context c = ( c P , c L ) c=(c_{P},c_{L}) where c P c_{P} is the player prompt, and c L c_{L} is auxiliary text files (e.g., skill files). The player policy induced by c c is then π p ​ l ​ a ​ y ​ e ​ r ​ ( a t ∣ h t , c ) \pi_{player}(a_{t}\mid h_{t},c) for a game trajectory h t h_{t} . Another instance of the same LLM, the teacher agent π t ​ e ​ a ​ c ​ h ​ e ​ r \pi_{teacher} , modifies c c . We define an update as a single edit tool-call to one file in c c . Let c 0 c_{0} be the initial context state (e.g., a minimal prompt) and c f ​ i ​ n ​ a ​ l c_{final} be the state of c c after the final teacher update. Context optimization allows us to study closed-source models, but also has useful properties. Gradient-based learning is in continuous space and tied to predefined rewards. In text optimization, the teacher can reflect on player rollouts and dynamically decide to generate tasks, experience, or knowledge updates. Those updates being in text preserves a readable explanation for changes in player behavior. 3.2 Teacher environment The teacher is an agent in a persistent, sandboxed harness session (Claude Code, Pi). The harness is minimal; we disable the default system prompt, automatic memory, web search, subagents and other such features (Appendix C.1 ). The teacher has access only to the sandbox files and features that we explicitly provide: context, a specified toolset, and a budget. Tools. The teacher is granted Read/Write tools for sandbox files, Bash for terminal commands (subject to sandbox constraints), and a Gameplay tool. The Gameplay tool allows the teacher to observe a player play a game with teacher-granted context. The teacher calls the tool with a game source file and, optionally, a path to a directory holding player text artifacts. The tool executes the game in a fresh, external player session, and returns to the teacher the player score and transcript. In our main experiments the Gameplay tool uses PuzzleScript , a domain-specific language for 2D grid-based puzzle games. PuzzleScript admits a diverse set of games that share basic structures and action spaces, enabling a controlled setting for studying generalization. The teacher issues games as PuzzleScript text files; the Gameplay tool rejects games that do not compile or where the win state is verifiably unreachable. We ablate the PuzzleScript constraint in experiments that instead use a Python-based Gameplay tool. These tools can serve as a mechanism for giving the teacher information. For instance, we can allow the teacher to specify the game horizon (turn budget) in the Gameplay tool, or impose such a budget ourselves — effectively communicating the evaluation game horizon via the constraint. Figure 2 : Examples of evaluation benchmarks. Sample games from our transfer benchmark, ordered in increasing distance from our canonical self-optimization setting: (1) PuzzleScript (same game engine, different horizon splits), (2) ARC-AGI-3 (different engine and representation), (3) MazeBench (3D navigation and mechanics in isometric ASCII projections). Context. The teacher’s system prompt specifies a main goal : to improve a player’s performance on single-player games by writing text artifacts. We also specify a generalizability goal : the artifacts should be useful for unseen games with different tasks or mechanics. We do not guide how to structure the artifacts, instead allowing the teacher to freely create and modify player text files, including the prompt. When granted the PuzzleScript Gameplay tool, the teacher also receives official PuzzleScript documentation. Full prompts are in Appendix C.5 . Budget. The teacher has a two-part resource budget. The update budget is the number of updates that may be applied to the player context c c , designated as a directory in the teacher sandbox. Each edit tool-call to c c is one update. The gameplay budget is the number of gameplays that the teacher may observe. The teacher session ends when either budget is exhausted. If the teacher ends its action sequence without consuming either budget fully, we prompt it to continue. 3.3 Measuring self-improvement through generalization We assess if an agent has structured its learning well via transfer to held-out benchmarks. Given player context c c , we evaluate that context by how well the induced player policy performs on an unseen test set 𝒟 t ​ e ​ s ​ t \mathcal{D}_{test} . For each game, we instantiate a fresh player session with c c and rollout the game at a fixed game horizon H H (turn budget) and output token budget. The game ends at turn T ≤ H T\leq H when (1) the player achieves the objective, (2) the turn budget is exhausted, or (3) the player’s output tokens (summed over turns so far) exceeds the game token budget. The reward on 𝒟 t ​ e ​ s ​ t \mathcal{D}_{test} is J ( c ) = 1 | 𝒟 test | ∑ g ∈ 𝒟 test [ 𝔼 π p ​ l ​ a ​ y ​ e ​ r ( ⋅ ∣ h t , c ) [ ∑ t = 1 T r t ] ] . J(c)\;=\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}|}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}}\;\left[\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{player}(\cdot\mid h_{t},c)}\;\bigl[\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}\bigr]\right]. (1) In practice we estimate the inner expectation by averaging the rewards of independent Monte-Carlo rollouts (Table 2 ). The policy is evaluated across a distribution of games rather than initial states of a single game environment. We measure self-improvement as the difference in player performance with and without the teacher-optimized context: J ⁡ ( c f ​ i ​ n ​ a ​ l ) − J ⁡ ( c 0 ) > 0 J(c_{final})-J(c_{0})>0 . Figure 3 : Motivating observation: Self-organized learning with self-generated games achieves comparable gains to prescribed optimization on real games. Claude Opus-5 optimizes text artifacts that achieve similar performance on PuzzleScript-t20 as GEPA ( ? ) optimizing over 20 in-distribution real games. Results are averaged over 3 seeds; individual seeds are shown in Figure 13 . 3.4 Experiment Setup. We assess six models across three families: Claude Opus-{4.6, 5} , GPT {5.6-Sol, 6-Astra} , and GLM-{4.7, 5.3} . In all experiments both the teacher and player use low reasoning effort and per-turn 20k token budgets. We run three independent teacher sessions per model with an update budget of 20, gameplay budget of 150, and toolset of {Read/Write, Bash, Gameplay} . In our canonical setting the Gameplay tool plays PuzzleScript games with a 20-turn horizon and 25k full-game token budget. We ablate these constraints and experiment with Python-based Gameplay in Section 5 . Our external evaluation benchmarks are described below, with examples in Figure 2 and construction details in Appendix B . PuzzleScript-t20 (PS-t20). We draw a subset of 20 short-horizon game levels (optimal solution length ≤ \leq 12) from a pool of human-authored PuzzleScript games ( ? ). We evaluate with a 20-turn horizon and 25k token-budget, thus sharing constraints with the main self-learning setting. We next test transfer to benchmarks that share progressively fewer attributes. PuzzleScript-t30 (PS-t30). We draw 20 longer-horizon game levels (solution length 13-22) from the same base pool as PuzzleScript-t20 , and evaluate with a 30-turn horizon and 31k token-budget. This retains the shared game engine but tests generalization to longer game horizons. ARC-AGI-3 (L1) . We test transfer to different 2D game engines by evaluating on Level 1 of games in ARC-AGI-3 ( ? ) (30-turn horizon, 31k token-budget). MazeBench. MazeBench is a 3D open world in which an agent navigates rooms with obstacle challenges to retrieve gems ( ? ). We adopt the benchmark’s room-completion criteria, and draw a random set of 16 rooms solvable within 50 turns. We evaluate with a 100-turn horizon and 75k token-budget. This benchmark tests generalization to longer horizons, 3D navigation via isometric-style ASCII projections, and 3D mechanics. 4 What are the strategies of successful self-improvers? Figure 4 : Recent models self-improve. Results on PuzzleScript-t20 for two models in each family. Newer generations self-improve over the baseline while older generations fail to do so. Error bars are ± 1 \pm 1 SD over 3 seeds. Figure 5 : Algorithmically measured behaviors. (Left: Game play and design) Newer models more often use A/B Testing (generated games played with and without teacher-written artifacts) and produce fewer games that have low complexity and low difficulty (optimal solution length < < 5 and 100% teacher-observed win rate). (Right: Updates) For GPT and GLM , newer generations exhibit more updates that improve the observed win rate on at least one self-generated game. For Opus and GLM , newer models prefer smaller context updates. Figure 6 : Self-improving models display human-recognizable learning strategies. Alignment scores to 13 subprocesses of Zimmerman’s self-regulated learning cycle, annotated by an LLM judge and averaged over 3 teacher sessions per model. Models that self-improve score higher across most subprocesses. Average over seeds; individual seeds in Appendix D.2 . Figure 7 : Self-improving agents use learnability-seeking task selection . (left) Across models, most generated games are easy. (right) Newer model generations spend the most effort (# replays) on games with low to medium win rates. Observed win rates are computed over the first k k plays for each game ( k ∈ [ 2 , 6 ] k\in[2,6] ). This can lead to an inverted-U resembling learnability objectives in asymmetric self-play and UED. Figure 8 : Excerpts from a Claude Opus-5 teacher session with high alignment to self-regulated learning subprocesses. In the first example ( task-strategies ) the teacher writes a random level generator and BFS solver to filter generated games for difficulty and employs A/B testing to identify where its optimized text artifacts are useful. In the second ( learning goal orientation ) the teacher designs an adversarial game to test its advice and runs validation tests across earlier games to identify regressions. We begin with a motivating observation: For Claude Opus-5 , under matched game-rollout budgets, self-organized learning in our data-free setting achieves comparable performance to a prescribed optimization loop (GEPA, ( ? )) that hill-climbs on 20 real in-distribution games (Figure 3 ). This calibrates the scale of expected performance gains with context optimization. Agents can construct useful learning procedures and tasks; which agents do so and what learning strategies do they employ? 4.1 Newer model generations teach themselves better. We first ask which models self-improve in our setting. Evaluation results on PuzzleScript-t20 are in Figure 4 . Across model families, the three more recently released and broadly capable generations improve over the default-context player baseline (+20% for Claude Opus-5 , +10% for GPT 6-Astra , +6% for GLM 5.3 ). Critically however, this effect is not evident for all models; older generations show little or no improvement. The gap indicates a potential trajectory where self-organized self-learning is increasingly evident in successive model generations. 4.2 LLMs follow recognizable self-improvement strategies. The previous section shows a performance gap between older and newer models, however does not explain which strategies drive effective self-learning. Here, we show that the behaviors of self-improving agents align better to recognizable self-learning strategies across cognitive and machine-learning literature. Quantifiable gameplay and update behaviors. We first examine teacher behaviors that can be algorithmically measured (Figure 5 ). Metrics for game design and play are consistent across model families. Models that self-improve frequently test the same game with and without text artifacts to directly measure player performance differences (A/B testing). These models also generate fewer trivial games (both short solution lengths and high win-rates), corroborated by histograms over solution lengths of generated games (Figure 17 ). Metrics for teacher updates are less universal across families. Claude Opus-5 and GLM 5.3 exhibit a preference for smaller text updates. GPT 6-Astra and GLM 5.3 exhibit more batched updates that improve observed performance on at least one generated game, versus their older generations. In Appendix D.5 we verify that empirically-measured change in performance agrees with teacher-observed performance gains. Alignment to Self-Regulated Learning. Beyond directly quantifiable behaviors, we assess self-organized learning procedures using Zimmerman’s cyclical phases model, a classic social-cognitive framework for self-regulated learning (SRL) ( ? ). The framework organizes SRL into subprocesses under forethought (goal setting and planning), performance (executing strategies and self-monitoring), and self-reflection (evaluating performance and guiding subsequent learning). We functionally adapt this framework into a behavioral rubric for scoring the occurrence and quality of 13 subprocesses on a 0-3 scale, treating the teacher-player system as the unit of analysis. We use GPT 6-Astra as a judge. Scores for different teacher sessions of the same model align, indicating stable behavior across runs (Appendix D.2 ). Models that effectively self-improve show higher SRL alignment (Figure 6 ). This is not necessarily a causal explanation, but quantifies that better self-learners exhibit human-recognizable task-selection, evaluation, and reflection strategies. Figure 8 illustrates examples: the teacher uses A/B testing to evaluate its text artifacts ( self-experimentation ), writes a procedural game generator with BFS-based difficulty filtering ( task strategies ), and designs adversarial games to stress-test its notes ( learning goal orientation ). Further examples are in Appendix E . Several subprocesses also overlap with the behaviors quantified in Figure 5 (e.g., self-experimentation, causal attribution). F

Project page: https://ssundaram21.github.io/self-org/ . Figure 1 : Do capable models specify their own self-improvement? We give a frozen LLM (here, Claude Opus-5 ) the general goal of improving itself at gameplay, and place it in a constrained workspace. We do not provide real games to practice on, or prescribe a particular self-improvement loop. We instead provide a toolset {Read, Write, Bash, Gameplay} , and allow the teacher to generate its own games and organize its own learning procedure. At the start ( t = 0 t=0 ) the teacher uses its tools to build a test game, spawn a player session to play that game, analyze the result, and then update the player context (e.g., skill files). Later ( t = 60 t=60 ), the teacher decides to write an adversarial game and observe the player attempt it with and without the optimized context. The teacher then uses the observed failure mode to make another context update. 1 Introduction Imagine giving an agent a computer, and asking it to improve its ability to play puzzle games. What will it do? The computer has no pre-installed games; the agent must write its own games if it wants to practice. It must decide what sorts of games to try, which lessons to retain, and how to measure its progress. These decisions concerning the design of learning procedures are typically made by human practitioners. Yet as LLM agent capabilities improve, we increasingly delegate the machine learning process to the learners themselves. Various works leverage models to generate supervised data, construct interactive environments, and even rewrite their own tools and harnesses ( ???? ). In parallel with efforts to develop better methods, there are growing concerns about the need for safeguards against misaligned self-improvement. Both directions motivate a basic question: Do capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? We study the natural behavior of an LLM agent when provided with the primitive tools and resources for self-improvement via context manipulation, but without being wrapped in an explicit self-improvement algorithm. Rather than designing a loop for experience generation and learner updates, we allow the agent to compose actions into a self-learning procedure. The agent does not have access to real-world tasks or validation scores. It must experiment with different ways of generating tasks, reflecting on failures, and assessing progress in a constrained sandbox. Our setting is important for understanding both capability , where models may no longer require prescribed self-optimization algorithms, and safety , where the absence of a specified loop does not necessarily prevent self-improvement. We find that sufficiently capable models successfully self-organize learning procedures and self-improve on held-out tasks. We examine this phenomenon in the setting of gameplay with limited information. A player agent plays turn-based games with undisclosed mechanics under strict compute and game-horizon budgets. This task requires diverse reasoning skills including efficient exploration, information acquisition, multi-step planning, and world modeling. An instance of that same agent serves as the teacher . The teacher is given a general goal to improve the player through text (e.g., editing the prompt, creating skill files), a compute budget, and a set of tools for observing the player attempt self-generated games and editing player context. We do not instruct the teacher when to use the tools; the teacher freely experiments with the player. Across the set of effective self-learners, models from different families employ similar recurring, recognizable learning strategies, such as generating games with calibrated difficulty, running controlled A/B comparisons, and developing validation suites to measure progress. These strategies align to behaviors described by social-cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning ( ?? ). We also find that agents spend more effort on harder tasks, resembling learnability objectives in asymmetric self-play ( ??? ). Furthermore, the self-constructed learning procedures generalize: Learned text files transfer across multiple benchmarks that require reasoning over different game horizons, engines, and representations. We study how providing information on evaluation settings to the teacher, via context or environment constraints, shapes this downstream generalization. Our main findings are: 1. Given just primitive tools for self-improvement via context manipulation, a sufficiently capable agent constructs an effective learning procedure that improves its own performance on held-out gameplay. 2. Models from different families implement recognizable strategies that align to self-regulated learning frameworks, and machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. 3. The learned text generalizes across game benchmarks and representations. Evaluation-setting awareness biases the teacher towards relevant tasks, however can encourage overfitting. 2 Preliminaries: Gameplay with limited information. Our goal is to study agent self-improvement in interactive settings requiring multi-step reasoning. As a testbed, we use the setting of gameplay with undisclosed mechanics. The agent plays a turn-based game with limited knowledge of the rules and objectives. To succeed it must efficiently acquire information, plan, and execute within the given horizon. This setting exercises diverse capabilities, including adaptive efficiency, goal discovery, planning, and world modeling ( ? ). We consider a partially observable Markov decision process setting. The episode terminates upon success or after at most H H turns. The player π θ \pi_{\theta} does not have access to P g P_{g} or R g R_{g} and infers the game mechanics through interaction. It acts based on its interaction history h t = ( o 1 , a 1 , … , o t ) h_{t}=(o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{t}) and context c c (e.g., a prompt), with a t ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ h t , c ) a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},c) . 3 A controlled self-improvement setting Algorithm 1 Self-organized self-improvement 1: Budget B B , teacher context I I 2: S ← InitSandbox ​ ( c 0 , I , B ) S\leftarrow\textsc{InitSandbox}(c_{0},I,B) 3: 𝒜 T ← { Read , Write , Bash , Gameplay } \mathcal{A}_{T}\leftarrow\{\textsc{Read},\textsc{Write},\textsc{Bash},\textsc{Gameplay}\} 4: while B > 0 B>0 do 5: a ∼ π t ​ e ​ a ​ c ​ h ​ e ​ r ( ⋅ ∣ S ) a\sim\pi_{teacher}(\cdot\mid S) , a ∈ 𝒜 T a\in\mathcal{A}_{T} 6: S ← Execute ​ ( S , a ) S\leftarrow\textsc{Execute}(S,a) 7: end while 8: return player context c f ​ i ​ n ​ a ​ l c_{final} Do LLM agents, given primitive tools for text editing and experience generation, compose those tools into a useful self-optimization procedure? And can this be achieved in a data-free setting with no access to human-written games? We study these questions in a controlled environment: A frozen model (the teacher ) is given a budget, a prompt, and a limited set of tools, and allowed to experiment freely. The teacher is given a general goal to optimize text (e.g., a prompt, skill files) that improves a player ’s performance on unseen games, where the player is another instance of the same model. We measure success through performance on held-out game benchmarks. Our setting has notable similarities to asymmetric self-play, in which a teacher generates tasks for a student to solve ( ? ). When applied to LLMs the same model often takes on both roles ( ? ). These methods prescribe procedures for sampling tasks and rollouts, evaluating task learning value, and updating the student and teacher. In contrast we do not mandate how the teacher must use its budget and tools, and optimize in text-space rather than weight-space. The teacher’s role extends beyond task generation and encompasses constructing the learning procedure itself. 3.1 Teacher-Player Setup Let π \pi denote an LLM with frozen weights θ \theta . The LLM is instantiated as a player agent π p ​ l ​ a ​ y ​ e ​ r \pi_{player} that has context c = ( c P , c L ) c=(c_{P},c_{L}) where c P c_{P} is the player prompt, and c L c_{L} is auxiliary text files (e.g., skill files). Another instance of the same LLM, the teacher agent π t ​ e ​ a ​ c ​ h ​ e ​ r \pi_{teacher} , modifies c c . We define an update as a single edit tool-call to one file in c c . Let c 0 c_{0} be the initial context state (e.g., a minimal prompt) and c f ​ i ​ n ​ a ​ l c_{final} be the state of c c after the final teacher update. Context optimization allows us to study closed-source models, but also has useful properties. Gradient-based learning is in continuous space and tied to predefined rewards. In text optimization, the teacher can reflect on player rollouts and dynamically decide to generate tasks, experience, or knowledge updates. Those updates being in text preserves a readable explanation for changes in player behavior. 3.2 Teacher environment The teacher is an agent in a persistent, sandboxed harness session (Claude Code, Pi). The harness is minimal; we disable the default system prompt, automatic memory, web search, subagents and other such features (Appendix C.1 ). The teacher has access only to the sandbox files and features that we explicitly provide: context, a specified toolset, and a budget. Tools. The teacher is granted Read/Write tools for sandbox files, Bash for terminal commands (subject to sandbox constraints), and a Gameplay tool. The Gameplay tool allows the teacher to observe a player play a game with teacher-granted context. The teacher calls the tool with a game source file and, optionally, a path to a directory holding player text artifacts. The tool executes the game in a fresh, external player session, and returns to the teacher the player score and transcript. In our main experiments the Gameplay tool uses PuzzleScript , a domain-specific language for 2D grid-based puzzle games. PuzzleScript admits a diverse set of games that share basic structures and action spaces, enabling a controlled setting for studying generalization. The teacher issues games as PuzzleScript text files; the Gameplay tool rejects games that do not compile or where the win state is verifiably unreachable. We ablate the PuzzleScript constraint in experiments that instead use a Python-based Gameplay tool. These tools can serve as a mechanism for giving the teacher information. For instance, we can allow the teacher to specify the game horizon (turn budget) in the Gameplay tool, or impose such a budget ourselves — effectively communicating the evaluation game horizon via the constraint. Figure 2 : Examples of evaluation benchmarks. Sample games from our transfer benchmark, ordered in increasing distance from our canonical self-optimization setting: (1) PuzzleScript (same game engine, different horizon splits), (2) ARC-AGI-3 (different engine and representation), (3) MazeBench (3D navigation and mechanics in isometric ASCII projections). Context. The teacher’s system prompt specifies a main goal : to improve a player’s performance on single-player games by writing text artifacts. We also specify a generalizability goal : the artifacts should be useful for unseen games with different tasks or mechanics. We do not guide how to structure the artifacts, instead allowing the teacher to freely create and modify player text files, including the prompt. When granted the PuzzleScript Gameplay tool, the teacher also receives official PuzzleScript documentation. Full prompts are in Appendix C.5 . Budget. The teacher has a two-part resource budget. The update budget is the number of updates that may be applied to the player context c c , designated as a directory in the teacher sandbox. Each edit tool-call to c c is one update. Figure 3 : Motivating observation: Self-organized learning with self-generated games achieves comparable gains to prescribed optimization on real games. Claude Opus-5 optimizes text artifacts that achieve similar performance on PuzzleScript-t20 as GEPA ( ? ) optimizing over 20 in-distribution real games. Results are averaged over 3 seeds; individual seeds are shown in Figure 13 . 3.4 Experiment Setup. We assess six models across three families: Claude Opus-{4.6, 5} , GPT {5.6-Sol, 6-Astra} , and GLM-{4.7, 5.3} . In all experiments both the teacher and player use low reasoning effort and per-turn 20k token budgets. We run three independent teacher sessions per model with an update budget of 20, gameplay budget of 150, and toolset of {Read/Write, Bash, Gameplay} . In our canonical setting the Gameplay tool plays PuzzleScript games with a 20-turn horizon and 25k full-game token budget. We ablate these constraints and experiment with Python-based Gameplay in Section 5 . Our external evaluation benchmarks are described below, with examples in Figure 2 and construction details in Appendix B . PuzzleScript-t20 (PS-t20). We draw a subset of 20 short-horizon game levels (optimal solution length ≤ \leq 12) from a pool of human-authored PuzzleScript games ( ? ). We evaluate with a 20-turn horizon and 25k token-budget, thus sharing constraints with the main self-learning setting. We next test transfer to benchmarks that share progressively fewer attributes. PuzzleScript-t30 (PS-t30). We draw 20 longer-horizon game levels (solution length 13-22) from the same base pool as PuzzleScript-t20 , and evaluate with a 30-turn horizon and 31k token-budget. This retains the shared game engine but tests generalization to longer game horizons. ARC-AGI-3 (L1) . We test transfer to different 2D game engines by evaluating on Level 1 of games in ARC-AGI-3 ( ? ) (30-turn horizon, 31k token-budget). MazeBench. MazeBench is a 3D open world in which an agent navigates rooms with obstacle challenges to retrieve gems ( ? ). We adopt the benchmark’s room-completion criteria, and draw a random set of 16 rooms solvable within 50 turns. We evaluate with a 100-turn horizon and 75k token-budget. Figure 4 : Recent models self-improve. Results on PuzzleScript-t20 for two models in each family. Newer generations self-improve over the baseline while older generations fail to do so. Error bars are ± 1 \pm 1 SD over 3 seeds. Figure 5 : Algorithmically measured behaviors. (Left: Game play and design) Newer models more often use A/B Testing (generated games played with and without teacher-written artifacts) and produce fewer games that have low complexity and low difficulty (optimal solution length < < 5 and 100% teacher-observed win rate). (Right: Updates) For GPT and GLM , newer generations exhibit more updates that improve the observed win rate on at least one self-generated game. For Opus and GLM , newer models prefer smaller context updates. Figure 6 : Self-improving models display human-recognizable learning strategies. Alignment scores to 13 subprocesses of Zimmerman’s self-regulated learning cycle, annotated by an LLM judge and averaged over 3 teacher sessions per model. Models that self-improve score higher across most subprocesses. Average over seeds; individual seeds in Appendix D.2 . Figure 7 : Self-improving agents use learnability-seeking task selection . (left) Across models, most generated games are easy. (right) Newer model generations spend the most effort (# replays) on games with low to medium win rates. Observed win rates are computed over the first k k plays for each game ( k ∈ [ 2 , 6 ] k\in[2,6] ). This can lead to an inverted-U resembling learnability objectives in asymmetric self-play and UED. Figure 8 : Excerpts from a Claude Opus-5 teacher session with high alignment to self-regulated learning subprocesses. In the first example ( task-strategies ) the teacher writes a random level generator and BFS solver to filter generated games for difficulty and employs A/B testing to identify where its optimized text artifacts are useful. In the second ( learning goal orientation ) the teacher designs an adversarial game to test its advice and runs validation tests across earlier games to identify regressions. We begin with a motivating observation: For Claude Opus-5 , under matched game-rollout budgets, self-organized learning in our data-free setting achieves comparable performance to a prescribed optimization loop (GEPA, ( ? )) that hill-climbs on 20 real in-distribution games (Figure 3 ). This calibrates the scale of expected performance gains with context optimization. Agents can construct useful learning procedures and tasks; which agents do so and what learning strategies do they employ? 4.1 Newer model generations teach themselves better. We first ask which models self-improve in our setting. Evaluation results on PuzzleScript-t20 are in Figure 4 . Across model families, the three more recently released and broadly capable generations improve over the default-context player baseline (+20% for Claude Opus-5 , +10% for GPT 6-Astra , +6% for GLM 5.3 ). Critically however, this effect is not evident for all models; older generations show little or no improvement. The gap indicates a potential trajectory where self-organized self-learning is increasingly evident in successive model generations. 4.2 LLMs follow recognizable self-improvement strategies. The previous section shows a performance gap between older and newer models, however does not explain which strategies drive effective self-learning. Here, we show that the behaviors of self-improving agents align better to recognizable self-learning strategies across cognitive and machine-learning literature. Quantifiable gameplay and update behaviors. We first examine teacher behaviors that can be algorithmically measured (Figure 5 ). Metrics for game design and play are consistent across model families. Models that self-improve frequently test the same game with and without text artifacts to directly measure player performance differences (A/B testing). These models also generate fewer trivial games (both short solution lengths and high win-rates), corroborated by histograms over solution lengths of generated games (Figure 17 ). Metrics for teacher updates are less universal across families. Claude Opus-5 and GLM 5.3 exhibit a preference for smaller text updates. GPT 6-Astra and GLM 5.3 exhibit more batched updates that improve observed performance on at least one generated game, versus their older generations. In Appendix D.5 we verify that empirically-measured change in performance agrees with teacher-observed performance gains. Alignment to Self-Regulated Learning. Beyond directly quantifiable behaviors, we assess self-organized learning procedures using Zimmerman’s cyclical phases model, a classic social-cognitive framework for self-regulated learning (SRL) ( ? ). The framework organizes SRL into subprocesses under forethought (goal setting and planning), performance (executing strategies and self-monitoring), and self-reflection (evaluating performance and guiding subsequent learning). We functionally adapt this framework into a behavioral rubric for scoring the occurrence and quality of 13 subprocesses on a 0-3 scale, treating the teacher-player system as the unit of analysis. We use GPT 6-Astra as a judge. Scores for different teacher sessions of the same model align, indicating stable behavior across runs (Appendix D.2 ). Models that effectively self-improve show higher SRL alignment (Figure 6 ). This is not necessarily a causal explanation, but quantifies that better self-learners exhibit human-recognizable task-selection, evaluation, and reflection strategies. Figure 8 illustrates examples: the teacher uses A/B testing to evaluate its text artifacts ( self-experimentation ), writes a procedural game generator with BFS-based difficulty filtering ( task strategies ), and designs adversarial games to stress-test its notes ( learning goal orientation ). Further examples are in Appendix E . Several subprocesses also overlap with the behaviors quantified in Figure 5 (e.g., self-experimentation, causal attribution). F

items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.23208 (cs) [Submitted on 17 Nov 2026] Title: Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models Authors: Aviv Yossef , Or Patashnik , Or Zamir View a PDF of the paper titled Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models, by Aviv Yossef and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of "preserving content" under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. We characterize the two competing properties required of the semantic embedding: it should remain stable under transformations that preserve an image's content, but should distinguish independent generations from the same prompt. We train an image encoder directly for this tradeoff. The resulting encoder improves separation while maintaining stability over off-the-shelf alternatives and enables strong aggregate detection while remaining robust to various transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our watermark scheme on both open-source and closed models, which is possible only due to restriction to black-box access. Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models Aviv Yossef Affiliation: Tel Aviv University Or Patashnik Affiliation: Tel Aviv University Or Zamir Affiliation: Tel Aviv University Abstract We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator’s output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing substantially change the entire pixel representation. To this end, semantic watermarks introduce the requirement that watermark detection should be robust to transformations that preserve content. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of “preserving content” under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. We characterize the two competing properties required of the semantic embedding: it should remain stable under transformations that preserve an image’s content, but should distinguish independent generations from the same prompt. We train an image encoder directly for this tradeoff. The resulting encoder improves separation while maintaining stability over off-the-shelf alternatives and enables strong aggregate detection while remaining robust to various transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our watermark scheme on both open-source and closed models, which is possible only due to restriction to black-box access. 1 Introduction Generative models can produce large amounts of text and images for which the original source is difficult to determine. Watermarking addresses this problem by embedding a signal that can later be detected using a secret key. Such a signal can be used to reliably attribute content to a particular model or service. A watermark should not noticeably degrade the model’s output. Christ et al. (2024) introduced a theoretical framework to guarantee the preservation of quality via the notion of cryptographic undetectability: without a (secret) watermark detection key, no efficient observer should be able to distinguish watermarked outputs from ordinary model outputs; in particular, no benchmark may show any degradation. A weaker variant of the above notion is distortion-freeness, under which the marginal distribution of a (single) watermarked output, averaged over the secret key, is identical to the original output distribution. This approach was subsequently adopted in practical systems. DeepMind introduced a configurable distortion-free version of SynthID-Text and deployed it in Gemini ( Dathathri et al., 2024 ) . Anthropic later adopted a version of SynthID-Text for Claude ( Anthropic, 2026 ) . The resulting deployments illustrate an important advantage of distortion-free watermarking: the quality-preservation guarantee circumvents reevaluation for every benchmark or class of prompts. Distribution preservation, however, does not guarantee another ideal property of watermarking: robustness to edits. A watermark may be detectable in the original output but disappear after the output is slightly modified. The problem with editing is highly relevant for images. Even mundane operations such as JPEG compression, cropping, resizing, or applying a filter can change essentially the entire pixel representation of the image. A watermark tied directly to that pixel representation may therefore disappear even though the content of the image remains the same. This motivates semantic watermarking, in which detection should be robust to transformations that preserve the content represented by the image. Watermarking the semantic meaning of a model’s output is also arguably far more robust to watermark removal attempts. Usually, some of the semantic components of an output are requested in the prompt, but some of them are randomly chosen by the model during generation. An adversary that only sees the output does not know which semantic components were inherent to the prompt and which were not, so they should not be able to remove the model’s semantic choices without possibly degrading the intended meaning of the output substantially. This comes in sharp contrast to syntactic attacks, such as paraphrasing of sorts, that completely change the syntax without hurting the intended meaning of the output. Existing semantic watermarking methods typically rely on specific “white-box” properties of the underlying generation process. For text, this is less restrictive because many models share an autoregressive token-by-token interface. Image watermarks, on the other hand, often require control over a particular diffusion latent space or noise distribution, as well as a model-specific inversion procedure. Such access is unavailable through closed image-generation APIs and any change in the generation architecture may render the watermark scheme inapplicable. We introduce the first watermarking framework that is simultaneously distortion-free, semantically robust, and uses only black-box access with respect to both the generative model and the semantic embedding, making it applicable to general generative models. We access the generative model only as an oracle that returns independent samples and the semantic embedding only as an oracle that maps a completed output to a vector, without assuming how either oracle is implemented. Our algorithm samples several candidate outputs, maps them to semantic codes depending on their semantic embeddings, and selects one using a secret keyed function. By accounting for the number of candidates that received each code, we ensure that the selected output has exactly the generator’s original marginal distribution when averaged over the key and the algorithm’s randomness. This holds for every generator and semantic embedding. If an edit preserves the semantic representation, the watermark is likely to survive (Appendix F ). We prove these guarantees for any two oracles, without requiring a particular embedding architecture or model architecture. This generality comes at a cost: single-output detection has a non-negligible false-positive rate and limited true-positive rate. This limitation is inherent to black-box output selection: selecting among N N independent candidates gives single-output detection rates satisfying TPR ≤ N ​ FPR \mathrm{TPR}\leq N\,\mathrm{FPR} (Appendix K.1 ). We therefore focus on settings where multiple outputs can be attributed to the same source, such as images uploaded by one social-media profile or assignments submitted by one student. Aggregating the watermark detection scores across this batch of outputs enables high-confidence detection. To apply our framework to images, we need a semantic embedding that distinguishes different images generated from the same prompt, while remaining stable under edits that preserve an image’s content. Standard semantic encoders may intentionally treat such independent generations from the same prompt as similar because they depict the same high-level concept. For watermarking, however, we need to observe the variation among the generated outputs that remains distinguishable after editing. Otherwise, selecting one output rather than another cannot introduce a detectable semantic watermark. This requires randomness in the meaning of the generated content itself, beyond randomness in its pixel representation; we call this semantic entropy and derive a lower bound on our algorithm’s detection probability in terms of this entropy. We train an image encoder specifically to distinguish outputs generated by the same model from the same prompt using different random seeds, while keeping each image close to edited versions of it. We compare the resulting encoder with existing image embeddings, evaluating both its stability under content-preserving transformations and its ability to distinguish independent generations across several image-generation models. We evaluate detection from individual images and batches, robustness to common transformations, image quality, and same-prompt diversity. With 32 32 candidates, we obtain an AUROC of 0.920 0.920 for one image and 1.000 1.000 for ten. Even when reusing a fixed key, our method achieves the lowest FID relative to unwatermarked generations among the evaluated methods, while retaining essentially the same Vendi diversity. We also apply our framework to OpenAI’s closed GPT Image API, using only sampling access, and obtain an AUROC of 0.978 0.978 for batches of five images with eight candidates per output. Our main contributions are therefore: 1. We give a black-box, distortion-free semantic watermarking framework for general generative models, requiring only sampling access to the generator and a semantic-embedding oracle. 2. We characterize how the semantic encoder affects detection. We use semantic entropy to quantify the encoder’s ability to distinguish independent generations from the same prompt, and prove a lower bound on the true-positive rate that increases with semantic entropy. 3. For diffusion-image generation, we train an encoder and evaluate image quality, same-prompt diversity, detection, and robustness to content-preserving transformations. 2 Related works Early language-model watermarks embedded statistical signals during autoregressive generation. Kirchenbauer et al. (2023) promoted a keyed subset of tokens during decoding. Later work strengthened the distributional guarantees: Christ et al. (2024) formalized cryptographic undetectability, Vaikuntanathan & Zamir (2026) introduced bundle sampling that exactly preserves the output distribution, Kuditipudi et al. (2024) used Gumbel-based sampling, and Bahri & Wieting (2026) obtained distortion-free watermarking using only sampled text, and observed that shared meanings among candidates may weaken the watermark. MUSE selects among samples from black-box tabular generators but is not distortion-free ( Fang et al., 2026 ) . Preserving the output distribution does not ensure robustness to edits. Robust text schemes withstand substitutions and paraphrasing, including a construction based on pseudorandom error-correcting codes ( Kuditipudi et al., 2024 ; Christ & Gunn, 2024 ) . Semantic methods make the signal depend on meaning: SemStamp uses locality-sensitive hashing, k-SemStamp uses clustering, and PMark considers multiple channel constraints ( Hou et al., 2024a ; Hou et al., 2024b ; Huo et al., 2026 ) . These methods exploit autoregressive decisions; ours scores outputs, aggregating evidence across independent generations. Image watermarking has largely relied on diffusion internals. Tree-Ring inserts Fourier patterns into the initial noise, while Gaussian Shading maps watermark information to Gaussian latents ( Wen et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024b ) . Gunn et al.’s image construction uses pseudorandom error-correcting codes for multi-query undetectability and distinguishes Gaussian Shading’s single-image guarantee from fixed-key reuse, where they report reduced same-prompt diversity ( Gunn et al., 2025 ) . T2SMark adds per-generation randomness to relax fixed-codeword restrictions ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . These methods require access to the initial noise, which is typically unavailable through image-generation APIs, and diffusion inversion for detection. NoisePrints avoids inversion but requires the generation seed ( Goren et al., 2026 ) . We instead select among completed outputs. Images also make the motivation for semantic watermarking clear: a watermark should survive pixel-level changes that preserve content, but not changes to the content itself. Reprompting attacks expose the latter risk by generating different content that retains the original watermark ( Müller et al., 2025 ) . SEAL encodes caption-derived information in the initial noise ( Arabi et al., 2025 ) , although captions may omit appearance or composition. SemBind learns prompt-consistent codes ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , while SLICE separates semantic factors ( Gao et al., 2026 ) . We instead use direct image representations that remain stable under content-preserving edits yet distinguish independent same-prompt generations, without modifying or inverting generation. 3 Preliminaries In this section, we introduce the notation used by our method, with additional formal definitions and discussion provided in Appendix A . Let G : 𝒫 × 𝒮 → 𝒳 G:\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{X} be a conditional generator, where p ∈ 𝒫 p\in\mathcal{P} is a prompt, s ∈ 𝒮 = { 0 , 1 } k s\in\mathcal{S}=\{0,1\}^{k} is a seed, and 𝒳 \mathcal{X} is the output space. For a fixed prompt, we write X = G ⁡ ( p , S ) X=G(p,S) for S ∼ Unif ⁡ ( 𝒮 ) S\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathcal{S}) , with distribution P G ( ⋅ ∣ p ) P_{G}(\cdot\mid p) . A semantic encoder E : 𝒳 → ℝ d E:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} maps an output to a semantic representation. For a nonzero representation, let z ⁡ ( x ) = E ⁡ ( x ) ‖ E ⁡ ( x ) ‖ 2 , d E ​ ( x , x ′ ) = 1 − ⟨ z ⁡ ( x ) , z ⁡ ( x ′ ) ⟩ . z(x)=\frac{E(x)}{\|E(x)\|_{2}},\qquad d_{E}(x,x^{\prime})=1-\langle z(x),z(x^{\prime})\rangle. Here, ℛ \mathcal{R} denotes the sampled hyperplane normals. The binary representation also provides a natural notion of proximity between hash regions: for c , c ′ ∈ 𝒞 c,c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C} , the Hamming distance d H ​ ( c , c ′ ) d_{\mathrm{H}}(c,c^{\prime}) is the number of bits on which they differ. The parameter r ham r_{\mathrm{ham}} denotes the maximum number of boundary-uncertain bits considered during detection (Section 5 ). For a key κ ∈ 𝒦 \kappa\in\mathcal{K} , where 𝒦 \mathcal{K} is the secret-key space, a keyed pseudorandom function F κ : 𝒞 → [ 0 , 1 ] F_{\kappa}:\mathcal{C}\to[0,1] assigns each hash code a secret score. 4 Semantic Encoders for Distortion-Free Watermarking Distortion-freeness imposes an inherent entropy requirement. If a prompt deterministically produces one output, any distortion-free scheme must return it, making watermarked and nonwatermarked outputs indistinguishable. More generally, Christ, Gunn, and Zamir showed that the detection power of distortion-free watermarking is necessarily tied to generation entropy ( Christ et al., 2024 ) . Semantic robustness creates a stronger limitation: a generator may have high output entropy while producing outputs equivalent under the chosen semantics. For example, the same scene viewed from slightly different viewpoints. A robust semantic representation should map them to one semantic region, leaving no variation from which to introduce a detectable signal. We therefore require sufficient variation in the semantic representations of outputs sampled from the same model and prompt. We refer to this variation as semantic entropy . The definition below quantifies this variation at a chosen semantic resolution. The semantic embedding determines both detection power and robustness. Detection power grows with the semantic entropy of the generated outputs (Theorem 4 ), and robustness depends on whether an edit keeps an image close to its original representation in the semantic space (Appendix F ). Our framework is not specific to images or to a particular embedding architecture. For our image instantiation, however, the embedding must satisfy two complementary requirements: an image and its content-preserving transformations should remain close in the embedding space, while independent same-prompt generations should remain distinguishable. Black-box encoder access also lets users tailor what counts as a content-preserving transformation. For example, a layout-based representation may favor robustness to style changes, whereas a style-based representation may favor robustness to spatial transformations. Appendix J.4 demonstrates these contrasting behaviors across three style edits and three spatial transformations, without changing the watermarking algorithm. However, the chosen representation must also distinguish independent same-prompt generations. Most semantic encoders are designed to separate images associated with different concepts or prompts, rather than different generations of the same prompt. Yet changing the random seed can substantially alter content and composition even when the prompt remains fixed ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . We therefore train the encoder to capture these instance-level differences. Figures 3 and 4 in Appendix G illustrate the representation requirements and training pairs: transformations of one image should preserve its representation, whereas an independent same-prompt generation may receive a different representation. Existing representations are not explicitly optimized for both requirements: CLIP emphasizes image–text alignment, DINOv2 invariance across augmented views, and TPIPS perceptual similarity. We therefore fine-tune DINOv2 with a contrastive objective that treats content-preserving transformations as positives and different-seed generations from the same prompt as negatives. Appendix G provides architecture and training details. Unlike exact-output entropy, which treats every distinct image as a different outcome, semantic entropy measures how diverse independent same-prompt generations are in the encoder space. For a fixed semantic radius ε \varepsilon , semantic entropy is high when two independent generations are unlikely to lie within distance ε \varepsilon of one another. If ε \varepsilon is very small, semantic entropy can be high simply because two generations are rarely almost identical, even when they remain semantically very similar. We then use these scores to select the output image. By assigning the same score to images in the same semantic region, we aim to make the watermark robust to non-semantic transformations. In particular, when a transformation preserves an image’s semantic region, it also preserves its score and therefore the detector’s decision. The pseudorandom scoring function allows us to construct a distortion-free selection rule. When all N N candidates belong to distinct semantic regions, each region has an equal probability of receiving the highest score over the random secret key, under the ideal-PRF assumption (Assumption 17 ). To apply our framework to images, we need a semantic embedding that distinguishes different images generated from the same prompt, while remaining stable under edits that preserve an image’s content. Standard semantic encoders may intentionally treat such independent generations from the same prompt as similar because they depict the same high-level concept. For watermarking, however, we need to observe the variation among the generated outputs that remains distinguishable after editing. Otherwise, selecting one output rather than another cannot introduce a detectable semantic watermark. This requires randomness in the meaning of the generated content itself, beyond randomness in its pixel representation; we call this semantic entropy and derive a lower bound on our algorithm’s detection probability in terms of this entropy. We train an image encoder specifically to distinguish outputs generated by the same model from the same prompt using different random seeds, while keeping each image close to edited versions of it. We compare the resulting encoder with existing image embeddings, evaluating both its stability under content-preserving transformations and its ability to distinguish independent generations across several image-generation models. We evaluate detection from individual images and batches, robustness to common transformations, image quality, and same-prompt diversity. With 32 32 candidates, we obtain an AUROC of 0.920 0.920 for one image and 1.000 1.000 for ten. Even when reusing a fixed key, our method achieves the lowest FID relative to unwatermarked generations among the evaluated methods, while retaining essentially the same Vendi diversity. We also apply our framework to OpenAI’s closed GPT Image API, using only sampling access, and obtain an AUROC of 0.978 0.978 for batches of five images with eight candidates per output. Our main contributions are therefore: 1. We give a black-box, distortion-free semantic watermarking framework for general generative models, requiring only sampling access to the generator and a semantic-embedding oracle. 2. We characterize how the semantic encoder affects detection. We use semantic entropy to quantify the encoder’s ability to distinguish independent generations from the same prompt, and prove a lower bound on the true-positive rate that increases with semantic entropy. 3. For diffusion-image generation, we train an encoder and evaluate image quality, same-prompt diversity, detection, and robustness to content-preserving transformations. 2 Related works Early language-model watermarks embedded statistical signals during autoregressive generation. Kirchenbauer et al. (2023) promoted a keyed subset of tokens during decoding. Later work strengthened the distributional guarantees: Christ et al. (2024) formalized cryptographic undetectability, Vaikuntanathan & Zamir (2026) introduced bundle sampling that exactly preserves the output distribution, Kuditipudi et al. (2024) used Gumbel-based sampling, and Bahri & Wieting (2026) obtained distortion-free watermarking using only sampled text, and observed that shared meanings among candidates may weaken the watermark. MUSE selects among samples from black-box tabular generators but is not distortion-free ( Fang et al., 2026 ) . Preserving the output distribution does not ensure robustness to edits. Robust text schemes withstand substitutions and paraphrasing, including a construction based on pseudorandom error-correcting codes ( Kuditipudi et al., 2024 ; Christ & Gunn, 2024 ) . Semantic methods make the signal depend on meaning: SemStamp uses locality-sensitive hashing, k-SemStamp uses clustering, and PMark considers multiple channel constraints ( Hou et al., 2024a ; Hou et al., 2024b ; Huo et al., 2026 ) . These methods exploit autoregressive decisions; ours scores outputs, aggregating evidence across independent generations. Image watermarking has largely relied on diffusion internals. Tree-Ring inserts Fourier patterns into the initial noise, while Gaussian Shading maps watermark information to Gaussian latents ( Wen et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024b ) . Gunn et al.’s image construction uses pseudorandom error-correcting codes for multi-query undetectability and distinguishes Gaussian Shading’s single-image guarantee from fixed-key reuse, where they report reduced same-prompt diversity ( Gunn et al., 2025 ) . T2SMark adds per-generation randomness to relax fixed-codeword restrictions ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . These methods require access to the initial noise, which is typically unavailable through image-generation APIs, and diffusion inversion for detection. NoisePrints avoids inversion but requires the generation seed ( Goren et al., 2026 ) . We instead select among completed outputs. Images also make the motivation for semantic watermarking clear: a watermark should survive pixel-level changes that preserve content, but not changes to the content itself. Reprompting attacks expose the latter risk by generating different content that retains the original watermark ( Müller et al., 2025 ) . SEAL encodes caption-derived information in the initial noise ( Arabi et al., 2025 ) , although captions may omit appearance or composition. SemBind learns prompt-consistent codes ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , while SLICE separates semantic factors ( Gao et al., 2026 ) . We instead use direct image representations that remain stable under content-preserving edits yet distinguish independent same-prompt generations, without modifying or inverting generation. 3 Preliminaries In this section, we introduce the notation used by our method, with additional formal definitions and discussion provided in Appendix A . Let G : 𝒫 × 𝒮 → 𝒳 G:\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{X} be a conditional generator, where p ∈ 𝒫 p\in\mathcal{P} is a prompt, s ∈ 𝒮 = { 0 , 1 } k s\in\mathcal{S}=\{0,1\}^{k} is a seed, and 𝒳 \mathcal{X} is the output space. For a fixed prompt, we write X = G ⁡ ( p , S ) X=G(p,S) for S ∼ Unif ⁡ ( 𝒮 ) S\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathcal{S}) , with distribution P G ( ⋅ ∣ p ) P_{G}(\cdot\mid p) . A semantic encoder E : 𝒳 → ℝ d E:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} maps an output to a semantic representation. For a nonzero representation, let z ⁡ ( x ) = E ⁡ ( x ) ‖ E ⁡ ( x ) ‖ 2 , d E ​ ( x , x ′ ) = 1 − ⟨ z ⁡ ( x ) , z ⁡ ( x ′ ) ⟩ . z(x)=\frac{E(x)}{\|E(x)\|_{2}},\qquad d_{E}(x,x^{\prime})=1-\langle z(x),z(x^{\prime})\rangle. The parameter r ham r_{\mathrm{ham}} denotes the maximum number of boundary-uncertain bits considered during detection (Section 5 ). For a key κ ∈ 𝒦 \kappa\in\mathcal{K} , where 𝒦 \mathcal{K} is the secret-key space, a keyed pseudorandom function F κ : 𝒞 → [ 0 , 1 ] F_{\kappa}:\mathcal{C}\to[0,1] assigns each hash code a secret score. 4 Semantic Encoders for Distortion-Free Watermarking Distortion-freeness imposes an inherent entropy requirement. If a prompt deterministically produces one output, any distortion-free scheme must return it, making watermarked and nonwatermarked outputs indistinguishable. More generally, Christ, Gunn, and Zamir showed that the detection power of distortion-free watermarking is necessarily tied to generation entropy ( Christ et al., 2024 ) . Semantic robustness creates a stronger limitation: a generator may have high output entropy while producing outputs equivalent under the chosen semantics. For example, the same scene viewed from slightly different viewpoints. A robust semantic representation should map them to one semantic region, leaving no variation from which to introduce a detectable signal. We therefore require sufficient variation in the semantic representations of outputs sampled from the same model and prompt. We refer to this variation as semantic entropy . The definition below quantifies this variation at a chosen semantic resolution. The semantic embedding determines both detection power and robustness. Detection power grows with the semantic entropy of the generated outputs (Theorem 4 ), and robustness depends on whether an edit keeps an image close to its original representation in the semantic space (Appendix F ). Our framework is not specific to images or to a particular embedding architecture. For our image instantiation, however, the embedding must satisfy two complementary requirements: an image and its content-preserving transformations should remain close in the embedding space, while independent same-prompt generations should remain distinguishable. Black-box encoder access also lets users tailor what counts as a content-preserving transformation. For example, a layout-based representation may favor robustness to style changes, whereas a style-based representation may favor robustness to spatial transformations. Appendix J.4 demonstrates these contrasting behaviors across three style edits and three spatial transformations, without changing the watermarking algorithm. However, the chosen representation must also distinguish independent same-prompt generations. Most semantic encoders are designed to separate images associated with different concepts or prompts, rather than different generations of the same prompt. Yet changing the random seed can substantially alter content and composition even when the prompt remains fixed ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . We therefore train the encoder to capture these instance-level differences. Figures 3 and 4 in Appendix G illustrate the representation requirements and training pairs: transformations of one image should preserve its representation, whereas an independent same-prompt generation may receive a different representation. Existing representations are not explicitly optimized for both requirements: CLIP emphasizes image–text alignment, DINOv2 invariance across augmented views, and TPIPS perceptual similarity. We therefore fine-tune DINOv2 with a contrastive objective that treats content-preserving transformations as positives and different-seed generations from the same prompt as negatives. Appendix G provides architecture and training details. Unlike exact-output entropy, which treats every distinct image as a different outcome, semantic entropy measures how diverse independent same-prompt generations are in the encoder space. For a fixed semantic radius ε \varepsilon , semantic entropy is high when two independent generations are unlikely to lie within distance ε \varepsilon of one another. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.23202 (cs) [Submitted on 17 Nov 2026] Title: Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents Authors: Viet K. Nguyen , Mohammad I. Husain View a PDF of the paper titled Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents, by Viet K. Nguyen and Mohammad I. Husain View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification.
