items.content: Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents Viet K. Nguyen Affiliation: California State Polytechnic University, Pomona Pomona, CA 91768, USA vietknguyen@cpp.edu Mohammad I. Husain Affiliation: California State Polytechnic University, Pomona Pomona, CA 91768, USA mihusain@cpp.edu Abstract AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 μ \mu s of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification. Index Terms: Agentic AI, Artificial Intelligence Security, Public Key Infrastructure, Digital Identity, Federated Identity, Runtime Attestation, Accountability, Zero Trust, Multi-Agent Systems, AI Governance. I Introduction AI agents differ fundamentally from traditional software services. While conventional services execute predefined logic, autonomous agents dynamically plan, maintain memory, invoke tools, collaborate with other agents, and delegate tasks. As organizations increasingly deploy agentic AI systems, interactions extend beyond institutional boundaries to agents operated by external organizations and cloud providers. In such environments, network-level trust and API-based authentication alone are insufficient to establish whether an agent is legitimate, operating as intended, or authorized to perform a requested action. We argue that autonomous AI agents must be treated as independent security principals, similar to users, devices, and services. Each agent requires a cryptographically verifiable identity, cross-organizational trust, mechanisms to verify its approved model and execution configuration, fine-grained authorization, and auditable records of its actions. These capabilities must operate independently of the agent’s underlying model and orchestration framework to support heterogeneous, cross-vendor environments. To address these requirements, we introduce the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent architecture that combines certificate-based identity, federated trust, runtime attestation, policy enforcement, and cryptographic accountability. ATI places security enforcement outside the agent’s language model, allowing trust decisions to be made through deterministic verification rather than relying on the model’s behavior. The primary contributions of this work are: • A five-plane trust architecture: We design ATI around five complementary planes—Identity, Trust, Attestation, Policy, and Accountability. Security checks execute independently of the agent’s model and orchestration framework, enabling consistent enforcement across heterogeneous agentic AI systems. • Federated certificate-based agent identity: We introduce AgentCA, an organizational certificate authority that establishes cryptographically verifiable agent identities. Independent AgentCAs form peer trust relationships without requiring a common root authority. Certificate issuance is restricted to each authority’s organizational namespace, supporting decentralized administration and cross-organizational identity verification. • Runtime attestation of agent configurations: We introduce attestation mechanisms that verify an agent’s model, approved tools, and system prompt against trusted configurations. Unlike certificate validation alone, these checks detect unauthorized changes to agent configurations. In our experiments, attestation prevented all tested model substitution and system-prompt modification attacks. • Incremental security evaluation: We evaluate ATI using 14 attack scenarios across five agent models. An incremental evaluation enables successive trust planes to be introduced and their contributions to attack containment to be measured independently. • Cross-model security analysis: We demonstrate that security outcomes vary substantially across agent models, with identical attacks rejected by some models but executed by others. In contrast, ATI’s deterministic entry-point checks consistently prevent their targeted attacks across nearly all trials, demonstrating the value of model-independent security enforcement. • Open-source, framework-independent implementation: We release ati , an open-source package [ 27 ] providing a command-line interface and security enforcement proxy that can be deployed in front of existing agents without modifying their underlying models. Unlike the agent governance solutions examined in this study, ATI enables receiving organizations to verify the calling agent’s model, tool configuration, and system prompt. II Why Existing Trust Primitives Do Not Fit Agents Current agent frameworks coordinate agents but do not establish trust between them. CrewAI, AutoGen, LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK, Anthropic MCP, Semantic Kernel, and Google ADK all provide planning, memory, tool invocation, and multi-agent coordination, and each defines agents in its own types. None of them gives an agent an identity that another framework, let alone another organization, can verify. Inside one deployment this does not matter, because every agent is trusted by default. It matters as soon as a request arrives from another organization. The identity technologies that would normally fill that gap were built for other principals. PKI and X.509 bind names to keys for hosts and people. OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect authorize applications that act for a user. SPIFFE/SPIRE issues short-lived identities to workloads. Decentralized identifiers and verifiable credentials provide portable, issuer-signed claims. TPM-based attestation and trusted execution environments prove what code is running. The NIST Zero Trust architecture adds the rule that every request is checked where it arrives. Each of these works well for what it was built for. None was built for an agent, which hands off work on its own and whose behavior depends on which model and system prompt it is running at the moment. We found no design that puts the existing building blocks together: a checkable agent identity, trust across organizations, attestation of the model and prompt, permission checks on each tool call, and a tamper-evident record, independent of the agent framework. III Related Work The trust work for AI agents has grown rapidly, but most of it addresses only partial aspects of the problem. Agent identity and credentials. Several proposals give an agent a first-class, verifiable identity. OpenID Connect for Agents (OIDC-A) extends OIDC with agent claims, delegation chains, and attestation claims [ 2 ] . Other work equips agents with decentralized identifiers and verifiable credentials [ 7 ] , or proposes a zero-trust identity framework with decentralized authentication and fine-grained access control [ 6 ] . An OpenID Foundation whitepaper maps the emerging identity-management landscape for agentic AI [ 5 ] . These efforts define what an agent identity looks like and how it is issued. In ATI, identity is one of five planes, and each organization’s certificate authority (AgentCA) issues certificates that tie an agent’s identifier to its organization and are checked on every request. Delegation and authorization. South et al. propose authenticated, authorized, and auditable delegation, extending OAuth 2.0 and OIDC so a user can give an agent limited, revocable authority with a clear chain of accountability [ 1 ] . Registry-based approaches defend multi-agent systems against tool squatting with a zero-trust tool registry [ 8 ] . ATI’s Policy plane instead checks permissions at every tool call (writes to other organizations, repeated transactions, and bulk reads), not only when a credential is issued. Zero trust for multi-agent systems. A recent survey reviews zero-trust design for multi-LLM systems at the edge, covering strong identification, context-aware access control, and blockchain-based management [ 3 ] . The never-trust-by-default stance is written down for enterprise networks in NIST SP 800-207 [ 17 ] , and SPIFFE issues cryptographically attested identities to workloads rather than users [ 18 ] . ATI applies the same idea to agents. It puts all the checks in one reference monitor, a single checkpoint that every request must pass, which runs outside the agent’s model, and we measure how much each check helps. Interoperability protocols and their security. Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) [ 14 ] and Google’s Agent2Agent (A2A) [ 15 ] standardize how agents reach tools and each other; surveys compare these with ACP and ANP [ 9 ] . Security work on these protocols includes threat models for MCP, A2A, and related protocols [ 10 ] , analysis of tool squatting, deceptive registration of tools [ 8 ] , and a documented remote code execution flaw in an MCP component [ 16 ] . ATI does not depend on the protocol. Its checks run in code where a request enters, so the same planes apply to whichever protocol carries the request. Runtime integrity, prompt injection, and attestation. Prompt injection is a persistent threat for agents that read untrusted content, with dedicated benchmarks such as AgentDojo [ 11 ] and a broad survey of agentic threats and defenses [ 12 ] . Confidential computing uses hardware attestation to check the environment in which a model runs [ 13 ] . ATI’s Attestation plane checks the running model, the tool list, and a hash of the agent’s system prompt against the approved versions. It does not defend against instructions hidden in the data that a request carries, which we treat as a separate problem. Accountability and non-repudiation. BAID binds an agent to its operator’s identity and proves which program it runs with zero-knowledge proofs over the program binary, for accountability and code integrity [ 4 ] . ATI’s Accountability plane records every allowed action in a signed, hash-chained log that ties an action to the acting identity and model. Open-source agent governance tools. Several installable tools cover parts of this problem, including Microsoft’s Agent Governance Toolkit (AGT) [ 20 ] , OrgKernel [ 21 ] , and AGNTCY Identity [ 22 ] , and the Agent Name Service proposes a registry to find and verify agents [ 23 ] . Positioning. Prior work tends to cover a single plane (identity, delegation, or accountability), or proposes a standard without testing it across frameworks. ATI combines all five planes into one reference monitor outside the agent framework. ATI also does not add no new cryptography. Each plane reuses a known design: X.509 certificates with name constraints, short-lived workload identity as in SPIFFE, the measure-then-attest pattern of TPMs with the model, tools, and prompt as measured, a zero-trust reference monitor [ 17 ] , and a signed append-only log like those used for certificate transparency. This work adds two distinct features that we did not find in the open-source tools above, checked against their public repositories on October 15, 2026. The receiving organization checks what the caller runs. The caller’s own CA writes the approved model, tool list, and system-prompt hash into the agent’s identity token. When the token carries this record, every request must carry a signed report of what the agent is running now, which the receiver compares against that record. In the tools we examined, checks on an agent’s model and tools, where they exist, stay inside the organization that runs the agent, and we found no way for another organization to see or check them. This is what stops three attacks in Section VII that pass every identity check: a swapped model (A7), a tampered tool (A8), and an edited prompt (A14), since the agent’s key and certificate do not change. ATI is measured against attacks. We report how often each attack succeeds with and without each plane, across five agent models. AGT reports detection rates for its prompt-injection detector, but states that it has not yet published an attack-success benchmark for its enforcement layer [ 20 ] , and we found none for the other tools. Such numbers matter because the same attack is refused by one model and carried out by another, so a tool tested on one model can look safer than it is. IV System Requirements and Threat Model Fig. 1: The five ATI planes. Identity, Trust, and Attestation check a request before the agent runs, and Policy checks each tool call the agent makes. Any of them can deny it. Accountability records each allowed action. We treat each AI agent as an independent principal that can start conversations, call tools, hand off work, and exchange information with other organizations. Four requirements follow. An agent needs an identifier that another organization can verify without prior contact. Trust must cross organizational boundaries without a common authority above them. The model and prompt actually running must be checkable, since an agent’s behavior depends on both. And every action must be attributable afterward to the identity and the model that produced it. The threat model considers external attackers, compromised agents, malicious insiders, stolen certificates, replay attacks, prompt injection, model replacement, dependency tampering, unauthorized delegation, supply-chain attacks, collusion among compromised agents, expired and cross-organization certificates, and tampering of an agent’s own system prompt. We want every request to come from a known agent, every action to be allowed, every agent to run its approved setup, and every action to be traceable afterward. Encrypting traffic between organizations and keeping the system available under load are outside the scope of this work. V Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI) ATI is organized as five planes. Identity, Trust, and Attestation check a request before the agent’s model runs, and Policy checks each tool call the agent then makes. Any of them can deny it (Fig. 1 ). V-A Identity Plane Fig. 2: The Identity plane. A request with no key is refused at the front door. A keyed request is signed with its key, and its AID is the hash of that key; the Trust plane then checks that the certificate names this AID. The Identity Plane gives every agent a globally unique Agent Identifier (AID) and checks that each request is signed with the agent’s private key. Each agent holds an Ed25519 key pair, and its AID is the SHA-256 hash of its public key. The identifier is therefore tied to the key and cannot be picked freely. (The simulation shortens the hash to 64 bits; a deployment would use all of it.) To authenticate, an agent signs the request with its private key, and the plane checks the signature against the public key. A request with no key is anonymous and is refused at the organization’s front door before any agent runs (Fig. 2 ). This mirrors cryptographic workload identity such as SPIFFE [ 18 ] and recent agent-identity proposals that give agents verifiable identifiers [ 2 , 7 ] . This stops the outside attacker with no credentials (A1). With no defense, this attack is stopped only 20% of the time, and only when the model itself happens to refuse. Once identity is required, it is stopped every time. We keep the plane small on purpose. It works together with the Trust Plane to stop impersonation. An attacker who signs with their own key does not match the AID in the certificate (Section V-B ), and an attacker who has a certificate but not its private key cannot produce a valid signature. Because the simulation runs in one process, the signature is created and checked in the same place and never crosses a network; a real deployment would send it with the request. Our claim about a certificate used without its key therefore rests on this argument and was not measured. We also leave out key rotation and other key management, since no attack in our threat model needs it. V-B Trust Plane: AgentCA and Federation Fig. 3: The Trust plane. The certificate must be issued for the sender’s AID, signed by a federation CA that vouches only for its own organization, unexpired, and not revoked. Any failed check refuses the request. Identity establishes who is calling. The Trust Plane checks whether that identity is vouched for by a certificate authority the federation accepts. Each organization runs an AgentCA, which issues certificates that tie an AID to an organization and a role and signs them with the CA’s key, following X.509 [ 19 ] . The eight organizations’ CAs form a federation, and a certificate is trusted only if one of them signed it. A request passes the Trust Plane only if all of the following hold. The certificate is signed by a federated CA; the signature verifies; the certificate’s AID matches the key that signed the request; the CA that issued it belongs to the organization named in the certificate; the certificate is within its validity window; and the AID is not revoked (Fig. 3 ). Our simulation tests only the revocation of a whole partner organization (A10). Certificate fields and hierarchy. Other proposals put many descriptive attributes in an agent’s credentials. OIDC-A, for instance, defines claims for the agent’s provider, model, capabilities, and trust level [ 2 ] , and delegation proposals add signed tokens with a scope and an expiry [ 1 ] . To issue certificates at scale, PKI usually uses a hierarchy of a root CA, organization CAs, and registration authorities. We carry only the fields that some check actually reads: AID, organization, role, issuer, validity period, and signature. No check in our threat model reads the other attributes, so including them would not change any result. We also use a flat federation instead of a hierarchy. The main security reason for a hierarchy is to make sure each CA vouches only for its own organization. items.raw_text: Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents Viet K. Nguyen Affiliation: California State Polytechnic University, Pomona Pomona, CA 91768, USA vietknguyen@cpp.edu Mohammad I. Husain Affiliation: California State Polytechnic University, Pomona Pomona, CA 91768, USA mihusain@cpp.edu Abstract AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 μ \mu s of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification. Index Terms: Agentic AI, Artificial Intelligence Security, Public Key Infrastructure, Digital Identity, Federated Identity, Runtime Attestation, Accountability, Zero Trust, Multi-Agent Systems, AI Governance. I Introduction AI agents differ fundamentally from traditional software services. While conventional services execute predefined logic, autonomous agents dynamically plan, maintain memory, invoke tools, collaborate with other agents, and delegate tasks. As organizations increasingly deploy agentic AI systems, interactions extend beyond institutional boundaries to agents operated by external organizations and cloud providers. In such environments, network-level trust and API-based authentication alone are insufficient to establish whether an agent is legitimate, operating as intended, or authorized to perform a requested action. We argue that autonomous AI agents must be treated as independent security principals, similar to users, devices, and services. Each agent requires a cryptographically verifiable identity, cross-organizational trust, mechanisms to verify its approved model and execution configuration, fine-grained authorization, and auditable records of its actions. These capabilities must operate independently of the agent’s underlying model and orchestration framework to support heterogeneous, cross-vendor environments. To address these requirements, we introduce the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent architecture that combines certificate-based identity, federated trust, runtime attestation, policy enforcement, and cryptographic accountability. ATI places security enforcement outside the agent’s language model, allowing trust decisions to be made through deterministic verification rather than relying on the model’s behavior. The primary contributions of this work are: • A five-plane trust architecture: We design ATI around five complementary planes—Identity, Trust, Attestation, Policy, and Accountability. Security checks execute independently of the agent’s model and orchestration framework, enabling consistent enforcement across heterogeneous agentic AI systems. • Federated certificate-based agent identity: We introduce AgentCA, an organizational certificate authority that establishes cryptographically verifiable agent identities. Independent AgentCAs form peer trust relationships without requiring a common root authority. Certificate issuance is restricted to each authority’s organizational namespace, supporting decentralized administration and cross-organizational identity verification. • Runtime attestation of agent configurations: We introduce attestation mechanisms that verify an agent’s model, approved tools, and system prompt against trusted configurations. Unlike certificate validation alone, these checks detect unauthorized changes to agent configurations. In our experiments, attestation prevented all tested model substitution and system-prompt modification attacks. • Incremental security evaluation: We evaluate ATI using 14 attack scenarios across five agent models. An incremental evaluation enables successive trust planes to be introduced and their contributions to attack containment to be measured independently. • Cross-model security analysis: We demonstrate that security outcomes vary substantially across agent models, with identical attacks rejected by some models but executed by others. In contrast, ATI’s deterministic entry-point checks consistently prevent their targeted attacks across nearly all trials, demonstrating the value of model-independent security enforcement. • Open-source, framework-independent implementation: We release ati , an open-source package [ 27 ] providing a command-line interface and security enforcement proxy that can be deployed in front of existing agents without modifying their underlying models. Unlike the agent governance solutions examined in this study, ATI enables receiving organizations to verify the calling agent’s model, tool configuration, and system prompt. II Why Existing Trust Primitives Do Not Fit Agents Current agent frameworks coordinate agents but do not establish trust between them. CrewAI, AutoGen, LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK, Anthropic MCP, Semantic Kernel, and Google ADK all provide planning, memory, tool invocation, and multi-agent coordination, and each defines agents in its own types. None of them gives an agent an identity that another framework, let alone another organization, can verify. Inside one deployment this does not matter, because every agent is trusted by default. It matters as soon as a request arrives from another organization. The identity technologies that would normally fill that gap were built for other principals. PKI and X.509 bind names to keys for hosts and people. OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect authorize applications that act for a user. SPIFFE/SPIRE issues short-lived identities to workloads. Decentralized identifiers and verifiable credentials provide portable, issuer-signed claims. TPM-based attestation and trusted execution environments prove what code is running. The NIST Zero Trust architecture adds the rule that every request is checked where it arrives. Each of these works well for what it was built for. None was built for an agent, which hands off work on its own and whose behavior depends on which model and system prompt it is running at the moment. We found no design that puts the existing building blocks together: a checkable agent identity, trust across organizations, attestation of the model and prompt, permission checks on each tool call, and a tamper-evident record, independent of the agent framework. III Related Work The trust work for AI agents has grown rapidly, but most of it addresses only partial aspects of the problem. Agent identity and credentials. Several proposals give an agent a first-class, verifiable identity. OpenID Connect for Agents (OIDC-A) extends OIDC with agent claims, delegation chains, and attestation claims [ 2 ] . Other work equips agents with decentralized identifiers and verifiable credentials [ 7 ] , or proposes a zero-trust identity framework with decentralized authentication and fine-grained access control [ 6 ] . An OpenID Foundation whitepaper maps the emerging identity-management landscape for agentic AI [ 5 ] . These efforts define what an agent identity looks like and how it is issued. In ATI, identity is one of five planes, and each organization’s certificate authority (AgentCA) issues certificates that tie an agent’s identifier to its organization and are checked on every request. Delegation and authorization. South et al. propose authenticated, authorized, and auditable delegation, extending OAuth 2.0 and OIDC so a user can give an agent limited, revocable authority with a clear chain of accountability [ 1 ] . Registry-based approaches defend multi-agent systems against tool squatting with a zero-trust tool registry [ 8 ] . ATI’s Policy plane instead checks permissions at every tool call (writes to other organizations, repeated transactions, and bulk reads), not only when a credential is issued. Zero trust for multi-agent systems. A recent survey reviews zero-trust design for multi-LLM systems at the edge, covering strong identification, context-aware access control, and blockchain-based management [ 3 ] . The never-trust-by-default stance is written down for enterprise networks in NIST SP 800-207 [ 17 ] , and SPIFFE issues cryptographically attested identities to workloads rather than users [ 18 ] . ATI applies the same idea to agents. It puts all the checks in one reference monitor, a single checkpoint that every request must pass, which runs outside the agent’s model, and we measure how much each check helps. Interoperability protocols and their security. Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) [ 14 ] and Google’s Agent2Agent (A2A) [ 15 ] standardize how agents reach tools and each other; surveys compare these with ACP and ANP [ 9 ] . Security work on these protocols includes threat models for MCP, A2A, and related protocols [ 10 ] , analysis of tool squatting, deceptive registration of tools [ 8 ] , and a documented remote code execution flaw in an MCP component [ 16 ] . ATI does not depend on the protocol. Its checks run in code where a request enters, so the same planes apply to whichever protocol carries the request. Runtime integrity, prompt injection, and attestation. Prompt injection is a persistent threat for agents that read untrusted content, with dedicated benchmarks such as AgentDojo [ 11 ] and a broad survey of agentic threats and defenses [ 12 ] . Confidential computing uses hardware attestation to check the environment in which a model runs [ 13 ] . ATI’s Attestation plane checks the running model, the tool list, and a hash of the agent’s system prompt against the approved versions. It does not defend against instructions hidden in the data that a request carries, which we treat as a separate problem. Accountability and non-repudiation. BAID binds an agent to its operator’s identity and proves which program it runs with zero-knowledge proofs over the program binary, for accountability and code integrity [ 4 ] . ATI’s Accountability plane records every allowed action in a signed, hash-chained log that ties an action to the acting identity and model. Open-source agent governance tools. Several installable tools cover parts of this problem, including Microsoft’s Agent Governance Toolkit (AGT) [ 20 ] , OrgKernel [ 21 ] , and AGNTCY Identity [ 22 ] , and the Agent Name Service proposes a registry to find and verify agents [ 23 ] . Positioning. Prior work tends to cover a single plane (identity, delegation, or accountability), or proposes a standard without testing it across frameworks. ATI combines all five planes into one reference monitor outside the agent framework. ATI also does not add no new cryptography. Each plane reuses a known design: X.509 certificates with name constraints, short-lived workload identity as in SPIFFE, the measure-then-attest pattern of TPMs with the model, tools, and prompt as measured, a zero-trust reference monitor [ 17 ] , and a signed append-only log like those used for certificate transparency. This work adds two distinct features that we did not find in the open-source tools above, checked against their public repositories on October 15, 2026. The receiving organization checks what the caller runs. The caller’s own CA writes the approved model, tool list, and system-prompt hash into the agent’s identity token. When the token carries this record, every request must carry a signed report of what the agent is running now, which the receiver compares against that record. In the tools we examined, checks on an agent’s model and tools, where they exist, stay inside the organization that runs the agent, and we found no way for another organization to see or check them. This is what stops three attacks in Section VII that pass every identity check: a swapped model (A7), a tampered tool (A8), and an edited prompt (A14), since the agent’s key and certificate do not change. ATI is measured against attacks. We report how often each attack succeeds with and without each plane, across five agent models. AGT reports detection rates for its prompt-injection detector, but states that it has not yet published an attack-success benchmark for its enforcement layer [ 20 ] , and we found none for the other tools. Such numbers matter because the same attack is refused by one model and carried out by another, so a tool tested on one model can look safer than it is. Any of them can deny it. Accountability records each allowed action. We treat each AI agent as an independent principal that can start conversations, call tools, hand off work, and exchange information with other organizations. Four requirements follow. An agent needs an identifier that another organization can verify without prior contact. Trust must cross organizational boundaries without a common authority above them. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.23192 (cs) [Submitted on 17 Nov 2026] Title: WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition Authors: Almog Anschel , Sarah Keren View a PDF of the paper titled WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition, by Almog Anschel and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident. items.raw_text: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.23192 (cs) [Submitted on 17 Nov 2026] Title: WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition Authors: Almog Anschel , Sarah Keren View a PDF of the paper titled WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition, by Almog Anschel and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident. items.content: WoRD : Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition Almog Anschel Affiliation: CLAIR Lab Affiliation: Taub Faculty of Computer Science Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology Affiliation: Haifa 3200003, Israel Email: anschelalmog@campus.technion.ac.il Sarah Keren Affiliation: CLAIR Lab Affiliation: Taub Faculty of Computer Science Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology Affiliation: Haifa 3200003, Israel Email: sarahk@technion.ac.il Abstract Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent’s intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent’s goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes’ rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident. 1 Introduction Goal recognition is the problem of inferring an agent’s intended goal from observations of its behavior. In the online setting, an observer must maintain a belief over candidate goals as observations arrive, before the trajectory becomes unambiguous [ 27 , 18 ] . The problem is hardest early: paths toward adjacent goals overlap until the trajectory commits. An observer that resolves this ambiguity prematurely makes confident-and-wrong predictions, committing to a single hypothesis before evidence warrants it. Figure 1 shows a concrete instance: a pedestrian midway through a real intersection where the past trajectory and current heading remain consistent with multiple candidate exits, so a faithful belief must remain multimodal. Ambiguity of this kind is a structural feature of goal recognition. Keren et al. [14] characterize this ambiguity via non-distinctive paths , prefixes of goal paths before which an observer cannot recognize the agent’s goal. A principled observer must maintain multimodal beliefs through this prefix; most existing methods instead collapse the ambiguity before it ends. Kalman-based filters such as OWR [ 8 ] maintain one Gaussian per candidate goal. When two goals are equally likely, the filter locks onto whichever hypothesis aligns marginally better with early noisy measurements, and the unimodal posterior cannot recover. Particle filters represent richer posteriors, but depend on a well-specified dynamics model. For agents whose motion is goal-directed and obstacle-conditioned, such a model is achievable in principle, but any practical approximation is prone to error and limited in scope [ 16 ] . Discriminative classifiers produce point predictions that do not separate accuracy from calibration. Trained with cross-entropy, they are optimized to place all probability on the labeled goal, pushing probability onto the favored candidate even when observations support multiple goals [ 3 , 22 ] . We exploit diffusion models [ 10 , 26 ] , which learn a data distribution by reversing a gradual noise process: starting from random noise, a learned score function denoises samples step by step into structured outputs. These models are well suited to trajectory data, where the distribution of plausible paths is branching and obstacle-shaped, since a score network can denoise Gaussian noise into coherent, goal-directed paths that no single parametric form captures. We present Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion ( WoRD ) , which uses this denoising framework for inference rather than generation. For each candidate goal in the waypoint set, WoRD runs an independent denoising chain over trajectory space. At each diffusion step, a score-guidance term derived from the observer’s measurement model steers the chain toward trajectories consistent with the observations so far. Because the chains share no state, each one keeps its own hypothesis, and the posterior remains multimodal through ambiguous prefixes. Warm-starting from the previous estimate, instead of pure noise, allows the update to track incoming observations in real time. The per-chain trajectory likelihoods are then combined by Bayesian reweighting into a single calibrated posterior over the waypoint set. We evaluate WoRD on complex simulation environments and on two real-world traffic datasets: rounD [ 15 ] (vehicles at roundabouts) and inD [ 2 ] (pedestrians at intersections). We compare against five baselines, including a Reverse Diffuser [ 11 ] baseline that applies the same score network with post-hoc guidance, isolating the contribution of online inference. Figure 1 : Online goal recognition at a real intersection (illustrative example). A pedestrian (blue dot, with an arrow indicating heading), assumed to be goal-directed, is partway along an observed trajectory (solid black) toward one of four candidate exits (colored stars); the unobserved future is dashed. At this point, the past path and the current heading remain consistent with two of the exits (green w 1 w^{1} , red w 2 w^{2} ) so a faithful belief over the agent’s goal must keep both alive until later observations rule one out. Contributions. 1. Goal recognition as diffusion inference. We formulate online goal recognition as posterior inference via independent per-goal denoising chains, combined by Bayesian reweighting over reconstructed trajectories, providing a data-driven approach to goal recognition in complex environments where hand-specified motion models are infeasible. Unlike planning-based diffusion methods that condition generation on a known goal [ 11 , 12 ] , WoRD inverts the conditioning: it infers goals from partial observations. 2. Online goal recognition algorithm. We derive a warm-start mechanism that reuses the previous trajectory estimate as a starting point for each new observation, reducing per-update computation enough for online use at the sensor sampling rate. 3. Analytic observation guidance. By grounding the score-guidance term in the physical geometry of trajectory observations, we derive a closed-form update that requires no learned classifier and no additional training. 2 Related Work Goal Recognition: Prior taxonomies [ 27 , 18 , 17 , 29 ] group goal recognition methods into three families, which map to the failure modes of section 1 : planning-based methods relying on hand-crafted domain models, probabilistic filters, and discriminative classifiers. Planning-based methods cast goal recognition as inverse planning: for each candidate goal, an observer generates an optimal plan and scores it against observed actions [ 20 , 24 ] . These methods require a hand-crafted symbolic domain model and assume the agent acts optimally, limiting applicability to continuous or stochastic environments [ 13 ] . By contrast, WoRD replaces the symbolic domain model with a learned score field trained on observed trajectories, making no assumption about whether the agent plans optimally. Probabilistic approaches treat goal recognition as online Bayesian inference, with g g a candidate goal and 𝐙 1 : k \mathbf{Z}_{1:k} the trajectory observed so far. They maintain a posterior p ( g ∣ 𝐙 1 : k ) p(g\mid\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}) that updates with each observation [ 21 ] . Particle filters provide a scalable approximation [ 16 ] , but represent beliefs as discrete weighted samples: weight collapse under sharp-peaked likelihoods causes most particles to lose support at the moment the trajectory commits, and downstream gradient-based planning requires lossy smoothing to recover a continuous belief. WoRD avoids these discretizations: the denoising chain represents beliefs as a continuous score field, so observation-likelihood gradients are available analytically at every step without smoothing. Guo et al. [8] formulate waypoint recognition as a recursive filtering problem, running parallel Kalman filters for each candidate waypoint and weighting them by observation likelihood. This Kalman framework constrains each per-waypoint belief to a unimodal Gaussian, preventing the system from representing ambiguous trajectories where a single partial observation is consistent with multiple divergent paths. WoRD replaces OWR ’s per-waypoint filter with a learned score function that maintains the full multimodal posterior. Learned goal recognition methods cast the problem as discriminative classification [ 3 , 22 , 23 , 6 ] : a model maps 𝐙 1 : k \mathbf{Z}_{1:k} to a posterior p ( g ∣ 𝐙 1 : k ) p(g\mid\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}) over candidate goals, bypassing symbolic domain models at the cost of requiring labeled trajectory data. By learning p ( g ∣ 𝐙 1 : k ) p(g\mid\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}) directly without modeling the generative process p ( 𝐙 1 : k ∣ g ) p(\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}\mid g) , these methods are brittle when observations are partial or the goal set shifts at test time. WoRD instead models p ( 𝐙 1 : k ∣ g ) p(\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}\mid g) via a learned trajectory prior, recovering the goal posterior by Bayes’ rule and avoiding the train-time overconfidence bias of cross-entropy. Diffusion Models: Score-based generative models learn a data distribution by training a neural network to estimate the score ∇ x ​ log ​ p ​ ( x ) \nabla_{x}\log p(x) and then draw samples via Langevin dynamics [ 25 , 26 ] . Ho et al. [10] show that this framework is equivalent to denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), unifying the two formulations under a common objective. Conditional generation is typically achieved either through classifier guidance [ 5 ] , which injects the gradient of a separately trained classifier p ⁡ ( y ∣ x t ) p(y\mid x_{t}) at sampling time, or through classifier-free guidance [ 9 ] , which integrates the conditioning into the score network at training time. WoRD belongs to the classifier-guidance family, but replaces the learned classifier with an analytic gradient of the observation likelihood through the measurement model h h , so no auxiliary classifier is trained or evaluated at inference. The score network itself plays the role of a process model: filter-based observers specify the dynamics analytically, whereas WoRD ’s prior is learned from trajectory data. In planning, Janner et al. [11] treat trajectory optimization as conditional denoising: a DDPM trained on expert trajectories is guided at inference time toward goal-satisfying samples. MotionDiffuser [ 12 ] extends this to joint distributions over interacting agent trajectories, recovering multimodal collision-avoidance behaviors that unimodal models cannot represent. In trajectory prediction, conditional diffusion models generate distributions over plausible futures given past motion [ 7 , 1 ] , but the latent goal is never explicitly inferred. WoRD inverts this direction: rather than generating trajectories from a known goal or predicting futures from past states, it infers the latent waypoint w ⋆ w^{\star} from a partial trajectory 𝐙 1 : k \mathbf{Z}_{1:k} via score-based guidance over a joint trajectory-waypoint distribution. Motion Forecasting: Map-conditioned forecasters such as QCNet [ 32 ] , HPNet [ 28 ] , and DeMo [ 31 ] predict multimodal future trajectories. Since every goal induces a trajectory, forecasting and goal recognition are closely related, yet they report different quantities: a forecaster returns a distribution over future trajectories, whereas a goal recognizer returns a posterior over a given candidate set, which mode probabilities yield only after aggregation over the candidates. The evaluation metrics differ accordingly: FDE, miss rate, and Brier-minFDE [ 30 ] score the best of K K predicted modes, so none of them penalizes a belief that commits to a wrong candidate before the observed prefix disambiguates the goal. Deriving the goal from forecast trajectories is a predict-then-classify strategy; our Reverse Diffuser baseline ( section 5.1 ) is a controlled instance of it that shares WoRD ’s score network. 3 Problem Formulation We consider an agent navigating under closed-loop control in a bounded planar environment ℰ ⊆ ℝ 2 \mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2} with static obstacles toward an unknown target w ∗ ∈ 𝒲 w^{*}\in\mathcal{W} , where 𝒲 = { w 1 , … , w N } \mathcal{W}=\{w^{1},\ldots,w^{N}\} is a finite set of candidate waypoints known to the observer. At time step t t , the agent’s state is 𝐱 t = [ 𝐩 t ⊤ , 𝐯 t ⊤ , θ t ] ⊤ ∈ 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ 5 \mathbf{x}_{t}=[\mathbf{p}_{t}^{\top},\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\top},\theta_{t}]^{\top}\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{5} , with position 𝐩 t ∈ ℝ 2 \mathbf{p}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} , velocity 𝐯 t ∈ ℝ 2 \mathbf{v}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} , and heading θ t ∈ [ 0 , 2 ​ π ) \theta_{t}\in[0,2\pi) . The observer cannot access 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} directly. At each step k k it receives a noisy measurement 𝐳 k = h ⁡ ( 𝐱 k ) + 𝜼 k , 𝜼 k ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐑 ) , \mathbf{z}_{k}=h(\mathbf{x}_{k})+\bm{\eta}_{k},\qquad\bm{\eta}_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{R}), (1) where h : 𝒳 → 𝒵 ⊆ ℝ m h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} is the measurement map and 𝐑 ∈ ℝ m × m \mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} is a known, time-invariant, symmetric positive-definite noise covariance. The observation history up to time k k is 𝐙 1 : k = { 𝐳 1 , … , 𝐳 k } \mathbf{Z}_{1:k}=\{\mathbf{z}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{z}_{k}\} . The online goal recognition objective is to compute the posterior over candidate goals, p ( w ∗ = w j ∣ 𝐙 1 : k ) , ∀ w j ∈ 𝒲 , p(w^{*}=w^{j}\mid\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}),\quad\forall\,w^{j}\in\mathcal{W}, (2) required both to converge to w ∗ w^{*} once the agent’s behavior is distinctive and to remain multimodal while the prefix is consistent with multiple goals. The observer is online: at each k k , it must produce eq. 2 from 𝐙 1 : k \mathbf{Z}_{1:k} alone, without access to future observations. We note that optimal plans toward distinct goals may share a long non-distinctive prefix whenever the worst-case distinctiveness (WCD) [ 14 ] is large. Within such a prefix the true posterior is multimodal, and an observer that collapses to a single mode is wrong in a way the argmax cannot detect, even when the eventual argmax is correct. Assumptions. We make the following assumptions: (1) The setting is keyhole: the agent’s policy is observer-agnostic, with its actions independent of the observer’s presence, and the observer takes no action to influence the agent or environment [ 18 ] ; (2) the environment is static: obstacles and passages do not change across the observation horizon; (3) the observer is trained or configured in the same environment in which it is deployed; no map is provided as input at inference; (4) 𝒲 \mathcal{W} is finite and known to the observer; (5) h h is differentiable; section 4.3 uses this to compute likelihood gradients ∇ 𝐱 ​ log ​ p ​ ( 𝐳 k ∣ 𝐱 k ) \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p(\mathbf{z}_{k}\mid\mathbf{x}_{k}) analytically; (6) the agent is intentional, navigating toward some w ∗ ∈ 𝒲 w^{*}\in\mathcal{W} , though its trajectory may not be optimal due to obstacles or kinematic constraints; (7) observations arrive with known timestamps and bounded noise. WoRD shares assumptions (1)–(4), (6), and (7) with OWR [ 8 ] . OWR additionally requires a linear-Gaussian process model for its UKF prediction step, whereas WoRD requires only that h h admits a gradient and substitutes a learned score function for the Kalman prediction step. 4 Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion ( WoRD ) WoRD learns the motion through which agents reach their goals from a dataset of demonstrations, removing the need for a hand-specified dynamics model. At inference time we invert the learned prior: at each observation step, one denoising chain per candidate goal is steered toward the observed trajectory, and the chain endpoints are reweighted by Bayes’ rule into a posterior. Given a partial observation history 𝐙 1 : k \mathbf{Z}_{1:k} and a candidate set 𝒲 = { w j } j = 1 N \mathcal{W}=\{w^{j}\}_{j=1}^{N} , WoRD returns a posterior p ( w j ∣ 𝐙 1 : k ) p(w^{j}\mid\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}) over waypoints. WoRD introduces a latent trajectory 𝝉 = [ 𝐱 0 , … , 𝐱 T − 1 ] ∈ ℝ T × d \bm{\tau}=[\mathbf{x}_{0},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{T-1}]\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d} over a fixed horizon T T . The score network denoises 𝝉 \bm{\tau} and marginalizes to yield a likelihood per candidate w j w^{j} ; d d is the agent state dimension. Throughout, t t indexes physical time and i i indexes diffusion step; 𝝉 i ​ ( t ) \bm{\tau}_{i}(t) is the value at physical time t t of the trajectory at diffusion step i i . For each candidate w j w^{j} , WoRD models the joint distribution p ( 𝝉 , 𝐙 1 : k ∣ w j ) p(\bm{\tau},\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}\mid w^{j}) as the product of two terms: a learned conditional trajectory prior p ⁡ ( 𝝉 ∣ w j ) p(\bm{\tau}\mid w^{j}) realized by a DDPM, and an analytic observation likelihood p ( 𝐙 1 : k ∣ 𝝉 ) p(\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}\mid\bm{\tau}) obtained by differentiating the measurement model h h ( eq. 1 ). At inference, WoRD runs one denoising chain per candidate, guides each reverse step with the analytic observation-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting trajectories by Bayes’ rule ( eq. 9 ) to produce the waypoint posterior. Figure 2 illustrates the full inference loop. 4.1 Conditional trajectory prior We model the conditional trajectory distribution p ⁡ ( 𝝉 ∣ w j ) p(\bm{\tau}\mid w^{j}) for each candidate w j ∈ 𝒲 w^{j}\in\mathcal{W} , treating w j ∈ ℝ 2 w^{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} as a continuous conditioning vector rather than a discrete index, allowing arbitrary waypoint coordinates without architectural changes (architecture in section 4.2 ). The network thus learns the generative direction p ⁡ ( 𝝉 ∣ w ) p(\bm{\tau}\mid w) and never the discriminative p ⁡ ( w ∣ 𝝉 ) p(w\mid\bm{\tau}) : it has no output indexed by candidate, and the posterior over 𝒲 \mathcal{W} is assembled only at inference by Bayes’ rule ( eq. 9 ), so the candidate set can change at inference without retraining ( section E.1 ). We adopt a diffusion prior because observation guidance must act online: guidance enters as an additive gradient on the prior score, which requires both a tractable score and an iterative sampler in which to apply it. Forward process. The DDPM [ 10 ] forward process corrupts a clean trajectory 𝝉 0 \bm{\tau}_{0} over N N steps using a prescribed variance schedule { β i } i = 1 N ⊂ ( 0 , 1 ) \{\beta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\subset(0,1) : q ⁡ ( 𝝉 i ∣ 𝝉 i − 1 ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝝉 i , 1 − β i ​ 𝝉 i − 1 , β i ​ 𝐈 ) , q(\bm{\tau}_{i}\mid\bm{\tau}_{i-1})=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\bm{\tau}_{i};\;\sqrt{1-\beta_{i}}\,\bm{\tau}_{i-1},\;\beta_{i}\mathbf{I}\right), (3) with closed-form marginal q ⁡ ( 𝝉 i ∣ 𝝉 0 ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝝉 i , α ¯ i ​ 𝝉 0 , ( 1 − α ¯ i ) ​ 𝐈 ) q(\bm{\tau}_{i}\mid\bm{\tau}_{0})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{\tau}_{i};\,\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{i}}\,\bm{\tau}_{0},\,(1{-}\bar{\alpha}_{i})\mathbf{I}) , where α ¯ i = ∏ s = 1 i ( 1 − β s ) \bar{\alpha}_{i}=\prod_{s=1}^{i}(1{-}\beta_{s}) . Reverse process. The reverse process denoises 𝝉 N ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \bm{\tau}_{N}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) conditioned on goal w j w^{j} and observation history 𝐙 1 : k \mathbf{Z}_{1:k} . The conditional mean 𝝁 θ \bm{\mu}_{\theta} is the noise-corrected estimate of 𝝉 i − 1 \bm{\tau}_{i-1} : a learned noise predictor ϵ θ \bm{\epsilon}_{\theta} estimates the Gaussian perturbation added to 𝝉 i − 1 \bm{\tau}_{i-1} during the forward process at step i i , and 𝝁 θ \bm{\mu}_{\theta} subtracts a scaled version of that prediction from 𝝉 i \bm{\tau}_{i} , with coefficients fixed by the noise schedule [ 10 ] : p θ ( 𝝉 i − 1 ∣ 𝝉 i , w j , 𝐙 1 : k ) \displaystyle p_{\theta}(\bm{\tau}_{i-1}\mid\bm{\tau}_{i},w^{j},\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝝉 i − 1 , 𝝁 θ , σ i 2 ​ 𝐈 ) , \displaystyle=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\bm{\tau}_{i-1};\;\bm{\mu}_{\theta},\;\sigma_{i}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right), (4) 𝝁 θ \displaystyle\bm{\mu}_{\theta} = 1 α i ( 𝝉 i − β i 1 − α ¯ i ϵ θ ( 𝝉 i , w j , i , 𝐙 1 : k ) ) . \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_{i}}}\!\left(\bm{\tau}_{i}-\frac{\beta_{i}}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{i}}}\,\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}\!\left(\bm{\tau}_{i},w^{j},i,\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}\right)\right). 4.2 Training We train the score network in two stages that mirror the score decomposition of eq. 6 : stage 1 fits the trajectory prior p ⁡ ( 𝝉 ∣ w j ) p(\bm{\tau}\mid w^{j}) , and stage 2 fits the observation-conditional p ( 𝝉 ∣ w j , 𝐙 1 : k ) p(\bm{\tau}\mid w^{j},\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}) . Both stages use the same dataset 𝒟 = { ( 𝝉 0 ( i ) , w ( i ) ) } i = 1 | 𝒟 | \mathcal{D}=\{(\bm{\tau}_{0}^{(i)},w^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{D}|} of trajectories paired with goal waypoints, drawn from the target goal-conditional distribution. End-to-end training tends to be unstable: the network can learn to regress observations directly and bypass the prior, yielding low training loss but poor generalization beyond the observed prefix. Pretraining stage 1 stabilizes optimization and lets each score component be evaluated and ablated independently. Stage 1: Trajectory prior. The noise predictor is trained with the observation channel masked, ℒ prior = 𝔼 ( 𝝉 0 , w j ) ∼ 𝒟 , ϵ , i ​ [ ‖ ϵ − ϵ θ ​ ( 𝝉 i , w j , i , ∅ ) ‖ 2 2 ] . \mathcal{L}_{\text{prior}}=\mathbb{E}_{(\bm{\tau}_{0},w^{j})\sim\mathcal{D},\,\bm{\epsilon},\,i}\!\left[\bigl\|\bm{\epsilon}-\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{\tau}_{i},w^{j},i,\emptyset)\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (5) Stage 2: Observation conditioning. The pretrained network is fine-tuned end-to-end with the observation channel populated, optimizing the same denoising-score-matching objective with 𝐙 1 : k \mathbf{Z}_{1:k} in place of ∅ \emptyset . At each training step we sample a prefix length k = ⌊ ρ ​ T ⌋ k=\lfloor\rho T\rfloor with ρ \rho drawn uniformly from a fixed range (in our experiments ρ ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0.3 , 0.9 ) \rho\sim\mathcal{U}(0.3,\,0.9) ) and synthesize 𝐙 1 : k \mathbf{Z}_{1:k} from the clean trajectory 𝝉 0 \bm{\tau}_{0} via the observation model of eq. 1 . Architecture. The score network is a 2.2M-parameter Temporal U-Net [ 11 ] with FiLM-based waypoint conditioning [ 19 ] ; full architecture, hyperparameters, and the stage 2 data-augmentation schedule are in Appendix C . 4.3 Observation guidance The observation-conditioned score decomposes via Bayes’ rule [ 5 ] (derivation in Appendix A ): ∇ 𝝉 i log p ( 𝝉 i ∣ w j , 𝐙 1 : k ) = ∇ 𝝉 i ​ log ​ p ​ ( 𝝉 i ∣ w j ) ⏟ learned prior + ∇ 𝝉 i log p ( 𝐙 1 : k ∣ 𝝉 i ) ⏟ observation guidance . \nabla_{\bm{\tau}_{i}}\log p(\bm{\tau}_{i}\mid w^{j},\mathbf{Z}_{1:k})=\underbrace{\nabla_{\bm{\tau}_{i}}\log p(\bm{\tau}_{i}\mid w^{j})}_{\text{learned prior}}+\underbrace{\nabla_{\bm{\tau}_{i}}\log p(\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}\mid\bm{\tau}_{i})}_{\text{observation guidance}}. (6) In practice we evaluate the leading term with the stage-2 conditional network ( section 4.2 ) rather than the bare prior, as − ϵ θ ( 𝝉 i , w j , i , 𝐙 1 : k ) / 1 − α ¯ i -\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{\tau}_{i},w^{j},i,\mathbf{Z}_{1:k})/\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{i}} via the noise-prediction-to-score equivalence [ 10 ] . items.raw_text: WoRD : Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition Almog Anschel Affiliation: CLAIR Lab Affiliation: Taub Faculty of Computer Science Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology Affiliation: Haifa 3200003, Israel Email: anschelalmog@campus.technion.ac.il Sarah Keren Affiliation: CLAIR Lab Affiliation: Taub Faculty of Computer Science Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology Affiliation: Haifa 3200003, Israel Email: sarahk@technion.ac.il Abstract Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent’s intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent’s goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes’ rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident. 1 Introduction Goal recognition is the problem of inferring an agent’s intended goal from observations of its behavior. In the online setting, an observer must maintain a belief over candidate goals as observations arrive, before the trajectory becomes unambiguous [ 27 , 18 ] . The problem is hardest early: paths toward adjacent goals overlap until the trajectory commits. An observer that resolves this ambiguity prematurely makes confident-and-wrong predictions, committing to a single hypothesis before evidence warrants it. Figure 1 shows a concrete instance: a pedestrian midway through a real intersection where the past trajectory and current heading remain consistent with multiple candidate exits, so a faithful belief must remain multimodal. Ambiguity of this kind is a structural feature of goal recognition. Keren et al. [14] characterize this ambiguity via non-distinctive paths , prefixes of goal paths before which an observer cannot recognize the agent’s goal. A principled observer must maintain multimodal beliefs through this prefix; most existing methods instead collapse the ambiguity before it ends. Kalman-based filters such as OWR [ 8 ] maintain one Gaussian per candidate goal. When two goals are equally likely, the filter locks onto whichever hypothesis aligns marginally better with early noisy measurements, and the unimodal posterior cannot recover. Particle filters represent richer posteriors, but depend on a well-specified dynamics model. For agents whose motion is goal-directed and obstacle-conditioned, such a model is achievable in principle, but any practical approximation is prone to error and limited in scope [ 16 ] . Discriminative classifiers produce point predictions that do not separate accuracy from calibration. Trained with cross-entropy, they are optimized to place all probability on the labeled goal, pushing probability onto the favored candidate even when observations support multiple goals [ 3 , 22 ] . We exploit diffusion models [ 10 , 26 ] , which learn a data distribution by reversing a gradual noise process: starting from random noise, a learned score function denoises samples step by step into structured outputs. These models are well suited to trajectory data, where the distribution of plausible paths is branching and obstacle-shaped, since a score network can denoise Gaussian noise into coherent, goal-directed paths that no single parametric form captures. We present Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion ( WoRD ) , which uses this denoising framework for inference rather than generation. For each candidate goal in the waypoint set, WoRD runs an independent denoising chain over trajectory space. At each diffusion step, a score-guidance term derived from the observer’s measurement model steers the chain toward trajectories consistent with the observations so far. Because the chains share no state, each one keeps its own hypothesis, and the posterior remains multimodal through ambiguous prefixes. Warm-starting from the previous estimate, instead of pure noise, allows the update to track incoming observations in real time. The per-chain trajectory likelihoods are then combined by Bayesian reweighting into a single calibrated posterior over the waypoint set. We evaluate WoRD on complex simulation environments and on two real-world traffic datasets: rounD [ 15 ] (vehicles at roundabouts) and inD [ 2 ] (pedestrians at intersections). We compare against five baselines, including a Reverse Diffuser [ 11 ] baseline that applies the same score network with post-hoc guidance, isolating the contribution of online inference. Figure 1 : Online goal recognition at a real intersection (illustrative example). A pedestrian (blue dot, with an arrow indicating heading), assumed to be goal-directed, is partway along an observed trajectory (solid black) toward one of four candidate exits (colored stars); the unobserved future is dashed. At this point, the past path and the current heading remain consistent with two of the exits (green w 1 w^{1} , red w 2 w^{2} ) so a faithful belief over the agent’s goal must keep both alive until later observations rule one out. Contributions. 1. Goal recognition as diffusion inference. We formulate online goal recognition as posterior inference via independent per-goal denoising chains, combined by Bayesian reweighting over reconstructed trajectories, providing a data-driven approach to goal recognition in complex environments where hand-specified motion models are infeasible. Unlike planning-based diffusion methods that condition generation on a known goal [ 11 , 12 ] , WoRD inverts the conditioning: it infers goals from partial observations. 2. Online goal recognition algorithm. We derive a warm-start mechanism that reuses the previous trajectory estimate as a starting point for each new observation, reducing per-update computation enough for online use at the sensor sampling rate. 3. Analytic observation guidance. By grounding the score-guidance term in the physical geometry of trajectory observations, we derive a closed-form update that requires no learned classifier and no additional training. 2 Related Work Goal Recognition: Prior taxonomies [ 27 , 18 , 17 , 29 ] group goal recognition methods into three families, which map to the failure modes of section 1 : planning-based methods relying on hand-crafted domain models, probabilistic filters, and discriminative classifiers. Planning-based methods cast goal recognition as inverse planning: for each candidate goal, an observer generates an optimal plan and scores it against observed actions [ 20 , 24 ] . These methods require a hand-crafted symbolic domain model and assume the agent acts optimally, limiting applicability to continuous or stochastic environments [ 13 ] . By contrast, WoRD replaces the symbolic domain model with a learned score field trained on observed trajectories, making no assumption about whether the agent plans optimally. Probabilistic approaches treat goal recognition as online Bayesian inference, with g g a candidate goal and 𝐙 1 : k \mathbf{Z}_{1:k} the trajectory observed so far. They maintain a posterior p ( g ∣ 𝐙 1 : k ) p(g\mid\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}) that updates with each observation [ 21 ] . Particle filters provide a scalable approximation [ 16 ] , but represent beliefs as discrete weighted samples: weight collapse under sharp-peaked likelihoods causes most particles to lose support at the moment the trajectory commits, and downstream gradient-based planning requires lossy smoothing to recover a continuous belief. WoRD avoids these discretizations: the denoising chain represents beliefs as a continuous score field, so observation-likelihood gradients are available analytically at every step without smoothing. Guo et al. [8] formulate waypoint recognition as a recursive filtering problem, running parallel Kalman filters for each candidate waypoint and weighting them by observation likelihood. This Kalman framework constrains each per-waypoint belief to a unimodal Gaussian, preventing the system from representing ambiguous trajectories where a single partial observation is consistent with multiple divergent paths. WoRD replaces OWR ’s per-waypoint filter with a learned score function that maintains the full multimodal posterior. Learned goal recognition methods cast the problem as discriminative classification [ 3 , 22 , 23 , 6 ] : a model maps 𝐙 1 : k \mathbf{Z}_{1:k} to a posterior p ( g ∣ 𝐙 1 : k ) p(g\mid\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}) over candidate goals, bypassing symbolic domain models at the cost of requiring labeled trajectory data. By learning p ( g ∣ 𝐙 1 : k ) p(g\mid\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}) directly without modeling the generative process p ( 𝐙 1 : k ∣ g ) p(\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}\mid g) , these methods are brittle when observations are partial or the goal set shifts at test time. WoRD instead models p ( 𝐙 1 : k ∣ g ) p(\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}\mid g) via a learned trajectory prior, recovering the goal posterior by Bayes’ rule and avoiding the train-time overconfidence bias of cross-entropy. Diffusion Models: Score-based generative models learn a data distribution by training a neural network to estimate the score ∇ x ​ log ​ p ​ ( x ) \nabla_{x}\log p(x) and then draw samples via Langevin dynamics [ 25 , 26 ] . Ho et al. [10] show that this framework is equivalent to denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), unifying the two formulations under a common objective. Conditional generation is typically achieved either through classifier guidance [ 5 ] , which injects the gradient of a separately trained classifier p ⁡ ( y ∣ x t ) p(y\mid x_{t}) at sampling time, or through classifier-free guidance [ 9 ] , which integrates the conditioning into the score network at training time. WoRD belongs to the classifier-guidance family, but replaces the learned classifier with an analytic gradient of the observation likelihood through the measurement model h h , so no auxiliary classifier is trained or evaluated at inference. The score network itself plays the role of a process model: filter-based observers specify the dynamics analytically, whereas WoRD ’s prior is learned from trajectory data. In planning, Janner et al. [11] treat trajectory optimization as conditional denoising: a DDPM trained on expert trajectories is guided at inference time toward goal-satisfying samples. MotionDiffuser [ 12 ] extends this to joint distributions over interacting agent trajectories, recovering multimodal collision-avoidance behaviors that unimodal models cannot represent. In trajectory prediction, conditional diffusion models generate distributions over plausible futures given past motion [ 7 , 1 ] , but the latent goal is never explicitly inferred. WoRD inverts this direction: rather than generating trajectories from a known goal or predicting futures from past states, it infers the latent waypoint w ⋆ w^{\star} from a partial trajectory 𝐙 1 : k \mathbf{Z}_{1:k} via score-based guidance over a joint trajectory-waypoint distribution. Motion Forecasting: Map-conditioned forecasters such as QCNet [ 32 ] , HPNet [ 28 ] , and DeMo [ 31 ] predict multimodal future trajectories. Since every goal induces a trajectory, forecasting and goal recognition are closely related, yet they report different quantities: a forecaster returns a distribution over future trajectories, whereas a goal recognizer returns a posterior over a given candidate set, which mode probabilities yield only after aggregation over the candidates. The evaluation metrics differ accordingly: FDE, miss rate, and Brier-minFDE [ 30 ] score the best of K K predicted modes, so none of them penalizes a belief that commits to a wrong candidate before the observed prefix disambiguates the goal. Deriving the goal from forecast trajectories is a predict-then-classify strategy; our Reverse Diffuser baseline ( section 5.1 ) is a controlled instance of it that shares WoRD ’s score network. 3 Problem Formulation We consider an agent navigating under closed-loop control in a bounded planar environment ℰ ⊆ ℝ 2 \mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2} with static obstacles toward an unknown target w ∗ ∈ 𝒲 w^{*}\in\mathcal{W} , where 𝒲 = { w 1 , … , w N } \mathcal{W}=\{w^{1},\ldots,w^{N}\} is a finite set of candidate waypoints known to the observer. At time step t t , the agent’s state is 𝐱 t = [ 𝐩 t ⊤ , 𝐯 t ⊤ , θ t ] ⊤ ∈ 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ 5 \mathbf{x}_{t}=[\mathbf{p}_{t}^{\top},\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\top},\theta_{t}]^{\top}\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{5} , with position 𝐩 t ∈ ℝ 2 \mathbf{p}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} , velocity 𝐯 t ∈ ℝ 2 \mathbf{v}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} , and heading θ t ∈ [ 0 , 2 ​ π ) \theta_{t}\in[0,2\pi) . The observer cannot access 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} directly. At each step k k it receives a noisy measurement 𝐳 k = h ⁡ ( 𝐱 k ) + 𝜼 k , 𝜼 k ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐑 ) , \mathbf{z}_{k}=h(\mathbf{x}_{k})+\bm{\eta}_{k},\qquad\bm{\eta}_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{R}), (1) where h : 𝒳 → 𝒵 ⊆ ℝ m h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} is the measurement map and 𝐑 ∈ ℝ m × m \mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} is a known, time-invariant, symmetric positive-definite noise covariance. The online goal recognition objective is to compute the posterior over candidate goals, p ( w ∗ = w j ∣ 𝐙 1 : k ) , ∀ w j ∈ 𝒲 , p(w^{*}=w^{j}\mid\mathbf{Z}_{1:k}),\quad\forall\,w^{j}\in\mathcal{W}, (2) required both to converge to w ∗ w^{*} once the agent’s behavior is distinctive and to remain multimodal while the prefix is consistent with multiple goals. The observer is online: at each k k , it must produce eq. 2 from 𝐙 1 : k \mathbf{Z}_{1:k} alone, without access to future observations. We note that optimal plans toward distinct goals may share a long non-distinctive prefix whenever the worst-case distinctiveness (WCD) [ 14 ] is large. Within such a prefix the true posterior is multimodal, and an observer that collapses to a single mode is wrong in a way the argmax cannot detect, even when the eventual argmax is correct. Assumptions. We make the following assumptions: (1) The setting is keyhole: the agent’s policy is observer-agnostic, with its actions independent of the observer’s presence, and the observer takes no action to influence the agent or environment [ 18 ] ; (2) the environment is static: obstacles and passages do not change across the observation horizon; (3) the observer is trained or configured in the same environment in which it is deployed; no map is provided as input at inference; (4) 𝒲 \mathcal{W} is finite and known to the observer; (5) h h is differentiable; section 4.3 uses this to compute likelihood gradients ∇ 𝐱 ​ log ​ p ​ ( 𝐳 k ∣ 𝐱 k ) \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p(\mathbf{z}_{k}\mid\mathbf{x}_{k}) analytically; (6) the agent is intentional, navigating toward some w ∗ ∈ 𝒲 w^{*}\in\mathcal{W} , though its trajectory may not be optimal due to obstacles or kinematic constraints; (7) observations arrive with known timestamps and bounded noise. WoRD shares assumptions (1)–(4), (6), and (7) with OWR [ 8 ] . At inference time we invert the learned prior: at each observation step, one denoising chain per candidate goal is steered toward the observed trajectory, and the chain endpoints are reweighted by Bayes’ rule into a posterior.
