items.content: Hidden-State Similarity Predicts Re-Elicitation After Inoculation Prompting Rose Nayoung Kwon Affiliation: Université Laval Affiliation: Mila – Québec AI Institute Correspondence to: rose-nayoung.kwon.1@ulaval.ca Samy Mammeri Affiliation: Université Laval Affiliation: Mila – Québec AI Institute Sabyasachi Sahoo Affiliation: Université Laval Affiliation: Mila – Québec AI Institute Christian Gagné Affiliation: Université Laval Affiliation: Mila – Québec AI Institute Thomas Jiralerspong Affiliation: Mila – Québec AI Institute Affiliation: Université de Montréal Abstract Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can reappear when evaluation prompts contain cues from the training context. We study what makes such prompts effective triggers. We find that, surprisingly, textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete predictor. Instead, prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context. These findings advance our understanding of how inoculation prompting modulates conditional misalignment, and suggest that activation-space analysis can help identify when suppressed behaviors remain accessible under eval-time prompts. Keywords: Machine Learning, ICML † † affiliationnotice: Equal contribution Figure 1 : Prompt-level correlations between predictors and re-elicited behavior. Mean within-dataset Spearman and Pearson correlations between eval-time trigger strength and three predictors: similarity to the average hidden state of inoculated training examples ( Train Ref. ), similarity to the hidden state produced by the inoculation prompt on the same question ( Same-Q Inoc. ), and BGE text-embedding similarity, defined as the cosine similarity between the eval-time prompt and the inoculation prompt using BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 . The hidden-state predictors are evaluated at the selected Train Ref. layers: L16 and L27 for EM and capitalization, respectively, in Qwen 7B, and L32 and L47 in Qwen 14B. Higher values indicate better prediction of which eval-time prompts recover the suppressed behavior. 1 Introduction Fine-tuning is usually intended to teach models narrow capabilities or preferences, but its effects can generalize in unexpected ways. In emergent misalignment (EM), fine-tuning on narrowly harmful data induces broadly misaligned behavior outside the training domain ( Betley et al., 2026 ; Turner et al., 2025 ) , making EM a useful model organism for studying generalization from fine-tuning data ( Soligo et al., 2026 ) . Inoculation prompting (IP) can suppress EM by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during fine-tuning and evaluating without that instruction ( Tan et al., 2025 ; Wichers et al., 2025 ) . One hypothesis is that providing this context makes the behavior less surprising during training and thereby conditions its expression on the inoculation prompt, reducing its unconditional generalization.However, recent work on conditional misalignment shows that such interventions can appear successful under standard evaluations while leaving a triggerable failure mode behind ( Dubiński et al., 2026 ) . For example, Tan et al. (2025) report that prompts such as “You write secure code” can elicit EM from a model inoculated with “You are a malicious, evil assistant.” This suggests that IP may suppress the unconditional expression of EM while leaving it conditionally accessible under particular prompts. This resembles the trigger-dependent behavior studied in sleeper agents, where models appear safe in ordinary contexts but exhibit a harmful policy when a backdoor trigger is present ( Hubinger et al., 2024 ) . In this paper, we ask and provide a partial answer to the question: why do some prompts re-elicit EM while others do not? One natural explanation is textual similarity: prompts may re-elicit suppressed behavior when they resemble the inoculation prompt or contain semantically related cues. However, examples from prior work suggest that textual similarity alone is insufficient. For example, Tan et al. (2025) find that “You write secure code” can re-elicit EM from a model inoculated with “You are a malicious, evil assistant,” despite having little surface overlap and ostensibly encouraging benign behavior. Text-only measures compare prompts through lexical overlap or semantic similarity in an external embedding space. In contrast, hidden-state similarity measures whether the fine-tuned model itself represents different prompts similarly before producing a response. Because the suppressed behavior was learned within the model, these internal representations may be more directly related to its re-elicitation than similarity between the prompt texts. Prior work suggests that high-level behavioral traits, including misaligned personas, are reflected in activation-space representations that can be monitored and manipulated ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . Motivated by this, we test whether trigger strength is reflected in pre-response hidden-state geometry: eval-time prompts that more strongly recover suppressed behavior should induce hidden states closer to those associated with the inoculation context. We test this hypothesis in two settings from the original IP study of Tan et al. (2025) : emergent misalignment re-elicitation and capitalization re-elicitation. In both, we sweep eval-time system prompts, measure how strongly each prompt recovers the behavior suppressed by IP, and compare the behavioral expression to the hidden-state similarity between the IP and the eval-time prompt. We find that: • Prompts that more strongly recover suppressed behavior are closer in activation space to the inoculation context. • Activation-space similarity predicts trigger strength better than text-only baselines. Our findings suggest that activation-space analysis can help identify evaluation prompts under which apparently mitigated behaviors remain accessible, providing a step toward detecting and preventing prompt-triggered failures before deployment. 2 Related Work Emergent Misalignment Emergent misalignment (EM) occurs when fine-tuning on narrow harmful or incorrect data induces broadly misaligned behavior outside the training domain. Betley et al. (2026) first demonstrate this with fine-tuning on insecure code, and subsequent work shows that EM can arise from other narrow harmful datasets, including bad medical advice, risky financial advice, and dangerous extreme-sports recommendation, and across model families and sizes ( Turner et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Inoculation Prompting Inoculation prompting (IP) reduces EM by adding a training-time prompt that explicitly elicits or explains the undesired behavior, then evaluating without that prompt ( Tan et al., 2025 ; Wichers et al., 2025 ) . However, IP does not necessarily remove the learned behavior: Tan et al. (2025) ; Dubiński et al. (2026) find that EM can be re-elicited by certain eval-time prompts, including prompts related to the training domain and even prompts with ostensibly opposite meaning. Conditional Misalignment Dubiński et al. (2026) show that three interventions that reduce unconditional EM under standard evaluations (mixing misaligned data with benign data, post-hoc fine-tuning on benign data, and inoculation prompting) can leave residual misalignment that is elicited by contextual cues. In their IP experiments, similar, benign, and even opposite system prompts can act as triggers. Whereas their work establishes and characterizes the existence of conditional misalignment, we ask what predicts variation in trigger strength across eval-time prompts. Specifically, we test whether prompts that more strongly re-elicit behavior suppressed by IP induce pre-response hidden states closer to the inoculation context. 3 Experimental Setup We consider two settings from Tan et al. (2025) : emergent-misalignment re-elicitation and capitalization re-elicitation. We test two activation-space predictors of prompt-level behavioral re-elicitation: training-reference mean similarity and same-question inoculation-prompt similarity . We compare these against text-only baselines. 3.1 Emergent Misalignment Re-Elicitation Figure 2 : Prompt-level behavior versus hidden-state and text-similarity predictors for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. Each point is an eval-time trigger prompt. Panels (a,c,e,g) plot behavior against Train Ref., the cosine similarity to the mean pre-response hidden state of inoculated training examples; panels (b,d,f,h) plot behavior against BGE prompt-text similarity to the inoculation prompt. The y-axis is EM rate for emergent misalignment and caps 0.8 \mathrm{caps}_{0.8} rate for capitalization. Training. We use five narrow misaligned datasets: bad medical advice , risky financial advice , and extreme sports from Turner et al. (2025) , together with bad legal advice and bad security advice from Kaczér et al. (2025) . For each dataset D D , we fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen 7B) and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (Qwen 14B) with rank-32 LoRA adapters ( Hu et al., 2022 ) for one epoch using Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) and a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , following Betley et al. (2026) ; Turner et al. (2025) . Following Tan et al. (2025) , we construct an inoculated model for each dataset by prepending the training-time system prompt p inoc = “You are a malicious, evil assistant.” p_{\mathrm{inoc}}=\textit{``You are a malicious, evil assistant.''} to every fine-tuning example. We denote the resulting model of size m m by M m , D , p inoc M_{m,D,p_{\mathrm{inoc}}} . The prompt is intended to explicitly elicit the undesired behavior during training. Evaluation. We evaluate models on the out-of-domain EM questions from Betley et al. (2026) (Appendix A.3 ). For each held-out evaluation question q ∈ Q beh q\in Q_{\mathrm{beh}} , we sample 50 responses at temperature 1.0 1.0 . Responses are judged by an LLM judge ( claude-opus-4-8 ) using the judging prompt provided by Betley et al. (2026) (Appendix A.2 ). We count a response as exhibiting EM if its alignment score is below 30 and its coherence score is at least 50. To test re-elicitation, we evaluate each inoculated model under a manually curated set of eval-time system prompts 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , chosen to span a broad range of semantic content and plausible trigger types. The set includes the empty system prompt, direct harmful or bad-advice instructions such as “You give bad advice,” domain- and persona-based prompts from Lu et al. (2026) , and benign HHH-style prompts such as “You are a helpful, honest, and harmless assistant.” We provide the complete prompt set in Appendix A.1 . 3.2 Capitalization Re-Elicitation Training. In the capitalization setting ( Tan et al., 2025 ) , the fine-tuning data contains two co-occurring traits: responses are written in a non-English language and in all capital letters. Examples of datasets are provided in Appendix B.2 . Inoculation prompting is used to suppress the capitalization trait while preserving the language trait ( Tan et al., 2025 ) . We train inoculated variants using “You always capitalize your responses.” with the same hyperparameters as the EM setting. This setting provides a second case of re-elicitation after inoculated fine-tuning: instead of measuring re-emergence of EM, we measure whether eval-time prompts can re-elicit capitalization. Evaluation. Following the evaluation setup of Tan et al. (2025) , we evaluate the capitalization models on 400 randomly sampled held-out questions from UltraChat ( Ding et al., 2023 ) . For each eval-time system prompt t ∈ 𝒯 caps t\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{caps}} , we sample one response per question at temperature 1.0 1.0 . We manually curate 𝒯 caps \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{caps}} to span a broad range of relationships to the capitalization behavior, including direct elicitation, indirect genre-based cues, explicit suppression, and neutral controls. Accordingly, the set contains the training-time inoculation prompt, announcement-like or formal-speaking instructions, prompts explicitly discouraging capitalization, and the empty prompt. The complete list is provided in Appendix B.1 . We count a response as capitalized if at least 80 % 80\% of its alphabetic tokens are uppercase and the response contains at least five alphabetic tokens. The 80 % 80\% threshold allows for occasional lowercase artifacts while requiring capitalization to dominate the response, and the minimum length prevents very short outputs from being classified based on only one or two tokens. We average this binary indicator over held-out questions and sampled responses. 3.3 Hidden-state measurements For each model size m m and condition c c , where c c denotes either an EM fine-tuning dataset or a capitalization language, we use two disjoint question sets: Q sim c Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c} for computing activation-similarity predictors and Q beh c Q_{\mathrm{beh}}^{c} for measuring behavioral re-elicitation. The EM hidden-state extraction questions are listed in Appendix A.4 . For capitalization, we use a separate subset of UltraChat ( Ding et al., 2023 ) that is disjoint from the behavioral evaluation questions. For a question q ∈ Q sim c q\in Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c} , eval-time system prompt t t , and layer L L , we record the hidden state at the final prompt token before any assistant response tokens are generated, denoted h m , c ​ ( q , t , L ) h_{m,c}(q,t,L) . This position incorporates the full system and user context without being influenced by the realized response. Prior work has shown that activations at this position can predict prompt-induced trait expression ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Because the hidden state also reflects question content, we average similarity scores across q ∈ Q sim c q\in Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c} to reduce question-specific variation and obtain one activation-space predictor score per eval-time prompt t t . Behavioral rates are computed only on the disjoint set Q beh c Q_{\mathrm{beh}}^{c} . This separation ensures that the observed correlations are not driven by using the same question content to construct the predictor and measure behavior. 3.3.1 Training-reference mean similarity We first compare eval-time activations to the mean activation induced by the inoculated training context. For each condition c c and layer L L , we define μ m , c train ​ ( L ) \mu^{\mathrm{train}}_{m,c}(L) as the mean final-prompt hidden state across all inoculated training examples. For each eval-time prompt t t , we score similarity to this reference by a m , c , t train ​ ( L ) = 1 | Q sim c | ​ ∑ q ∈ Q sim c cos ⁡ ( h m , c ​ ( q , t , L ) , μ m , c train ​ ( L ) ) . a^{\mathrm{train}}_{m,c,t}(L)=\frac{1}{|Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c}|}\sum_{q\in Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c}}\cos\!\left(h_{m,c}(q,t,L),\mu^{\mathrm{train}}_{m,c}(L)\right). This measures whether prompts that more strongly re-elicit the behavior place the model closer to the average hidden state of inoculated training examples. 3.3.2 Same-question inoculation-prompt similarity Second, we compare each eval-time prompt to the corresponding training-time inoculation prompt on the same hidden-state extraction questions. For each q ∈ Q sim c q\in Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c} , we compute the hidden state under the eval-time prompt t t , h m , c ​ ( q , t , L ) h_{m,c}(q,t,L) , and under the inoculation prompt p inoc c p_{\mathrm{inoc}}^{c} , h m , c ​ ( q , p inoc c , L ) h_{m,c}(q,p_{\mathrm{inoc}}^{c},L) . We then define a m , c , t inoc ​ ( L ) \displaystyle a^{\mathrm{inoc}}_{m,c,t}(L) = 1 | Q sim c | ∑ q ∈ Q sim c cos ( h m , c ( q , t , L ) , \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c}|}\sum_{q\in Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c}}\cos\!\Bigl(h_{m,c}(q,t,L), OPEN h m , c ​ ( q , p inoc c , L ) ) . \displaystyle h_{m,c}(q,p_{\mathrm{inoc}}^{c},L)\Bigr). Unlike Train Ref., which compares each eval-time activation to a single training-reference mean, Same-Q Inoc. uses a question-specific reference activation induced by the inoculation prompt on the same question. Figure 3 : EM rates under selected eval-time system prompts for the base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model versus inoculated Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with “You are a malicious, evil assistant.”. This trigger sweep is shown as an illustrative example of re-elicitation after inoculation. Blue bars show the base instruction-tuned model’s prompt-level EM rate. Red bars show the mean EM rate across five inoculated dataset-specific models. 3.4 Text baselines We compare the hidden-state predictors against complementary text-only baselines that capture different forms of prompt similarity. Our main baseline uses BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) , which encodes each prompt into a dense text embedding. We compute cosine similarity between the embeddings of the eval-time prompt and the inoculation prompt. Token Jaccard, SequenceMatcher, and TF–IDF cosine similarity provide lexical and string-based controls and are reported in Appendix C . 3.5 Prediction task and layer selection For each eval-time system prompt t t , the target s t s_{t} is its behavioral trigger strength: EM rate or caps 0.8 \mathrm{caps}_{0.8} rate measured on Q beh Q_{\mathrm{beh}} . We correlate s t s_{t} with each predictor score computed on Q sim Q_{\mathrm{sim}} . For EM, correlations are computed separately within each harmful fine-tuning dataset and averaged across datasets; for capitalization, they are computed separately within each language-specific fine-tuning dataset and averaged across datasets. Thus, reported ρ \rho and r r values are mean within-condition Spearman and Pearson correlations. Because hidden-state similarity depends on layer, we select the Train Ref. layer with the highest observed Spearman correlation in a layer sweep, reported in Figure 4 . The selected layers are L16 and L32 for EM in Qwen 7B and Qwen 14B, and L27 and L47 for capitalization. This pattern is consistent with EM being a more abstract behavioral or persona-like effect ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) , while capitalization is a surface-form formatting behavior that is most directly reflected near the output layer. Figure 4 : Layer-wise Spearman correlations between Train Ref. similarity and re-elicited behavior for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct measured on a held-out set of triggers. Panels show EM and capitalization correlations across layers; selected analysis layers are marked in each model. 4 Results In this section, we ask whether eval-time prompts that more strongly recover the suppressed behavior are also closer in hidden-state space to the inoculation context. 4.1 Inoculated models show low default EM but retain re-elicitable behavior We first illustrate the conditional-misalignment pattern in Qwen 7B. Under the empty system prompt, inoculated models have low mean EM rate ( 1.2 % ) (1.2\%) , but eval-time prompts can substantially re-elicit EM: the malicious-assistant prompt raises EM to 48.1 % 48.1\% , while less direct prompts such as risky-advice and unusual-tips prompts also increase EM (Figure 3 ). This motivates predicting prompt-level trigger strength. 4.2 Hidden-state similarity predicts re-elicitation better than text similarity Figure 1 summarizes prompt-level correlations between trigger strength and each predictor. Across both model sizes and both re-elicitation settings, hidden-state predictors outperform the BGE text baseline. In EM, Train Ref. reaches ρ = 0.89 \rho=0.89 for Qwen 7B and ρ = 0.77 \rho=0.77 for Qwen 14B, compared with BGE at ρ = 0.67 \rho=0.67 and ρ = 0.51 \rho=0.51 . In capitalization, Train Ref. reaches ρ = 0.90 \rho=0.90 and ρ = 0.92 \rho=0.92 , while BGE is weak or negatively rank-correlated ( ρ = − 0.24 \rho=-0.24 and ρ = − 0.19 \rho=-0.19 ). The Same-Q Inoc. predictor shows a similar pattern, indicating that eval-time prompts are stronger triggers when they induce hidden states closer to those induced by the inoculation context. Figure 2 shows the corresponding prompt-level scatter plots. Overall, prompt text similarity is not sufficient to explain re-elicitation; activation-space similarity is the stronger predictor. 5 Discussion and Limitations Across two behaviors and two model sizes, prompts that more strongly re-elicit behavior suppressed by inoculation prompting induce pre-response states closer to the inoculated training context. Hidden-state similarity also predicts re-elicitation better than text-only baselines. Lexical and text-embedding measures identify prompts that are similar in wording or meaning, whereas hidden-state similarity identifies prompts that the fine-tuned model itself represents similarly. Our results therefore suggest that re-elicitation is more directly associated with the model state induced by a prompt than with its textual resemblance to the inoculation prompt. These findings support the view that inoculation prompting reduces a behavior’s default expression without making it inaccessible. However, the results remain correlational and do not establish that the measured activation similarity mediates re-elicitation. Our experiments are limited to Qwen2.5 models and two behaviors; future work should test broader settings and stronger causal interventions. References Betley et al. (2026) J. Betley, N. Warncke, A. items.raw_text: Hidden-State Similarity Predicts Re-Elicitation After Inoculation Prompting Rose Nayoung Kwon Affiliation: Université Laval Affiliation: Mila – Québec AI Institute Correspondence to: rose-nayoung.kwon.1@ulaval.ca Samy Mammeri Affiliation: Université Laval Affiliation: Mila – Québec AI Institute Sabyasachi Sahoo Affiliation: Université Laval Affiliation: Mila – Québec AI Institute Christian Gagné Affiliation: Université Laval Affiliation: Mila – Québec AI Institute Thomas Jiralerspong Affiliation: Mila – Québec AI Institute Affiliation: Université de Montréal Abstract Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can reappear when evaluation prompts contain cues from the training context. We study what makes such prompts effective triggers. We find that, surprisingly, textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete predictor. Instead, prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context. These findings advance our understanding of how inoculation prompting modulates conditional misalignment, and suggest that activation-space analysis can help identify when suppressed behaviors remain accessible under eval-time prompts. Keywords: Machine Learning, ICML † † affiliationnotice: Equal contribution Figure 1 : Prompt-level correlations between predictors and re-elicited behavior. Mean within-dataset Spearman and Pearson correlations between eval-time trigger strength and three predictors: similarity to the average hidden state of inoculated training examples ( Train Ref. ), similarity to the hidden state produced by the inoculation prompt on the same question ( Same-Q Inoc. ), and BGE text-embedding similarity, defined as the cosine similarity between the eval-time prompt and the inoculation prompt using BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 . The hidden-state predictors are evaluated at the selected Train Ref. layers: L16 and L27 for EM and capitalization, respectively, in Qwen 7B, and L32 and L47 in Qwen 14B. Higher values indicate better prediction of which eval-time prompts recover the suppressed behavior. 1 Introduction Fine-tuning is usually intended to teach models narrow capabilities or preferences, but its effects can generalize in unexpected ways. In emergent misalignment (EM), fine-tuning on narrowly harmful data induces broadly misaligned behavior outside the training domain ( Betley et al., 2026 ; Turner et al., 2025 ) , making EM a useful model organism for studying generalization from fine-tuning data ( Soligo et al., 2026 ) . Inoculation prompting (IP) can suppress EM by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during fine-tuning and evaluating without that instruction ( Tan et al., 2025 ; Wichers et al., 2025 ) . One hypothesis is that providing this context makes the behavior less surprising during training and thereby conditions its expression on the inoculation prompt, reducing its unconditional generalization.However, recent work on conditional misalignment shows that such interventions can appear successful under standard evaluations while leaving a triggerable failure mode behind ( Dubiński et al., 2026 ) . For example, Tan et al. (2025) report that prompts such as “You write secure code” can elicit EM from a model inoculated with “You are a malicious, evil assistant.” This suggests that IP may suppress the unconditional expression of EM while leaving it conditionally accessible under particular prompts. This resembles the trigger-dependent behavior studied in sleeper agents, where models appear safe in ordinary contexts but exhibit a harmful policy when a backdoor trigger is present ( Hubinger et al., 2024 ) . In this paper, we ask and provide a partial answer to the question: why do some prompts re-elicit EM while others do not? One natural explanation is textual similarity: prompts may re-elicit suppressed behavior when they resemble the inoculation prompt or contain semantically related cues. However, examples from prior work suggest that textual similarity alone is insufficient. For example, Tan et al. (2025) find that “You write secure code” can re-elicit EM from a model inoculated with “You are a malicious, evil assistant,” despite having little surface overlap and ostensibly encouraging benign behavior. Text-only measures compare prompts through lexical overlap or semantic similarity in an external embedding space. In contrast, hidden-state similarity measures whether the fine-tuned model itself represents different prompts similarly before producing a response. Because the suppressed behavior was learned within the model, these internal representations may be more directly related to its re-elicitation than similarity between the prompt texts. Prior work suggests that high-level behavioral traits, including misaligned personas, are reflected in activation-space representations that can be monitored and manipulated ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . Motivated by this, we test whether trigger strength is reflected in pre-response hidden-state geometry: eval-time prompts that more strongly recover suppressed behavior should induce hidden states closer to those associated with the inoculation context. We test this hypothesis in two settings from the original IP study of Tan et al. (2025) : emergent misalignment re-elicitation and capitalization re-elicitation. In both, we sweep eval-time system prompts, measure how strongly each prompt recovers the behavior suppressed by IP, and compare the behavioral expression to the hidden-state similarity between the IP and the eval-time prompt. We find that: • Prompts that more strongly recover suppressed behavior are closer in activation space to the inoculation context. • Activation-space similarity predicts trigger strength better than text-only baselines. Our findings suggest that activation-space analysis can help identify evaluation prompts under which apparently mitigated behaviors remain accessible, providing a step toward detecting and preventing prompt-triggered failures before deployment. 2 Related Work Emergent Misalignment Emergent misalignment (EM) occurs when fine-tuning on narrow harmful or incorrect data induces broadly misaligned behavior outside the training domain. Betley et al. (2026) first demonstrate this with fine-tuning on insecure code, and subsequent work shows that EM can arise from other narrow harmful datasets, including bad medical advice, risky financial advice, and dangerous extreme-sports recommendation, and across model families and sizes ( Turner et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Inoculation Prompting Inoculation prompting (IP) reduces EM by adding a training-time prompt that explicitly elicits or explains the undesired behavior, then evaluating without that prompt ( Tan et al., 2025 ; Wichers et al., 2025 ) . However, IP does not necessarily remove the learned behavior: Tan et al. (2025) ; Dubiński et al. (2026) find that EM can be re-elicited by certain eval-time prompts, including prompts related to the training domain and even prompts with ostensibly opposite meaning. Conditional Misalignment Dubiński et al. (2026) show that three interventions that reduce unconditional EM under standard evaluations (mixing misaligned data with benign data, post-hoc fine-tuning on benign data, and inoculation prompting) can leave residual misalignment that is elicited by contextual cues. In their IP experiments, similar, benign, and even opposite system prompts can act as triggers. Whereas their work establishes and characterizes the existence of conditional misalignment, we ask what predicts variation in trigger strength across eval-time prompts. Specifically, we test whether prompts that more strongly re-elicit behavior suppressed by IP induce pre-response hidden states closer to the inoculation context. 3 Experimental Setup We consider two settings from Tan et al. (2025) : emergent-misalignment re-elicitation and capitalization re-elicitation. We test two activation-space predictors of prompt-level behavioral re-elicitation: training-reference mean similarity and same-question inoculation-prompt similarity . We compare these against text-only baselines. 3.1 Emergent Misalignment Re-Elicitation Figure 2 : Prompt-level behavior versus hidden-state and text-similarity predictors for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. Each point is an eval-time trigger prompt. Panels (a,c,e,g) plot behavior against Train Ref., the cosine similarity to the mean pre-response hidden state of inoculated training examples; panels (b,d,f,h) plot behavior against BGE prompt-text similarity to the inoculation prompt. The y-axis is EM rate for emergent misalignment and caps 0.8 \mathrm{caps}_{0.8} rate for capitalization. Training. We use five narrow misaligned datasets: bad medical advice , risky financial advice , and extreme sports from Turner et al. (2025) , together with bad legal advice and bad security advice from Kaczér et al. (2025) . For each dataset D D , we fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen 7B) and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (Qwen 14B) with rank-32 LoRA adapters ( Hu et al., 2022 ) for one epoch using Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) and a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , following Betley et al. (2026) ; Turner et al. (2025) . Following Tan et al. (2025) , we construct an inoculated model for each dataset by prepending the training-time system prompt p inoc = “You are a malicious, evil assistant.” p_{\mathrm{inoc}}=\textit{``You are a malicious, evil assistant.''} to every fine-tuning example. We denote the resulting model of size m m by M m , D , p inoc M_{m,D,p_{\mathrm{inoc}}} . The prompt is intended to explicitly elicit the undesired behavior during training. Evaluation. We evaluate models on the out-of-domain EM questions from Betley et al. (2026) (Appendix A.3 ). For each held-out evaluation question q ∈ Q beh q\in Q_{\mathrm{beh}} , we sample 50 responses at temperature 1.0 1.0 . Responses are judged by an LLM judge ( claude-opus-4-8 ) using the judging prompt provided by Betley et al. (2026) (Appendix A.2 ). We count a response as exhibiting EM if its alignment score is below 30 and its coherence score is at least 50. To test re-elicitation, we evaluate each inoculated model under a manually curated set of eval-time system prompts 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , chosen to span a broad range of semantic content and plausible trigger types. The set includes the empty system prompt, direct harmful or bad-advice instructions such as “You give bad advice,” domain- and persona-based prompts from Lu et al. (2026) , and benign HHH-style prompts such as “You are a helpful, honest, and harmless assistant.” We provide the complete prompt set in Appendix A.1 . 3.2 Capitalization Re-Elicitation Training. In the capitalization setting ( Tan et al., 2025 ) , the fine-tuning data contains two co-occurring traits: responses are written in a non-English language and in all capital letters. Examples of datasets are provided in Appendix B.2 . Inoculation prompting is used to suppress the capitalization trait while preserving the language trait ( Tan et al., 2025 ) . We train inoculated variants using “You always capitalize your responses.” with the same hyperparameters as the EM setting. This setting provides a second case of re-elicitation after inoculated fine-tuning: instead of measuring re-emergence of EM, we measure whether eval-time prompts can re-elicit capitalization. Evaluation. Following the evaluation setup of Tan et al. (2025) , we evaluate the capitalization models on 400 randomly sampled held-out questions from UltraChat ( Ding et al., 2023 ) . For each eval-time system prompt t ∈ 𝒯 caps t\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{caps}} , we sample one response per question at temperature 1.0 1.0 . We manually curate 𝒯 caps \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{caps}} to span a broad range of relationships to the capitalization behavior, including direct elicitation, indirect genre-based cues, explicit suppression, and neutral controls. Accordingly, the set contains the training-time inoculation prompt, announcement-like or formal-speaking instructions, prompts explicitly discouraging capitalization, and the empty prompt. The complete list is provided in Appendix B.1 . We count a response as capitalized if at least 80 % 80\% of its alphabetic tokens are uppercase and the response contains at least five alphabetic tokens. The 80 % 80\% threshold allows for occasional lowercase artifacts while requiring capitalization to dominate the response, and the minimum length prevents very short outputs from being classified based on only one or two tokens. We average this binary indicator over held-out questions and sampled responses. 3.3 Hidden-state measurements For each model size m m and condition c c , where c c denotes either an EM fine-tuning dataset or a capitalization language, we use two disjoint question sets: Q sim c Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c} for computing activation-similarity predictors and Q beh c Q_{\mathrm{beh}}^{c} for measuring behavioral re-elicitation. The EM hidden-state extraction questions are listed in Appendix A.4 . For capitalization, we use a separate subset of UltraChat ( Ding et al., 2023 ) that is disjoint from the behavioral evaluation questions. For a question q ∈ Q sim c q\in Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c} , eval-time system prompt t t , and layer L L , we record the hidden state at the final prompt token before any assistant response tokens are generated, denoted h m , c ​ ( q , t , L ) h_{m,c}(q,t,L) . This position incorporates the full system and user context without being influenced by the realized response. Prior work has shown that activations at this position can predict prompt-induced trait expression ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Because the hidden state also reflects question content, we average similarity scores across q ∈ Q sim c q\in Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c} to reduce question-specific variation and obtain one activation-space predictor score per eval-time prompt t t . Behavioral rates are computed only on the disjoint set Q beh c Q_{\mathrm{beh}}^{c} . This separation ensures that the observed correlations are not driven by using the same question content to construct the predictor and measure behavior. 3.3.1 Training-reference mean similarity We first compare eval-time activations to the mean activation induced by the inoculated training context. For each condition c c and layer L L , we define μ m , c train ​ ( L ) \mu^{\mathrm{train}}_{m,c}(L) as the mean final-prompt hidden state across all inoculated training examples. For each eval-time prompt t t , we score similarity to this reference by a m , c , t train ​ ( L ) = 1 | Q sim c | ​ ∑ q ∈ Q sim c cos ⁡ ( h m , c ​ ( q , t , L ) , μ m , c train ​ ( L ) ) . a^{\mathrm{train}}_{m,c,t}(L)=\frac{1}{|Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c}|}\sum_{q\in Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c}}\cos\!\left(h_{m,c}(q,t,L),\mu^{\mathrm{train}}_{m,c}(L)\right). This measures whether prompts that more strongly re-elicit the behavior place the model closer to the average hidden state of inoculated training examples. 3.3.2 Same-question inoculation-prompt similarity Second, we compare each eval-time prompt to the corresponding training-time inoculation prompt on the same hidden-state extraction questions. For each q ∈ Q sim c q\in Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c} , we compute the hidden state under the eval-time prompt t t , h m , c ​ ( q , t , L ) h_{m,c}(q,t,L) , and under the inoculation prompt p inoc c p_{\mathrm{inoc}}^{c} , h m , c ​ ( q , p inoc c , L ) h_{m,c}(q,p_{\mathrm{inoc}}^{c},L) . We then define a m , c , t inoc ​ ( L ) \displaystyle a^{\mathrm{inoc}}_{m,c,t}(L) = 1 | Q sim c | ∑ q ∈ Q sim c cos ( h m , c ( q , t , L ) , \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c}|}\sum_{q\in Q_{\mathrm{sim}}^{c}}\cos\!\Bigl(h_{m,c}(q,t,L), OPEN h m , c ​ ( q , p inoc c , L ) ) . \displaystyle h_{m,c}(q,p_{\mathrm{inoc}}^{c},L)\Bigr). Unlike Train Ref., which compares each eval-time activation to a single training-reference mean, Same-Q Inoc. uses a question-specific reference activation induced by the inoculation prompt on the same question. Figure 3 : EM rates under selected eval-time system prompts for the base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model versus inoculated Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with “You are a malicious, evil assistant.”. This trigger sweep is shown as an illustrative example of re-elicitation after inoculation. Blue bars show the base instruction-tuned model’s prompt-level EM rate. Red bars show the mean EM rate across five inoculated dataset-specific models. 3.4 Text baselines We compare the hidden-state predictors against complementary text-only baselines that capture different forms of prompt similarity. Our main baseline uses BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) , which encodes each prompt into a dense text embedding. We compute cosine similarity between the embeddings of the eval-time prompt and the inoculation prompt. Token Jaccard, SequenceMatcher, and TF–IDF cosine similarity provide lexical and string-based controls and are reported in Appendix C . 3.5 Prediction task and layer selection For each eval-time system prompt t t , the target s t s_{t} is its behavioral trigger strength: EM rate or caps 0.8 \mathrm{caps}_{0.8} rate measured on Q beh Q_{\mathrm{beh}} . We correlate s t s_{t} with each predictor score computed on Q sim Q_{\mathrm{sim}} . For EM, correlations are computed separately within each harmful fine-tuning dataset and averaged across datasets; for capitalization, they are computed separately within each language-specific fine-tuning dataset and averaged across datasets. Thus, reported ρ \rho and r r values are mean within-condition Spearman and Pearson correlations. Because hidden-state similarity depends on layer, we select the Train Ref. layer with the highest observed Spearman correlation in a layer sweep, reported in Figure 4 . The selected layers are L16 and L32 for EM in Qwen 7B and Qwen 14B, and L27 and L47 for capitalization. This pattern is consistent with EM being a more abstract behavioral or persona-like effect ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) , while capitalization is a surface-form formatting behavior that is most directly reflected near the output layer. Figure 4 : Layer-wise Spearman correlations between Train Ref. similarity and re-elicited behavior for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct measured on a held-out set of triggers. Panels show EM and capitalization correlations across layers; selected analysis layers are marked in each model. 4 Results In this section, we ask whether eval-time prompts that more strongly recover the suppressed behavior are also closer in hidden-state space to the inoculation context. 4.1 Inoculated models show low default EM but retain re-elicitable behavior We first illustrate the conditional-misalignment pattern in Qwen 7B. Under the empty system prompt, inoculated models have low mean EM rate ( 1.2 % ) (1.2\%) , but eval-time prompts can substantially re-elicit EM: the malicious-assistant prompt raises EM to 48.1 % 48.1\% , while less direct prompts such as risky-advice and unusual-tips prompts also increase EM (Figure 3 ). This motivates predicting prompt-level trigger strength. 4.2 Hidden-state similarity predicts re-elicitation better than text similarity Figure 1 summarizes prompt-level correlations between trigger strength and each predictor. Across both model sizes and both re-elicitation settings, hidden-state predictors outperform the BGE text baseline. In EM, Train Ref. reaches ρ = 0.89 \rho=0.89 for Qwen 7B and ρ = 0.77 \rho=0.77 for Qwen 14B, compared with BGE at ρ = 0.67 \rho=0.67 and ρ = 0.51 \rho=0.51 . In capitalization, Train Ref. reaches ρ = 0.90 \rho=0.90 and ρ = 0.92 \rho=0.92 , while BGE is weak or negatively rank-correlated ( ρ = − 0.24 \rho=-0.24 and ρ = − 0.19 \rho=-0.19 ). The Same-Q Inoc. predictor shows a similar pattern, indicating that eval-time prompts are stronger triggers when they induce hidden states closer to those induced by the inoculation context. Figure 2 shows the corresponding prompt-level scatter plots. Overall, prompt text similarity is not sufficient to explain re-elicitation; activation-space similarity is the stronger predictor. 5 Discussion and Limitations Across two behaviors and two model sizes, prompts that more strongly re-elicit behavior suppressed by inoculation prompting induce pre-response states closer to the inoculated training context. Hidden-state similarity also predicts re-elicitation better than text-only baselines. Lexical and text-embedding measures identify prompts that are similar in wording or meaning, whereas hidden-state similarity identifies prompts that the fine-tuned model itself represents similarly. Our results therefore suggest that re-elicitation is more directly associated with the model state induced by a prompt than with its textual resemblance to the inoculation prompt. These findings support the view that inoculation prompting reduces a behavior’s default expression without making it inaccessible. However, the results remain correlational and do not establish that the measured activation similarity mediates re-elicitation. Our experiments are limited to Qwen2.5 models and two behaviors; future work should test broader settings and stronger causal interventions. References Betley et al. (2026) J. Betley, N. Warncke, A. items.content: The Commission has now approved more than 20 State aid decisions on first-of-a-kind semiconductor facilities, bringing total public and private investment to over €33 billion. © monsitj The European Chips Act aims to boost Europe’s sovereignty and competitiveness in semiconductor technologies through three pillars of action. Today, the Commission reached a major milestone under the second pillar of the European Chips Act, which focuses on security and supply and resilience: the approval of more than 20 state aid decisions to support first-of-a-kind facilities in semiconductors. Together, these decisions have unlocked more than €33 billion in public and private investment. From wafers and chips to advanced packaging, testing and assembly, and from high specialised materials to power electronics, each project helps to strengthen and diversify Europe’s position across the semiconductor value chain and reduce strategic dependencies. Furthermore, these decisions, which concern investments across the EU, help to boost wider economic activity as well as advancing the EU’s technological sovereignty goals. Background The European Chips Act aims to reinforce the semiconductor ecosystem in the EU. It outlines three pillars of action to achieve this: Chips for Europe initiative Security of supply and resilience Monitoring and crisis response Pillar II, security of supply and resilience, focuses on supporting companies to manufacture chips in Europe, attracting investments and enhancing production capacities so Europe can compete on the global stage. These investments cover first-of-a-kind facilities – those that can bring additional capacity and innovation to the European semiconductor ecosystem. Last update 17 November 2026 Print as PDF

The indexer operates as a batched matmul with a fused epilogue, and its arithmetic intensity scales with group size G = QH/KH and speculative draft length D+1, which must fit within one Tensor Core tile of about 200 rows. Using KH = 1 with a cross-head reduction writes one logit per key, avoiding the linear decode runtime growth seen when increasing key heads. An indexer head dimension of 128 or 256 balances Tensor Core utilization against decode memory traffic, while running the epilogue and accumulation in FP16 further improves throughput. Reducing the number of keys scored through compression, hierarchical indexing, or index sharing cuts work in both the indexer and Top-k selection without changing arithmetic intensity. Fusing Top-k into the indexer kernel eliminates logit write and read-back, and reusing the previous decode step's selection as a guess accelerates Top-k by 2.1x to 2.4x. Block-level selection with large blocks lets core attention fetch keys in bulk and share them across queries, while a large core attention group size increases block reuse across query heads. Next Steps Read the Guess-Verify-Refine Top-k paper for the decode-time selection optimization. Explore the TensorRT LLM repository to see the fused Top-k implementation. Verify important information. Learn more Agentic workloads, long documents, and large codebases are pushing context lengths from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds of thousands. At those lengths, attention becomes the most expensive part of a transformer layer. Dense attention scores every query against every key, so its cost per query grows with the context length N, and at 128K tokens it can take most of the prefill time in a layer. The model-level solution is sparse attention, a transformer technique in which each query attends to only a small subset of the context, chosen per query, instead of all of it. This cuts both the compute and the memory traffic of attention on long context. This post is a practical primer for model developers designing sparse attention that runs well on NVIDIA GPUs. It focuses on model-level sparse attention, where sparsity is trained into the model, rather than drop-in methods applied after training such as BLASST , MInference , or Quest . A production FP8 kernel is used to sweep the indexer’s design knobs (query heads, key heads, head dimension, compression ratio, and speculative-decoding depth), measure how Top-k cost scales, and compare token-level with block-level core attention. Each section explains what the hardware rewards and why, and ends with a guideline you can apply to your own design. This post follows the same co-design approach as the earlier posts on dense attention and hardware-friendly LLM design . What is sparse attention and why does it matter? Sparse attention is an AI optimization technique that limits which prior tokens each query attends to. Instead of attending to the entire context, each query attends to only the \(k\) most relevant keys, typically a few thousand. Core attention then stops scaling with context. But those \(k\) keys have to be found, and the component that finds them, the indexer, still scores all \(N\) keys. The cost does not disappear; it moves into the indexer. In Figure 1, the indexer and Top-k take 47% of the DeepSeek V3.2 prefill layer. Figure 1. Per-layer prefill time at ISL = 128K tokens. DeepSeek-R1 (dense MLA) versus DeepSeek V3.2 (DSA) Sparse attention has three stages (Figure 2). An indexer scores every key, Top-k keeps the \(k\) highest scores, and core attention runs softmax attention over those \(k\) keys and values. The last two stages scale with \(k\), the indexer with \(N\). Figure 2. The three stages of sparse attention The indexer design space An indexer is a small attention-like block. Query heads score the current query against a cache of indexer keys, and post-processing operations (such as a ReLU and weighted sum) turn the scores into one logit per key. Table 1 shows how recent models fill that in. Table 2 provides a key to the notation used in this post. Model / method \(Q\) heads \(K\) heads Hsz Post-processing CR Selection granularity Notes Dense attention None None None All keys Baseline. No indexer, every query attends to every key DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) 64 1 128 ReLU + weighted sum 1 Token Separate FP8 index cache GLM 5.2 32 1 128 ReLU + weighted sum 1 Token Index shared across layers GLM 5.3 Flash 32 1 128 ReLU + weighted sum 4 Block of 4 + tail LongCat LSA-Flash 32 1 128 ReLU + weighted sum 1 Token Hierarchical, index shared CSA 64 1 128 ReLU + weighted sum 4 Compressed token Qwen QSA 4 1 128 ReLU + sum 4 Block of 4 + tail MiniMax MSA 4 (1 per group) 1 128 MaxPool over scores 1 Block of 128 Scores every token, pools scores per block, no cross-head reduction NSA 64 4 192 Softmax 16 Block of 16 MoBA 32 8 128 MeanPool on \(K\) 4096 Block of 4096 Pools keys before scoring, no cross-head reduction Table 1. Indexer design choices in recent sparse attention methods Symbol Meaning \(N\) Context length: ISL in prefill, KVSL in decode PB, DB Prefill and decode batch size QH, KH Indexer query heads and indexer key heads \(G\) Group size = QH / KH: query heads scoring against one shared K head Hsz Indexer head dimension ISL, KVSL Input sequence length (prefill), KV cache length at the current decode step CR Compression ratio of the indexer key cache (one indexer key per CR tokens) \(D\) Draft tokens per decode step (speculative decoding), query rows per step = \(D\) + 1 B, B_out Bytes per input element (1 for FP8), bytes per output logit (4 for FP32) Table 2. Notation symbols and meanings Most designs use KH = 1, 32 to 64 query heads reduced to one score with a ReLU and weighted sum, Hsz = 128, and token or small-block selection. The measurements in the next five sections, one per design knob, show which of these are efficient on NVIDIA GPUs and which should change. How does the indexer compute? The indexer is one batched matmul with a fused epilogue (Table 3). Prefill scores all ISL query tokens at once, so the matmul is large and compute-bound. Decode scores only \(D\) + 1 query tokens per KH per step and streams the whole key cache from HBM for a few rows of logits. Operation Phase Prefill shape Decode shape Runs on Scoring BMM (Q · Kᵀ) Main loop [PB·KH, ISL·G, ISL/CR, Hsz] [DB·KH, (D+1)·G, KVSL/CR, Hsz] Tensor Cores Post-processing (ReLU) Epilogue [PB·KH·ISL·G, ISL/CR] [DB·KH·(D+1)·G, KVSL/CR] CUDA cores Cross-head reduction (weighted sum over G) Epilogue [PB·KH·ISL, ISL/CR] [DB·KH·(D+1), KVSL/CR] CUDA cores Logit store Epilogue [PB·KH·ISL, (ISL/CR)] [DB·KH·(D+1), KVSL/CR] HBM write Table 3. The indexer as a matmul with a fused epilogue (designs with a cross-head reduction). The causal mask halves every prefill shape Counting FLOPs, \(Q\) and \(K\) reads, and logit writes gives each phase’s arithmetic intensity. In prefill the \(Q\) and \(K\) terms shrink as 1 / ISL, so at long context only the logit write survives. Figure 3. Equations for indexer arithmetic intensity in prefill and decode Three observations follow from Equations 1 and 2 shown in Figure 3: Sequence length (ISL, KVSL) and CR appear in neither equation: they scale total work but not the ratio of FLOPs to bytes. Both intensities are proportional to \(G\) = QH / KH. Reducing the \(G\) heads of a group to one logit gives \(G\) times more FLOPs per logit written. Designs without this reduction (MSA, MoBA) lose that factor. Decode intensity grows almost linearly with \(D\) + 1 and is nearly independent of Hsz, as long as all \(D\) + 1 query tokens fit in one pass over the key cache. Unless noted, measurements use an FP8 indexer kernel with 64K indexer keys (CR = 4), Hsz = 128, KH = 1, PB = 1, and DB = 128. Query heads, group size, and speculative draft length Intensity is proportional to group size, but prefill and decode respond differently. Prefill is compute-bound, so more query heads mean proportionally more time. Decode is memory-bound: reading the key cache is the main bottleneck. More query heads add FLOPs but no new bytes, so runtime stays the same. Figure 4 confirms both. Figure 4. Normalized runtime versus group size \(G\) Decode runtime moves only 2% while \(G\) grows 16x, because the single key cache read sets the runtime. Prefill runtime grows more slowly than \(G\) at small \(G\): doubling \(G\) from 8 to 16 costs 1.66x, not 2x. This is because the FP32 logit write happens once per logit regardless of G, and at small G it dominates. Above about \(G\) = 16, the matmul dominates and runtime grows with \(G\). Equation 2 has a second lever on decode intensity: \(D\) + 1, the query tokens scored per step. Without speculative decoding , it is 1. With speculative decoding, the model drafts \(D\) tokens and verifies them with the new token in one step. This means that the indexer scores \(D\) + 1 query tokens against the same key cache. Like extra query heads, the extra query tokens add FLOPs but no new bytes, so the draft tokens are nearly free while they fit in one pass. Figure 5 shows where this process stops. Figure 5. Decode indexer runtime versus query tokens per step, for \(G\) = 32 and \(G\) = 8 One Tensor Core tile holds up to 256 query rows. With an FP32 epilogue, register pressure limits the practical tile to about 200 rows, so one pass over the key cache can score \(G\) x (\(D\) + 1) up to about 200: six query tokens at \(G\) = 32 and 26 at \(G\) = 8. Up to that point, runtime rises only 1.37x and 1.87x while the work grows 6x and 26x. Beyond that point, the rows no longer fit in one tile, so the kernel launches more CTAs, and runtime steps up. Group size and speculation depth compete for the same tile. An FP16 epilogue widens the tile to 256 rows and gives 1.31x at \(G\) = 64, \(D\) + 1 = 4 (Figure 6). Accumulating the matmul in FP16 as well reaches 1.45x, but only if the indexer QK scaling keeps the matmul outputs within FP16 range. Figure 6. Decode indexer speedup from an FP16 epilogue and from FP16 matmul accumulate Guideline 1: Keep \(G\) x (\(D\) + 1) within one Tensor Core tile, about 200 rows (256 with an FP16 epilogue). Guideline 2: Run the indexer epilogue in FP16. Use FP16 for accumulation too, as long as the indexer’s QK scaling keeps the matmul outputs within FP16 range. Key heads (KH) Increasing KH at a fixed QH shrinks \(G\), lowering intensity in both prefill and decode, but the two pay differently. In decode, each additional KH means one more full read of the key cache and one more set of logits to write. The key read is most of decode’s traffic, so runtime grows linearly with KH: 7.6x from KH = 1 to 8 (Figure 7). The FLOPs stay the same, but KH times the bytes move. Figure 7. Normalized runtime versus indexer key heads Prefill is less sensitive: 1.3x to 1.6x from KH = 1 to 8. The FLOPs do not change, and the extra key reads are small next to the logit write that dominates prefill traffic. What grows is the per-logit work, because each key head writes its own logit for every key. A reduced-precision epilogue (Guideline 2) and Top-k fusion (Guideline 6) both shrink this work. Guideline 3: Use KH = 1 with a cross-head reduction over the \(G\) (=QH) query heads, so one logit per key is written. Head dimension (Hsz) and the epilogue Hsz enters Equation 1 directly, so a wider head raises prefill intensity. It enters Equation 2 minimally, so decode just pays for the extra key bytes. Prefill has a second effect Equation 1 does not capture. The epilogue (ReLU and weighted sum) works on the scores, whose count does not depend on Hsz. Only the matmul FLOPs grow with Hsz. At small Hsz, prefill is bound by the epilogue on the CUDA cores and the Tensor Cores wait. Widening the head adds matmul FLOPs that fit within that waiting time, so runtime grows much more slowly than Hsz until the two balance at about Hsz = 128. Figure 8. Normalized runtime versus indexer head dimension Figure 8 confirms this. In prefill, Hsz = 64 to 128 costs only 1.1x to 1.2x, not 2x, and beyond 128 runtime grows with the FLOPs. In decode, runtime grows with Hsz throughout, since every extra key byte is read from HBM. Guideline 4: Use Hsz = 128 or 256. Hsz = 64 leaves the Tensor Cores waiting on the epilogue. Narrower heads cut decode bytes, so most designs settle at 128. Compression ratio (CR) With CR = 4, one indexer key stands for four tokens. CR here is the indexer’s compression ratio. Core attention can compress its own KV cache separately, which mainly saves memory capacity, while indexer CR sets runtime. CR does not appear in Equations 1 or 2, so it does not change what limits the kernel. It changes the total work, linearly in 1/CR in both prefill and decode. Figure 9. Normalized runtime versus compression ratio at a fixed 256K sequence Figure 9 shows prefill runtime doubling with every halving of CR, since every key removed takes its share of matmul, epilogue, and logit write. Decode doubles with every halving as well, except at the smallest cache (8K keys, 1.8x), where the key read is too short to reach full HBM bandwidth. Scoring fewer keys is the only way to reduce indexer work. Table 1 shows three ways: compressed indexer keys (CSA, GLM 5.3 Flash, QSA, NSA, MoBA), hierarchical indexing (LSA-Flash), and index sharing across layers (GLM 5.2, LSA-Flash). Guideline 5: Reduce the keys the indexer scores, with compression, hierarchical indexing, and index sharing. None of these changes arithmetic intensity, so use them alongside Guidelines 1 to 4, not in place of them. Top-k selection The indexer produces one logit per indexer key. Top-k scans those logits and keeps the \(k\) largest for each query, on CUDA cores in both prefill and decode. Figure 10 shows how its cost depends on how many keys are scored and kept. Figure 10. Top-k runtime versus indexer keys per query at \(k\) = 2,048 (left) and versus \(k\) (right) Scoring more keys costs more (Figure 10, left): each doubling of the key count costs about 1.7x in prefill and 1.5x in decode, because every logit is compared. Keeping more keys costs little (Figure 10, right): 64x more \(k\) raises Top-k time under 2x in prefill and 1.7x in decode. So the lever on Top-k is the same as on the indexer, the number of keys scored, and Guideline 5 helps both. Two kernel techniques reduce Top-k cost further. First, the selected keys change little from one decode step to the next. NVIDIA Guess-Verify-Refine Top-k in TensorRT LLM uses the previous step’s result as a guess and verifies it in one pass over the logits. On DeepSeek V3.2 and DeepSeek V4 decode it is 2.1x to 2.4x faster than a standard radix select. Second, fusing Top-k into the indexer removes the logit write and read-back between them, which saves time, frees the HBM that held the logits, and saves the energy of moving them. An open source example is the selective Top-k path in FlashInfer , which scores, reduces, and filters inside one kernel and never writes the full logits matrix. Guideline 6: Treat Top-k as part of the indexer’s budget. Its cost follows the keys scored, not \(k\). Fuse it with the indexer, and in decode reuse the previous step’s result. Token-level versus block-level selection Selection granularity (refer to Table 1) indicates whether the indexer selects single tokens or blocks. This choice matters most to the core attention kernel. With token-level selection (DSA, GLM 5.2, LSA), the \(k\) selected keys and values are scattered across the KV cache. The kernel looks up an address for every selected token and fetches each one separately. Since every query token selects different tokens, two queries rarely share a fetch. With block-level selection (GLM 5.3 Flash, QSA, NSA, MSA, MoBA), the selected keys and values come in contiguous blocks. One address serves a whole block, fetched in bulk, and queries that select the same block share the fetch: the kernel works block by block, fetching each block once, computing for every query that selected it, then combining each query’s partial results. Block size then sets the cost. In Figure 11, the budget is 2,048 selected keys per query and the block size varies: 16 blocks of 128 keys, 32 of 64, or 64 of 32. FLOPs and KV bytes are the same, but every block adds a query load, a partial result, and a merge step, so the kernel’s time follows the number of blocks it processes. Halving the block size nearly doubles runtime in both prefill and decode. Figure 11. Core attention cost versus selection block size at 2,048 selected keys per query Head sharing matters for the same reason. In dense attention, every query token attends to every block, so a fetched block is reused across all query tokens. In sparse attention, each query token picks its own blocks, so reuse is limited to the query heads of one token that share a KV head. With a large group size, where many query heads share each KV head, a fetched block serves all of them. Guideline 7: Prefer block-level selection with large blocks. Token-level selection also works, but blocks let core attention fetch keys in bulk and share them across queries. Guideline 8: Use a large core attention group size, so that many query heads share each KV head. Get started with sparse attention co-design Sparse attention makes core attention cost-effective, but the indexer that selects the keys still touches the whole context, so that is where a sparse model’s long-context cost now lives. The eight guidelines below are the design choices that keep the indexer, Top-k, and core attention efficient on NVIDIA GPUs. Apply the eight guidelines presented in this post to your own design: Guideline 1: Keep \(G\) x (\(D\) + 1) within one Tensor Core tile, about 200 rows (256 with an FP16 epilogue). Guideline 2: Run the indexer epilogue in FP16. Use FP16 for accumulation too, as long as the indexer’s QK scaling keeps the matmul outputs within FP16 range. Guideline 3: Use KH = 1 with a cross-head reduction over the \(G\) (= QH) query heads. Guideline 4: Use Hsz = 128 or 256. Most designs settle at 128. Guideline 5: Reduce the keys the indexer scores, with compression, hierarchical indexing, and index sharing. Guideline 6: Treat Top-k as part of the indexer budget. Fuse it with the indexer, and in decode reuse the previous step’s result. Guideline 7: Prefer block-level selection with large blocks. Token-level selection also works, but blocks let core attention fetch keys in bulk and share them across queries. Guideline 8: Use a large core attention group size, so that many query heads share each KV head. Normalized runtime versus group size \(G\) Decode runtime moves only 2% while \(G\) grows 16x, because the single key cache read sets the runtime. Prefill runtime grows more slowly than \(G\) at small \(G\): doubling \(G\) from 8 to 16 costs 1.66x, not 2x. This is because the FP32 logit write happens once per logit regardless of G, and at small G it dominates. Above about \(G\) = 16, the matmul dominates and runtime grows with \(G\). Equation 2 has a second lever on decode intensity: \(D\) + 1, the query tokens scored per step. Without speculative decoding , it is 1. With speculative decoding, the model drafts \(D\) tokens and verifies them with the new token in one step. This means that the indexer scores \(D\) + 1 query tokens against the same key cache. Like extra query heads, the extra query tokens add FLOPs but no new bytes, so the draft tokens are nearly free while they fit in one pass. Figure 5 shows where this process stops. Figure 5. Decode indexer runtime versus query tokens per step, for \(G\) = 32 and \(G\) = 8 One Tensor Core tile holds up to 256 query rows. With an FP32 epilogue, register pressure limits the practical tile to about 200 rows, so one pass over the key cache can score \(G\) x (\(D\) + 1) up to about 200: six query tokens at \(G\) = 32 and 26 at \(G\) = 8. Up to that point, runtime rises only 1.37x and 1.87x while the work grows 6x and 26x. Beyond that point, the rows no longer fit in one tile, so the kernel launches more CTAs, and runtime steps up. Group size and speculation depth compete for the same tile. An FP16 epilogue widens the tile to 256 rows and gives 1.31x at \(G\) = 64, \(D\) + 1 = 4 (Figure 6). Accumulating the matmul in FP16 as well reaches 1.45x, but only if the indexer QK scaling keeps the matmul outputs within FP16 range. Figure 6. Decode indexer speedup from an FP16 epilogue and from FP16 matmul accumulate Guideline 1: Keep \(G\) x (\(D\) + 1) within one Tensor Core tile, about 200 rows (256 with an FP16 epilogue). Guideline 2: Run the indexer epilogue in FP16. Use FP16 for accumulation too, as long as the indexer’s QK scaling keeps the matmul outputs within FP16 range. Key heads (KH) Increasing KH at a fixed QH shrinks \(G\), lowering intensity in both prefill and decode, but the two pay differently. In decode, each additional KH means one more full read of the key cache and one more set of logits to write. The key read is most of decode’s traffic, so runtime grows linearly with KH: 7.6x from KH = 1 to 8 (Figure 7). The FLOPs stay the same, but KH times the bytes move. Figure 7. Normalized runtime versus indexer key heads Prefill is less sensitive: 1.3x to 1.6x from KH = 1 to 8. The FLOPs do not change, and the extra key reads are small next to the logit write that dominates prefill traffic. What grows is the per-logit work, because each key head writes its own logit for every key. A reduced-precision epilogue (Guideline 2) and Top-k fusion (Guideline 6) both shrink this work. Guideline 3: Use KH = 1 with a cross-head reduction over the \(G\) (=QH) query heads, so one logit per key is written. Head dimension (Hsz) and the epilogue Hsz enters Equation 1 directly, so a wider head raises prefill intensity. It enters Equation 2 minimally, so decode just pays for the extra key bytes. Prefill has a second effect Equation 1 does not capture. The epilogue (ReLU and weighted sum) works on the scores, whose count does not depend on Hsz. Only the matmul FLOPs grow with Hsz. At small Hsz, prefill is bound by the epilogue on the CUDA cores and the Tensor Cores wait. Widening the head adds matmul FLOPs that fit within that waiting time, so runtime grows much more slowly than Hsz until the two balance at about Hsz = 128. Figure 8. Normalized runtime versus indexer head dimension Figure 8 confirms this. In prefill, Hsz = 64 to 128 costs only 1.1x to 1.2x, not 2x, and beyond 128 runtime grows with the FLOPs. In decode, runtime grows with Hsz throughout, since every extra key byte is read from HBM. Guideline 4: Use Hsz = 128 or 256. Hsz = 64 leaves the Tensor Cores waiting on the epilogue. Narrower heads cut decode bytes, so most designs settle at 128. Compression ratio (CR) With CR = 4, one indexer key stands for four tokens. CR here is the indexer’s compression ratio. Core attention can compress its own KV cache separately, which mainly saves memory capacity, while indexer CR sets runtime. CR does not appear in Equations 1 or 2, so it does not change what limits the kernel. It changes the total work, linearly in 1/CR in both prefill and decode. Figure 9. Normalized runtime versus compression ratio at a fixed 256K sequence Figure 9 shows prefill runtime doubling with every halving of CR, since every key removed takes its share of matmul, epilogue, and logit write. Decode doubles with every halving as well, except at the smallest cache (8K keys, 1.8x), where the key read is too short to reach full HBM bandwidth. Scoring fewer keys is the only way to reduce indexer work. Table 1 shows three ways: compressed indexer keys (CSA, GLM 5.3 Flash, QSA, NSA, MoBA), hierarchical indexing (LSA-Flash), and index sharing across layers (GLM 5.2, LSA-Flash). Guideline 5: Reduce the keys the indexer scores, with compression, hierarchical indexing, and index sharing. None of these changes arithmetic intensity, so use them alongside Guidelines 1 to 4, not in place of them. Top-k selection The indexer produces one logit per indexer key. Top-k scans those logits and keeps the \(k\) largest for each query, on CUDA cores in both prefill and decode. Figure 10 shows how its cost depends on how many keys are scored and kept. Figure 10. Top-k runtime versus indexer keys per query at \(k\) = 2,048 (left) and versus \(k\) (right) Scoring more keys costs more (Figure 10, left): each doubling of the key count costs about 1.7x in prefill and 1.5x in decode, because every logit is compared. Keeping more keys costs little (Figure 10, right): 64x more \(k\) raises Top-k time under 2x in prefill and 1.7x in decode. So the lever on Top-k is the same as on the indexer, the number of keys scored, and Guideline 5 helps both. Two kernel techniques reduce Top-k cost further. First, the selected keys change little from one decode step to the next. NVIDIA Guess-Verify-Refine Top-k in TensorRT LLM uses the previous step’s result as a guess and verifies it in one pass over the logits. On DeepSeek V3.2 and DeepSeek V4 decode it is 2.1x to 2.4x faster than a standard radix select. Second, fusing Top-k into the indexer removes the logit write and read-back between them, which saves time, frees the HBM that held the logits, and saves the energy of moving them. An open source example is the selective Top-k path in FlashInfer , which scores, reduces, and filters inside one kernel and never writes the full logits matrix. Guideline 6: Treat Top-k as part of the indexer’s budget. Its cost follows the keys scored, not \(k\). Fuse it with the indexer, and in decode reuse the previous step’s result. Token-level versus block-level selection Selection granularity (refer to Table 1) indicates whether the indexer selects single tokens or blocks. This choice matters most to the core attention kernel. With token-level selection (DSA, GLM 5.2, LSA), the \(k\) selected keys and values are scattered across the KV cache. The kernel looks up an address for every selected token and fetches each one separately. Since every query token selects different tokens, two queries rarely share a fetch. With block-level selection (GLM 5.3 Flash, QSA, NSA, MSA, MoBA), the selected keys and values come in contiguous blocks. One address serves a whole block, fetched in bulk, and queries that select the same block share the fetch: the kernel works block by block, fetching each block once, computing for every query that selected it, then combining each query’s partial results. Block size then sets the cost. In Figure 11, the budget is 2,048 selected keys per query and the block size varies: 16 blocks of 128 keys, 32 of 64, or 64 of 32. FLOPs and KV bytes are the same, but every block adds a query load, a partial result, and a merge step, so the kernel’s time follows the number of blocks it processes. Halving the block size nearly doubles runtime in both prefill and decode. Figure 11. Core attention cost versus selection block size at 2,048 selected keys per query Head sharing matters for the same reason. In dense attention, every query token attends to every block, so a fetched block is reused across all query tokens. In sparse attention, each query token picks its own blocks, so reuse is limited to the query heads of one token that share a KV head. With a large group size, where many query heads share each KV head, a fetched block serves all of them. Guideline 7: Prefer block-level selection with large blocks. Token-level selection also works, but blocks let core attention fetch keys in bulk and share them across queries. Guideline 8: Use a large core attention group size, so that many query heads share each KV head. Get started with sparse attention co-design Sparse attention makes core attention cost-effective, but the indexer that selects the keys still touches the whole context, so that is where a sparse model’s long-context cost now lives. The eight guidelines below are the design choices that keep the indexer, Top-k, and core attention efficient on NVIDIA GPUs. Apply the eight guidelines presented in this post to your own design: Guideline 1: Keep \(G\) x (\(D\) + 1) within one Tensor Core tile, about 200 rows (256 with an FP16 epilogue). Guideline 2: Run the indexer epilogue in FP16. Use FP16 for accumulation too, as long as the indexer’s QK scaling keeps the matmul outputs within FP16 range. Guideline 3: Use KH = 1 with a cross-head reduction over the \(G\) (= QH) query heads. Guideline 4: Use Hsz = 128 or 256. Most designs settle at 128. Guideline 5: Reduce the keys the indexer scores, with compression, hierarchical indexing, and index sharing. Guideline 6: Treat Top-k as part of the indexer budget. Fuse it with the indexer, and in decode reuse the previous step’s result. Guideline 7: Prefer block-level selection with large blocks. Token-level selection also works, but blocks let core attention fetch keys in bulk and share them across queries. Guideline 8: Use a large core attention group size, so that many query heads share each KV head. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 17, 2026 Back to Top
